q1-01.stem: A clinician slides the probe in and reads 5 mm, counting from the edge of the gum down to the bottom of the pocket. Which value has just been recorded?
choices: The probing depth
The clinical attachment level
The gingival recession
Radiographic bone loss
why: The edge of the gum to the base of the pocket is exactly how probing depth is measured.
Attachment level is counted from the CEJ, not the gum edge; it is the probing depth plus the recession.
Recession is the distance from the CEJ to the gum edge, and it says nothing about how deep the pocket goes.
Bone loss on a radiograph is read from a film, not taken with a probe in the pocket.

q1-02.stem: There is no visible recession: the CEJ is felt 4 mm below the gingival margin, and the probe sinks 7 mm. How much attachment has this site lost?
choices: 3 mm
7 mm
11 mm
4 mm
why: The covered CEJ makes recession -4, so the attachment level is 7 + (-4) = 3 mm.
That is just the pocket depth; it counts the 4 mm of pocket lying above the CEJ on enamel.
This adds the 4 mm rather than subtracting it; when the CEJ is under the gum, recession is negative.
That is only the gap from the CEJ to the margin (the negative recession), not the attachment lost.

q1-03.stem: Tooth X has 4 mm of root showing and a 2 mm pocket, for 6 mm of CAL. Tooth Y has no root showing, the CEJ 4 mm under the gum and a 7 mm pocket, for 3 mm of CAL. Which tooth will the patient find easier to keep clean and stable?
choices: Tooth X, the one with 6 mm of CAL
Tooth Y, the one with 3 mm of CAL
Neither; they are equally easy to keep
Neither; both are beyond maintenance
why: Its 2 mm pocket is within reach of a brush and floss, so it is the easier tooth to keep despite the larger CAL on paper.
A 7 mm pocket is deeper than home care reaches, so this tooth is the harder one to keep even with less CAL.
They are not equal: what the patient can reach and clean decides maintainability, not the CAL number alone.
Both teeth can be kept; the question is which is easier, and the shallow pocket is.

q1-04.stem: When bone loss is the concern, which film should replace the horizontal bitewing, and what is its advantage?
choices: Vertical bitewing, as it rarely misses an arch
Panoramic, since it shows each site best
Occlusal film, since it shows bone between teeth
Horizontal bitewing, since it reads fastest
why: The vertical bitewing covers a taller field, so bone loss in either jaw is less likely to fall off the film.
A panoramic is a broad overview and gives the least detail at any one site among these films.
An occlusal film looks down on the arch and is not used to read the crestal bone between teeth.
This is the film being replaced, because it can leave out the bone loss in one of the two jaws.

q1-09.stem: The 2018 World Workshop retired the labels 'chronic periodontitis' and 'aggressive periodontitis'. How are those patients classified now?
choices: As one Periodontitis category with a stage and grade
As two new groups, 'slow' and 'fast' periodontitis
Still with the old labels, which remain in clinical use
As necrotizing periodontitis, which absorbed both
why: The two were merged into a single Periodontitis category, with each case described by its stage and grade.
No 'slow' or 'fast' categories exist; how quickly the disease moves is what the grade records.
The old labels were dropped in the 2017/2018 classification, and staging and grading took their place.
Necrotizing periodontitis is a separate category of its own, not a merger of the two old ones.

q1-10.stem: Because examiners press the probe with different force, a minimum share of bleeding sites is required before gingivitis is diagnosed. What is that minimum?
choices: 10% of sites or more
A single bleeding site
50% of sites or more
25% of sites or more
why: Bleeding at 10% or more of sites is needed, so two or three stray bleeding spots don't make the diagnosis.
One bleeding spot would over-diagnose; a few bleeding sites can come from probing pressure alone.
Half the mouth is far past the cutoff, which is 10% of sites.
A quarter of sites is not the cutoff; gingivitis is called from 10% of sites bleeding.

q1-12.stem: Years after periodontitis treatment, a patient keeps 3-month maintenance visits. The pockets are shallow and nothing bleeds, but the films still show the old bone loss. How is this patient diagnosed at today's visit?
choices: Healthy on a reduced periodontium
Active Stage 3 periodontitis
Gingivitis on an intact periodontium
Necrotizing periodontitis
why: A stable, maintained patient with shallow, non-bleeding pockets is healthy on a reduced periodontium.
Nothing here is active: no bleeding and shallow pockets; old bone loss on its own doesn't make this active Stage 3.
The periodontium isn't intact, since the old bone loss means it is reduced.
Necrotizing disease is painful with dead papillae, nothing like this calm, stable mouth.

q1-13.stem: Plaque control is started for one patient with gingivitis and one with periodontitis. Which describes what each can get back?
choices: Gingivitis can fully resolve; periodontitis cannot
Both can return fully to their original state
Neither can return fully to its original state
Periodontitis can fully resolve; gingivitis cannot
why: Gingivitis clears completely once plaque is controlled; periodontitis leaves lost attachment, so the best result is health on a reduced periodontium.
Periodontitis does not fully reverse: treatment stabilizes it, but the lost attachment doesn't come back to where it was.
Gingivitis does reverse: it is confined to the gingiva and resolves with plaque control.
This swaps the two: gingivitis is the reversible disease, and periodontitis is not.

q1-16.stem: A clinician begins grading a periodontitis case and has not yet found any evidence to move it up or down. Which grade is the working assumption?
choices: Grade B
Grade A
Grade C
No grade is assumed
why: Grade B, moderate progression, is the starting point; evidence then moves it to A or C.
Grade A has to be earned with evidence of slow progression; it isn't where you start.
Grade C needs evidence of fast progression or a risk factor; it isn't the starting point.
There is a starting point: Grade B is assumed until the evidence shifts it.

q1-17.stem: The worst tooth of a 30-year-old has lost 50% of its bone. With no other information, what grade does the bone-loss/age ratio point to?
choices: Roughly 1.7, pointing to Grade C
Roughly 0.6, pointing to Grade B
Roughly 1.7, still within Grade B
No grade; serial records are needed
why: 50 divided by 30 is about 1.7, over the 1.0 cutoff, so the ratio points to Grade C.
0.6 is age divided by bone loss (30 / 50); the ratio is percent bone loss divided by age, about 1.7.
Grade B runs from 0.25 to 1.0, so a ratio near 1.7 is past it and lands in Grade C.
Serial records are best when they exist; without them, this ratio is exactly the tool you use.

q1-18.stem: Case A is 30, systemically healthy, and neither smokes nor has diabetes. Only #30 is affected: a 7 mm pocket over bone loss that reaches the middle third of the root. How is she diagnosed?
choices: Localized Stage 3 Grade C periodontitis
Localized Stage 3 Grade B periodontitis
Generalized Stage 3 Grade C periodontitis
Localized Stage 2 Grade C periodontitis
why: Middle-third loss with a 7 mm pocket is Stage 3, one tooth is localized, and more than a third of the root lost by age 30 gives a ratio over 1, which is Grade C.
She doesn't need a modifier to reach Grade C: losing over a third of the root by 30 puts the ratio above 1 on its own.
Only #30 is involved, well under 30% of her teeth, so the extent is localized.
Stage 2 ends at coronal-third bone loss; loss into the middle third with a 7 mm pocket is Stage 3.

q1-20.stem: Case E has diabetes with an HbA1c of 6.1%, yet her grade is left at B. What explains this?
choices: 6.1% is under the 7% level that forces Grade C
Diabetes is never used to modify the grade
Only heavy smoking is able to force Grade C
Diabetes changes the stage, not the grade
why: The diabetes modifier only applies at an HbA1c of 7% or higher, so 6.1% doesn't push her to Grade C.
Diabetes is a grade modifier: an HbA1c of 7% or more moves a case to Grade C.
Heavy smoking is one route to Grade C; an HbA1c of 7% or more and a ratio over 1.0 are others.
Diabetes acts on the grade; the stage comes from CAL, bone loss, teeth lost and complexity.

q1-22.stem: Once the flap is raised, the only bare surface in the defect is the root itself; bone still stands buccally, lingually and against the adjacent tooth. How would you classify this defect, and how likely is it to regenerate?
choices: Three-wall, the best regenerative prognosis
One-wall, the worst regenerative prognosis
Two-wall, the interdental shape called a crater
Four-wall, with bone surrounding every side
why: Buccal, lingual and proximal walls are all present, a 3-wall defect, which regenerates best.
A 1-wall defect keeps just one wall and does worst; this one keeps three.
A crater is a 2-wall defect with both proximal walls lost; here the wall against the next tooth is still there.
The fourth side is the bare root, not bone, so this counts as a 3-wall defect.

q1-23.stem: Between two teeth, the bone is gone from both proximal surfaces, and only a buccal and a lingual wall are left. What name is given to this 2-wall defect?
choices: Crater
Hemiseptum
Furcation
Dehiscence
why: A 2-wall defect that has lost both proximal walls, leaving buccal and lingual, is a crater.
A hemiseptum is a 1-wall defect between teeth; a crater still has two walls, buccal and lingual.
A furcation is bone loss between the roots of one multirooted tooth, not between neighboring teeth.
A dehiscence is bone missing over the facial or lingual surface of a root, not an interdental crater.

q1-25.stem: One tooth needs a crown and also needs periodontal treatment. In what order should the care go?
choices: Provisional crown, finish perio therapy, then final crown
Final crown first, followed by the periodontal therapy
No crown or temporary at all until therapy is done
Provisional and final crowns both placed during SRP
why: A temporary goes on, periodontal therapy is finished, and the final crown follows once the tissue is stable.
A permanent crown never goes on before periodontal therapy is done; its margins rely on healed tissue.
The tooth still needs protection and function in the meantime, which is what the temporary crown provides.
Only the temporary is placed during therapy; the final crown waits until therapy is complete.

q1-26.stem: A periodontitis patient also has several open carious lesions. When in the treatment plan are they restored?
choices: In Phase I, before or alongside SRP
Only once all surgery is completed
Never; caries is outside the perio plan
Only after the final RPD is delivered
why: Caries control is part of Phase I with SRP, because open lesions are hard to instrument and to keep clean.
Caries isn't put off until after surgery; cavitated surfaces hold plaque and undercut Phase I.
Caries control does belong in periodontal treatment planning, because open lesions trap plaque.
The final RPD comes late; caries control is done early, in Phase I.

q1-27.stem: A Stage 3 patient asks when it will be decided whether gum surgery is needed. Which visit is the right answer?
choices: The re-evaluation after Phase I
The first comprehensive exam
The first maintenance visit
The first SRP appointment
why: The Phase I re-evaluation shows how the tissue healed and how the patient complied, so that is where the surgical call is made.
At the first exam no one yet knows how the tissue will respond to Phase I.
Maintenance comes after active therapy; the surgical decision has already been made at re-evaluation.
The first SRP visit is part of Phase I, and its result isn't known until the re-evaluation.

q1-29.stem: In the Becker et al. tooth-loss data from lecture, one group lost teeth about twice as fast as patients who kept their maintenance visits. Which group was it?
choices: Treated patients who stopped coming to maintenance
Patients who declined periodontal treatment entirely
Treated patients who were also given antibiotics
Gingivitis patients who missed their recall visits
why: Treated patients who skipped maintenance lost teeth at about double the rate of those who kept recalls (about 0.22 vs 0.11 teeth a year).
Untreated patients fared worse still, losing about three times as many teeth as treated patients, more than a twofold gap.
Antibiotics weren't one of the groups; the comparison was untreated, treated without maintenance, and maintained.
The groups were periodontitis patients; the twofold gap is between treated patients with and without maintenance.

q1-31.stem: Two patients share the same numbers: interdental CAL of 5 mm or more, bone loss into the middle third and 7 mm pockets. What finding would make one of them Stage 4 instead of Stage 3?
choices: Five or more teeth lost to perio, or complex rehab needed
At least one vertical bone defect of 3 mm or deeper
A bone-loss/age ratio greater than 1.0 at the worst tooth
A habit of smoking 10 or more cigarettes each day
why: Stage 4 comes from losing 5 or more teeth to periodontitis or from needing complex rehabilitation.
A vertical defect of 3 mm or more is a Stage 3 finding; it doesn't split Stage 3 from Stage 4.
The bone-loss/age ratio decides the grade, not the stage.
Smoking modifies the grade, so it cannot move a case from Stage 3 to Stage 4.

q1-32.stem: Staging and grading each answer a different question. Which is the one only grading answers?
choices: How fast it progresses and how it will respond
How severe and extensive the attachment loss is
How complex the case will be to treat
Whether the disease is localized or generalized
why: Grading estimates the speed of the disease and the patient's likely response, which is where risk factors come in.
How severe and widespread the attachment loss is at presentation is what staging records.
Complexity of management is part of the stage, not the grade.
Localized or generalized is the extent, written in front of the stage, not what the grade tells you.

q2-01.stem: On the course's six-material suture chart, one option is a natural monofilament that is gone in 7-10 days, the quickest of the six, but its handling is very poor. Which one is it?
choices: Chromic gut
Poly-glycolic acid (PGA)
Silk
PTFE
why: Right: chromic gut is the natural monofilament that resorbs in 7-10 days and has very bad handling.
PGA is a braided synthetic that lasts the longest of the resorbables (55-70 days) and handles very well.
Silk is natural, but it is braided, never resorbs and handles beautifully.
PTFE is a synthetic that never resorbs, and its handling is good.

q2-02.stem: A surgeon closing a ridge or sinus augmentation wants a synthetic, braided suture that lasts the longest of all the resorbable choices, about 55-70 days. Which material matches?
choices: Poly-glycolic acid (PGA)
Silk
PGCL, poly(glycolide-co-caprolactone)
Chromic gut
why: Right: PGA is the braided synthetic resorbable that takes 55-70 days, a fit for slow-healing ridge and sinus grafts.
Silk is braided as well, but it is a natural material and it never resorbs.
PGCL is a synthetic resorbable, but it is a single strand and is gone sooner (22-55 days).
Chromic gut is a natural monofilament and the quickest to resorb (7-10 days).

q2-03.stem: Among the sutures that never resorb, one behaves like nylon and does not stick to the tissue at all. Which is it?
choices: Poly-propylene
Silk
PTFE
PGCL, poly(glycolide-co-caprolactone)
why: Right: poly-propylene is the non-resorbable monofilament that, like nylon, has no tissue adherence.
Silk does not resorb either, but it is a natural braided thread whose tissue reaction is very bad.
PTFE is another non-resorbable monofilament, but the chart singles it out as the high-cost option for every surgery except pure soft-tissue grafts.
PGCL resorbs over 22-55 days, so it is not in the non-resorbable group at all.

q2-04.stem: One of the six chart sutures handles beautifully but irritates tissue more than any of the others. Which is it?
choices: Silk
PGCL, poly(glycolide-co-caprolactone)
PTFE
Chromic gut
why: Right: silk's tissue reaction is rated very bad, the worst of the six, even though its handling is great.
PGCL's tissue reaction is rated great, so it is one of the gentlest.
PTFE's tissue reaction is rated great, so it is one of the gentlest.
Chromic gut causes only a mild reaction; its problem is very bad handling.

q2-05.stem: The course chart lists one non-resorbable suture that is natural and braided and gives it a specific removal time. Which suture is it, and when does it come out?
choices: Silk, removed at 7 days
PTFE, removed at 7 days
Poly-propylene, removed at 10 days
Silk, removed at 14 days
why: Right: silk is the natural, braided non-resorbable, and the chart has it removed at 7 days.
PTFE never resorbs, but it is a synthetic monofilament; the 7-day removal on the chart belongs to silk.
Poly-propylene must be removed too, but it is a synthetic monofilament, not the natural braided material described; that is silk, which comes out at 7 days.
The material is right, but the chart gives silk a 7-day removal; 10-14 days is the general window for non-absorbables.

q2-09.stem: A suture labeled 5-0 is compared with one labeled 3-0. Going up in size number, how does the thread change, and what does that mean for the knot?
choices: It gets thinner and needs more knots
It gets thicker and needs fewer knots
It gets thicker and needs more knots
It gets thinner and needs fewer knots
why: Right: the numbers run in reverse, so a higher number is a thinner thread, and a thinner thread needs more knots to hold.
A higher number is a thinner thread, not a thicker one.
More knots is right for a higher number, but the thread is thinner, not thicker.
Thinner is right, but thinner thread slips more easily, so it needs more knots, not fewer.

q2-13.stem: A surgeon makes only an intrasulcular incision, with no vertical release. The tissue stays attached at the sides, so access is limited and the flap is hard to advance. What is this design called, and what is it good for?
choices: A sulcular flap, for minor augmentation or a single implant
A trapezoidal flap, for major vertical augmentation
A pyramidal flap, for an implant with an onlay graft
An envelope flap, for root coverage with a soft-tissue graft
why: Right: with no vertical release, the sulcular flap stays attached laterally; it is the smallest option, used for minor augmentation or a single implant.
A trapezoidal flap has two vertical releases, giving wide access and easy coronal advancement.
A pyramidal flap adds one vertical release, so it gives more access than intrasulcular alone.
An envelope flap lifts only the buccal tissue to tuck a soft-tissue graft over a root; it isn't the intrasulcular-only design for minor augmentation.

q2-14.stem: An exam question says "partial-thickness flap." Which description is it referring to?
choices: The same as split thickness: periosteum stays on the bone
A full-thickness flap that is lifted only part of the way
A pyramidal flap, released by one vertical on one side
An envelope flap, with the papillae left in place
why: Right: partial and split thickness are two names for one thing; the periosteum is left on the bone and only the tissue above it is lifted.
How far a flap is lifted doesn't make it partial; if it takes the periosteum it is full thickness and bares the bone.
Pyramidal describes the flap's outline (one vertical release), not its thickness.
Envelope describes the outline (buccal only, papillae untouched), not whether the periosteum comes up.

q2-17.stem: One of the five surgical principles says a flap's base should be at least as wide as its free edge. What is that principle protecting?
choices: The blood supply reaching the flap
The free edge from rolling inward at closure
The placement of verticals at the line angles
The periosteum from being lifted with the flap
why: Right: after reflection, blood enters the flap only through its base, so a narrow base starves the free edge.
Edges rolling inward is a closure problem (a horizontal mattress prevents it), not what base width addresses.
Line-angle placement is a separate principle, there to spare the papilla and avoid recession.
Whether the periosteum comes up is the full vs partial thickness decision; base width is about blood supply.

q2-18.stem: Tooth #8 is present and #9 is missing. One continuous straight cut runs around #8 and then along the ridge at #9. How is each part of that cut named?
choices: Intrasulcular at #8 and crestal at #9, named by tooth presence
Crestal at #8 and intrasulcular at #9, named by where the blade goes in
Vertical at both, since each part follows the long axis
Pouch at both, since neither part releases the flap sideways
why: Right: it is one incision; around a tooth it is intrasulcular, and on the edentulous ridge it is crestal.
This swaps them: intrasulcular is the name around a tooth, and crestal is the name on an edentulous ridge.
Vertical incisions are releasing cuts that run apically; they don't follow the sulcus or the crest.
Pouch is the name of a flap design; the incisions themselves are intrasulcular and crestal.

q2-19.stem: The intrasulcular incision isn't giving enough exposure. Instead of carrying it onto more teeth, the surgeon adds a vertical release. What does that choice achieve?
choices: More apical access without including teeth that don't need it
An incision line placed right over the bony defect
A flap that stays split thickness, leaving the periosteum
Quicker healing than an intrasulcular incision gives
why: Right: a vertical release opens the flap apically for access, so uninvolved teeth don't have to be pulled into the horizontal cut.
Incisions are kept away from the bony defect, never over it; that is one of the five principles.
Adding a vertical doesn't change thickness; a major augmentation flap with verticals is full thickness.
Verticals aren't chosen to heal faster; they are added only for access.

q2-20.stem: A root-coverage case calls for a soft-tissue graft, and the papillae must not be disturbed at all. Which flap design suits it?
choices: An envelope (pouch) flap
A trapezoidal flap
A full-thickness flap that bares the bone
A sulcular flap carried across 4 teeth
why: Right: the envelope (pouch) flap lifts only the buccal tissue and never reflects the papillae.
A trapezoidal flap opens widely with two vertical releases, which disturbs the area.
A soft-tissue graft needs a split-thickness bed for its blood supply, and baring bone doesn't spare the papillae.
Carrying a sulcular flap across 4 teeth reflects the papillae as it goes.

q2-21.stem: For a large vertical ridge graft, the flap has to slide coronally and close passively, with no tension at all. Which design gives that?
choices: A trapezoidal flap
A sulcular flap
A pyramidal flap
An envelope flap
why: Right: its two releasing incisions let the flap advance coronally and close tension-free over a large graft.
A sulcular flap has no release and is hard to advance; it suits only minor augmentation.
A pyramidal flap has one release, which often can't stretch far enough for a major vertical graft without tearing.
An envelope flap has no vertical release and doesn't advance far.

q2-22.stem: An implant will get an onlay bone graft. The sulcular flap won't give enough room, but the surgeon doesn't want releases on both sides. Which flap fits?
choices: A pyramidal flap
A trapezoidal flap
An envelope flap
A split-thickness flap
why: Right: one vertical plus intrasulcular across three teeth gives more access than a sulcular flap without opening both sides.
A trapezoidal flap opens both sides with two releases; it is kept for major augmentation.
An envelope flap has no vertical release, so it gives even less room than needed.
Grafting bone needs the bone exposed, which means full thickness, not split thickness.

q2-24.stem: A 6 mm pocket is to be removed outright: the pocket wall will be cut away rather than lifted and put back. Which incision is meant for this?
choices: A sub-marginal incision
An intrasulcular incision
A crestal incision
A vertical releasing incision
why: Right: it is placed below the gingival margin and excises a strip of pocket wall, eliminating the pocket.
An intrasulcular incision keeps the pocket wall and reflects it rather than removing it.
A crestal incision is the same straight cut on an edentulous ridge; it removes no pocket wall.
A vertical incision only releases the flap for access; it takes no pocket tissue away.

q2-25.stem: After healing, a site treated with a sub-marginal incision shows recession. What explains it, and where is this incision appropriate?
choices: The pocket wall was removed deliberately; use it for deep pockets, never for recession
The flap was set too far apically by accident; it's an error to avoid
The pocket wall was removed deliberately; it's also the first choice for treating recession
The tissue was only lifted, so the margin returns to its old level in weeks
why: Right: the tissue coronal to the incision is excised on purpose, so the recession is intended; it fits a deep pocket and is never used where recession is the problem.
Nothing was misplaced: the tissue above the incision is cut away by design, so the recession isn't a mistake.
Removing pocket wall on purpose is right, and that is exactly why it is never used on a recession site; thin or receded tissue calls for a graft.
The tissue isn't lifted and replaced; it is excised, so the margin does not rebound.

q2-27.stem: At the recipient site of a soft-tissue graft meant to thicken the keratinized tissue around a tooth, how thick a flap is raised, and what is the reason?
choices: Partial thickness, so the periosteum stays as a blood-rich bed
Full thickness, so the graft can sit straight on bare bone
Partial thickness, so the epithelium stays for the graft to join
Full thickness, since periosteum left behind would reject the graft
why: Right: partial (split) thickness leaves the periosteum on the bone, and its vessels anastomose with the graft's.
Bare bone gives a soft-tissue graft no blood supply from below; full thickness is for bone work.
Partial thickness is right, but grafts fuse only to cut, epithelium-free surfaces; intact epithelium blocks the vessels from joining.
Periosteum doesn't reject a graft; it is the vascular bed that feeds it.

q2-28.stem: Where on the palate should a connective tissue graft be taken from, and what is the reason?
choices: Molar area, since less fat there means less graft shrinkage
Premolar area, since its thinner tissue is easier to suture
Molar area, since thicker epithelium there makes a bulkier graft
Premolar area, since its extra fat adds useful bulk
why: Right: the premolar area has more adipose tissue, which resorbs after transplanting, so molar-area grafts shrink less.
The premolar area isn't preferred: it carries more fat, and that fat resorbs and shrinks the graft.
The molar area is right, but not because of epithelium: a connective tissue graft has its epithelium trimmed off.
Fat isn't useful bulk: it resorbs quickly once moved, which is why the premolar area is avoided.

q2-32.stem: An orthodontist plans to move a patient's lower incisors further buccally, and the buccal tissue over them is thin. How should the periodontal care be timed?
choices: Graft to thicken the tissue first, before the teeth are moved
Begin the tooth movement and graft only if recession shows up
Hold off on orthodontics for good, since thin tissue rules it out
Wait until orthodontics ends, then graft no matter what happened
why: Right: thickening the tissue before the movement prevents the recession that pushing teeth through thin tissue tends to cause.
Waiting for recession means treating damage that an earlier graft would have prevented.
Thin tissue isn't a permanent contraindication; grafting first lets orthodontics go ahead.
Grafting afterward misses the window; the recession risk comes during the movement.

q3-01.stem: A patient asks what will happen to her teeth if she leaves without any treatment. Which prognosis system or systems can answer that kind of question?
choices: Only McGuire & Nunn
Only Kwok & Caton
Both McGuire & Nunn and Kwok & Caton
Every one of the three systems
why: Right: a no-treatment forecast is a diagnostic prognosis, and McGuire & Nunn is the only system that can give one (it can be therapeutic as well).
Kwok & Caton judges whether stability is reachable with treatment, so it is therapeutic only and can't forecast the untreated course.
Kwok & Caton can't be diagnostic, since it rates the outcome of treatment; McGuire & Nunn alone has a diagnostic version.
All three work as therapeutic prognoses, but only McGuire & Nunn can be diagnostic, so 'every one' is wrong here.

q3-04.stem: When a clinician assigns a McGuire & Nunn prognosis, what question about the tooth is being answered?
choices: How easily can it be maintained in the mouth?
What is its numeric chance of retention as a molar?
How likely is periodontal stability with treatment?
How fast is the disease progressing at this site?
why: Right: McGuire & Nunn rates how easy the tooth will be to maintain.
A numeric retention score for molars is Miller & McEntire; McGuire & Nunn rates any tooth by how easily it can be kept.
The likelihood of periodontal stability is Kwok & Caton's question.
Speed of progression is what grading describes; it isn't a prognosis system's question.

q3-08.stem: One prognosis system is assigned only at the level of the entire dentition rather than to individual teeth. Which one?
choices: Kwok & Caton
McGuire & Nunn
Miller & McEntire
Each of the three
why: Right: Kwok & Caton rates the whole dentition, asking whether periodontal stability can be reached with treatment.
McGuire & Nunn can be given for the whole mouth, but it is also assigned tooth by tooth.
Miller & McEntire is scored on single molars.
Only Kwok & Caton stays at the whole-dentition level; McGuire & Nunn is also per tooth and Miller & McEntire per molar.

q3-09.stem: The lecture contrasts P4 medicine with reactive, Hippocratic-style care. Which list gives the four P's as the lecture defines them?
choices: Predictive, Participatory, Personalized, Preventive
Progressive, Preventive, Participatory, Prophylactic
Predictive, Periodontal, Proactive, Personalized
Prophylactic, Periodontal, Preventive, Predictive
why: Right: the four P's are personalized, preventive, predictive and participatory; periodontal is the fifth P the lecture adds for P5.
Progressive and prophylactic aren't among the P's; personalized and predictive belong instead.
Proactive isn't a P, and periodontal is the fifth P (P5), not one of the four.
Personalized and participatory are missing, and prophylactic and periodontal aren't in P4.

q3-10.stem: Many patients who turn out to have periodontitis first walk in asking for nothing more than a routine cleaning. Roughly what percentage is that?
choices: About 72%
About 42%
About 25%
About 95%
why: Right: about 72% of patients later diagnosed with periodontitis came in asking only for a cleaning.
About 42% (42.5%) is the share of US adults over 30 who have periodontitis, a different number.
25% is far too low; the point was that most of these patients, about 72%, had no idea.
95% is the D1110 share of cleanings at ages 50-64, a different number.

q3-11.stem: Among patients aged 50 to 64, the prophylaxis code (D1110) accounts for 95.4% of cleanings. Why does the lecture treat this as a warning sign?
choices: Its share rises with age, while disease prevalence says it should shrink
It lines up with the periodontitis prevalence expected at those ages
It is below the prophy share seen in patients aged 19 to 34
It shows periodontitis grows less common past about age 50
why: Right: periodontitis gets more common with age, so prophy should make up less of the cleanings; instead it climbs to 95.4%, which points to missed disease.
It runs opposite to the epidemiology: prevalence rises with age while the prophy share also rises.
The 19-34 share is lower (72.3%); the share climbs with age, 87.5% at 35-49 and 95.4% at 50-64.
Periodontitis becomes more common with age (70.1% at 65 and older), which is exactly why the rising D1110 share doesn't fit.

q3-12.stem: Next to a periodontally healthy mouth (healthy value first), how big is the periodontal inflamed surface area (PISA) in a mouth with mild-to-moderate periodontitis?
choices: Roughly 60-70 times bigger: about 34 mm² vs 2,309 mm²
Roughly double: about 34 mm² vs 70 mm²
Roughly 10 times bigger: about 34 mm² vs 340 mm²
Roughly equal: a healthy sulcus is inflamed as well
why: Right: about 34 mm² in health vs about 2,309 mm² in mild-to-moderate periodontitis, around 60-70 times larger.
Double badly understates it; the inflamed area in periodontitis is about 2,309 mm².
Ten times is still far too small; about 2,309 mm² is close to 60-70 times the healthy value.
A healthy sulcus isn't inflamed; PISA counts inflamed pocket lining only, about 34 mm² in health, a small paper cut.

q3-16.stem: A risk tool gives 0 to 4 points each for cigarettes a day, HbA1c, how many pockets are 5 mm or deeper, BOP %, and bone loss divided by age, then adds them up into one patient score. What is this tool?
choices: UniFe
The PRA
PreViser/PAT
Miller & McEntire
why: Right: UniFe adds five 0-4 scores into a five-tier risk score.
The PRA (Lang & Tonetti) is drawn as a spider-web plot; five summed 0-4 items are UniFe's.
PreViser/PAT (Page et al.) also gives a risk tier from clinical, radiographic and behavioral inputs, but the five summed 0-4 items describe UniFe.
Miller & McEntire is a molar prognosis system, not a summed whole-patient risk score.

q3-17.stem: A patient has been placed in the low-risk tier. Under the risk-stratified maintenance protocol, what interval is set for professional removal of biofilm and calculus?
choices: Once every 6 months
Once every 3 months
Once every 2-4 months
Once every 4-6 months
why: Right: low risk means biofilm and calculus removal every 6 months.
Every 3 months is more often than low risk calls for; high risk is every 2-4 months.
Every 2-4 months is the high-risk interval.
Every 4-6 months is the moderate-risk interval.

q3-18.stem: For a patient in the high-risk tier, how often does the risk-stratified protocol schedule a separate oral exam and periodontal screening, apart from the comprehensive exam?
choices: Every 3 months
Every 6 months
Every 12 months
Never; high risk has no separate screening
why: Right: high risk adds a screening every 3 months on top of the comprehensive exam.
Every 6 months is the moderate-risk screening interval.
12 months is the outer limit of the comprehensive exam, not the high-risk screening.
High-risk patients do get a separate screening; it's the low-risk tier that has none.

q3-19.stem: A patient finished periodontal therapy, and today every site probes 3 mm. Why does she still not qualify for a routine prophylaxis by default?
choices: She healed with a long junctional epithelium, a weaker seal
A 3 mm reading after periodontal therapy can't be trusted
Insurance stops paying for a prophy after perio therapy
Her sites healed with new but immature connective tissue
why: Right: treated pockets heal with a long junctional epithelium, which breaks down under inflammation more easily than connective-tissue attachment with a short junctional epithelium.
The 3 mm reading can be accurate; what's different is the attachment beneath it.
The reason is biology, not billing: the healed attachment is weaker, so the maintenance code and schedule still apply.
Treatment doesn't rebuild connective-tissue attachment here; the pocket heals with a long junctional epithelium, the weaker seal.

q3-22.stem: A patient in active orthodontic tooth movement is booked for periodontal maintenance about every 4-6 weeks instead of every 3 months. What is the main biological reason?
choices: Inflammation while teeth move can uncouple bone formation and resorption
Brackets make it physically impossible to schedule 3-month visits
Orthodontic force alone causes bone loss, however good the biofilm control
Insurance bills braces patients on a fixed 4-6 week cycle
why: Right: inflammation during active movement can tip remodeling toward resorption and cause real bone loss, so biofilm is controlled every 4-6 weeks.
Brackets don't prevent 3-month visits; the visits do coincide with adjustments, but the shorter interval is about the bone.
Tooth movement remodels bone; the loss happens when inflammation uncouples formation from resorption, which is why tight biofilm control matters.
The interval comes from bone biology, not an insurance cycle.

q3-23.stem: According to the lecture's data on patient trust, what most often leads a patient to turn down a recommended periodontal treatment plan?
choices: Distrust of their dental provider
The price of the proposed treatment
Being afraid treatment will hurt
Lacking time for the appointments
why: Right: distrust is the top reason; 62% delay, switch providers, get a second opinion or refuse because they doubt the diagnosis.
Cost is rarely the real barrier (patients said they'd pay about $633 a tooth to keep it); it becomes one when they feel rushed or unheard.
Fear of pain wasn't the leading reason in the lecture's data; distrust of the provider or diagnosis was.
Time wasn't the leading reason either; distrust was, which is why the whole team needs to give one consistent message.

q3-26.stem: Two teeth receive different McGuire & Nunn categories. Which factor is the system actually sorting them by?
choices: How well each tooth can be maintained
How likely each tooth is to keep progressing
How likely each tooth is to loosen untreated
How often each tooth will need retreatment
why: Right: maintainability, how hard it will be to keep the tooth, sets the McGuire & Nunn category.
Disease progression was the class's most common pick, but the system sorts by maintainability.
Mobility feeds into it, but the category reflects overall maintainability, not mobility alone.
Retreatment frequency isn't what the categories measure; maintainability is.

q3-28.stem: Students often expect 'poor' to be the category just above hopeless in McGuire & Nunn, yet 'questionable' holds that spot. What explains the order?
choices: The scale is about keeping the tooth, and a questionable tooth won't stay put: it slides to hopeless or recovers to poor
A questionable tooth always has more attachment loss and mobility than a poor one, so the list runs from least to most damage
The order copies Kwok & Caton, where questionable also sits next to hopeless, so the two scales match up
Questionable is reserved for molars, so it is set apart near the end of the scale as a molar-only group
why: Right: the categories sort by whether a tooth can be kept, and a questionable tooth doesn't stay there; it gets worse or improves.
Questionable isn't defined by more destruction than poor; it reflects genuine doubt that the tooth can be kept.
In Kwok & Caton questionable sits in the middle (stability unknown); only McGuire & Nunn puts it right before hopeless.
Questionable applies to any tooth, not just molars; the molar-only system is Miller & McEntire.

q3-30.stem: Leave out every tooth rated 'good' and look only at the rest. How accurate are McGuire & Nunn prognoses then?
choices: Right about half the time
Right about 80% of the time
Right about 95% of the time
Right about 20% of the time
why: Right: without the easy 'good' teeth, predictions are right only about 50% of the time, a coin flip.
About 80% is the overall figure, with the good teeth counted.
95% is far too high; even the overall accuracy is about 80%.
20% is too low; the figure is about 50%, a coin flip.

q3-31.stem: A patient who keeps up with maintenance has a tooth rated hopeless. Over the long term, what did follow-up data show for teeth like this?
choices: They often last well beyond what was predicted
They nearly always fall out within a year
They have to come out before maintenance can begin
They lead to failure of the teeth next to them
why: Right: in well-maintained patients, hopeless teeth are often kept much longer than predicted.
They rarely exfoliate; most teeth leave the mouth because a dentist extracts them.
Extraction isn't required first; many such teeth stay in maintenance for years.
That isn't what the follow-up showed; the point was that they outlast expectations.

q3-32.stem: A clinician gives a diagnostic prognosis. What is she predicting?
choices: What happens if the patient gets no treatment
What happens after the recommended treatment
A forecast made for molars only
A forecast made only at maintenance visits
why: Right: a diagnostic prognosis forecasts the outcome if the patient leaves untreated.
The outcome after recommended treatment is a therapeutic prognosis.
Molars only describes Miller & McEntire, not the diagnostic vs therapeutic split.
It isn't tied to maintenance visits; it's the no-treatment forecast.

q3-34.stem: On the Kwok & Caton scale, 'questionable' falls between favorable and unfavorable rather than next to hopeless. What about the system puts it there?
choices: It rates whether stability with treatment is likely, uncertain or unlikely
It rates how much effort each tooth will take to keep in the mouth
It ranks its categories by the deepest probing depth found
Questionable is the one category of it that can be diagnostic
why: Right: Kwok & Caton asks whether periodontal stability is achievable with treatment (likely, don't know, unlikely), so questionable, the don't-know answer, lands in the middle.
Effort to keep a tooth is McGuire & Nunn's question, which is why its questionable sits right before hopeless.
It isn't ordered by probing depth; it's ordered by how likely stability is with treatment.
Kwok & Caton is therapeutic only, so none of its categories can be diagnostic.

q3-35.stem: Kwok & Caton would add the most for which of these patients?
choices: A smoker with complex medical history and an elevated A1c
Someone asking what happens if they decline all treatment
One mandibular molar that has a Class II furcation
A healthy nonsmoker with no systemic risk factors at all
why: Right: Kwok & Caton judges stability with treatment, so quitting smoking and getting the A1c under control become part of the plan it rates.
A forecast with no treatment is a diagnostic prognosis, which only McGuire & Nunn can give.
A single tooth calls for a per-tooth system such as McGuire & Nunn; Kwok & Caton rates the whole dentition.
With no systemic factors to fold into the plan, Kwok & Caton's advantage adds little here.

q3-38.stem: In the class case, a 78-year-old ASA II woman has generalized Stage 3 Grade B periodontitis, with bone loss that is mostly horizontal and furcations involved. What Kwok & Caton prognosis was she given?
choices: Questionable
Favorable
Unfavorable
Hopeless
why: Right: horizontal loss and furcations are hard to regenerate, so it is uncertain whether stability can be reached.
Favorable means stability is likely, but her horizontal loss and furcations leave it uncertain.
Unfavorable means stability is unlikely; her case was judged uncertain rather than unlikely.
Hopeless wasn't assigned; with treatment, stability is uncertain, not out of reach.

q3-39.stem: The class put the 78-year-old Stage 3 patient on a 3-month recall. What reasoning supports that interval?
choices: Subgingival bacteria repopulate in about 9-11 weeks, and a periodontitis patient stays higher risk even when healthy
Every patient older than 75 gets a 3-month recall whatever their periodontal diagnosis or risk level turns out to be
Her PRA put her in the extraction range, so the 3-month visits only monitor the remaining teeth until they come out
Her insurance pays for four visits a year, so coverage, not biology, is what fixed the length of the interval
why: Right: subgingival bacteria return in about 9-11 weeks, and a treated periodontitis patient remains higher risk.
Age alone doesn't set the recall; periodontal risk and repopulation time do.
She wasn't in an extraction range; the recall maintains health on a reduced periodontium (her PRA said to keep doing what she was doing).
The interval comes from biology (repopulation), not insurance coverage.

q3-40.stem: A deep, narrow vertical defect is treated with a bone replacement graft and a membrane. About what percentage of the defect should fill with bone?
choices: Roughly 70-75%
Roughly 10-20%
All of it, 100%
Roughly 40%
why: Right: a graft plus membrane fills about 70-75% of a deep, narrow vertical defect.
10-20% is far too low for a graft and membrane in a favorable defect.
Complete fill isn't expected; about 70-75% is.
About 40% is too low; the figure taught was about 70-75%.

q3-41.stem: In the class case, a 13-year-old has localized vertical defects on her first molars (molar-incisor pattern, Grade C) and regeneration is in the plan. Which overall therapeutic McGuire & Nunn prognosis fits?
choices: Good to fair overall, the involved teeth fair
The involved molars hopeless, the rest of the mouth good
Poor to questionable, the involved teeth questionable
Every tooth questionable pending re-evaluation
why: Right: deep, narrow vertical defects regenerate well (about 70-75% fill) and she is young, so with treatment the overall prognosis is good to fair, the involved teeth fair.
Grade C in a young patient with regenerable vertical defects doesn't make those molars hopeless.
Poor to questionable is her diagnostic prognosis, with no treatment; the question asks for the therapeutic one.
Only the involved teeth are in doubt, and regeneration is expected to work; the rest of her mouth isn't questionable.

q3-42.stem: Circumpubertal periodontitis with a molar-incisor pattern is linked to a specific underlying problem in about 70% of patients. What is it?
choices: Defective neutrophil chemotaxis
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
A deficiency of vitamin C
Past orthodontic treatment
why: Right: about 70% have a neutrophil chemotactic defect, which is why the first teeth to erupt are hit hardest.
Type 1 diabetes isn't the defect behind 70% of molar-incisor cases.
Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) affects the gingiva but isn't behind this pattern.
Orthodontic history isn't the common factor; a neutrophil chemotactic defect is.

q3-43.stem: Some patients with localized molar-incisor periodontitis go on to a generalized form. About 70% of that group have which risk factor in common?
choices: They use nicotine
They have diabetes
They are over age 40
They breathe through the mouth
why: Right: about 70% of patients whose molar-incisor pattern generalizes use nicotine.
Diabetes isn't the factor shared by 70%; nicotine is.
These are young patients; being over 40 isn't the shared factor.
Mouth breathing isn't the shared factor; nicotine is.

q3-44.stem: A patient has been staged at Stage 3. Under what circumstance, and only that one, can the stage be lowered?
choices: The vertical defect or furcation that set the stage is regenerated
The patient stops smoking, because smoking is one of the staging criteria
A year of 3-month maintenance passes with no new attachment loss at any site
Every probing depth falls below 4 mm after SRP when re-evaluated
why: Right: the stage comes down only when the stage-defining lesion, a vertical defect or furcation, is regenerated.
Smoking modifies grade, not stage, so quitting can't lower it.
Stable maintenance doesn't lower the stage; attachment already lost stays counted.
Shallower pockets after SRP don't reverse the stage.

q3-45.stem: Class case: a 75-year-old former smoker bleeds on probing at about 80% of sites and has both vertical and horizontal defects. What overall diagnostic McGuire & Nunn prognosis was she given?
choices: Poor
Good
Hopeless
Fair
why: Right: with about 80% BOP and vertical plus horizontal defects, the overall diagnostic prognosis was poor.
Good doesn't fit 80% BOP and several defects in an untreated mouth.
Some teeth were hopeless, but the overall prognosis was poor, not hopeless.
Fair is the therapeutic prognosis with compliance and surgery, not the no-treatment one.

q3-46.stem: A patient already graded C is newly found to have diabetes, with an A1c of 8.8%. How does this change her assessment?
choices: The grade stays C, but a risk tool such as the PRA shows a much bigger risk footprint
She moves up to Grade D, the grade set aside for patients with poorly controlled diabetes
Her stage falls to 2, since the diabetes rather than periodontitis now accounts for the bone loss
Nothing changes anywhere, because grading and risk tools both disregard systemic conditions
why: Right: Grade C is already the top grade, so it stays, but a tool like the PRA shows a larger risk footprint.
There is no Grade D; grades run A, B and C.
Diabetes doesn't lower the stage; stage reflects damage already done.
Risk tools like the PRA do take systemic factors such as diabetes into account.

q3-47.stem: Some people never develop periodontitis whether their oral hygiene is good or bad. About what fraction of people is that?
choices: Around 10%
Around 50%
Around 1%
Around 25%
why: Right: about 10% resist periodontitis regardless of hygiene.
50% is far too high for disease resistance.
1% is too low; about 10% are resistant.
20-25% is the share who don't respond to standard therapy, a different group.

q3-48.stem: If you were shown a Periodontal Risk Assessment (PRA) result, what kind of figure would you be looking at?
choices: A spider web whose footprint widens as risk rises
A bar chart with one probing-depth bar per sextant
A five-tier score added up from items scored 0-4
A decision flowchart that ends at a recall interval
why: Right: the PRA plots BOP, sites ≥5 mm, missing teeth, % bone loss and smoking (with systemic factors) on a spider web; the bigger the footprint, the higher the risk.
Probing depths feed it (sites ≥5 mm), but the PRA isn't a bar chart; it's a spider-web plot.
Five 0-4 items summed into a five-tier score is UniFe, not the PRA.
Its output does guide recall (keep current measures, or see the patient more or less often), but it's drawn as a spider web, not a flowchart.

q4-01.stem: You need to check how far a probe enters between the roots of a lower molar. Which instrument do you reach for?
choices: The Nabers probe
The ODU 11/12 explorer
The Gracey 11/12
The Columbia 13/14
why: Its curved shape follows the root into the furcation entrance, which is exactly what it is made for.
This explorer is for feeling root-surface roughness; it isn't the furcation instrument.
This is a curette for posterior mesial surfaces, used to instrument, not to examine furcations.
This is a universal curette for scaling, not an instrument for examining furcations.

q4-02.stem: During the exam you want to feel every surface of every root for roughness. Which instrument does that job?
choices: The ODU 11/12 explorer
A periodontal probe
The Nabers probe
A sickle scaler
why: This explorer is the one used to check root roughness on all surfaces of all teeth.
A periodontal probe records pocket depth; it isn't used to judge root roughness.
The Nabers probe is for furcations, not root roughness everywhere.
A sickle scaler takes off supragingival calculus; it is a working instrument, not an evaluation one.

q4-03.stem: You are working below the gingival margin on the distal surface of a lower first molar. Which Gracey fits that surface?
choices: The Gracey 13/14
The Gracey 11/12
The Gracey 3/4
The Gracey 15/16
why: Its shank has more bends than the 11/12's, so it wraps around to reach posterior distal surfaces.
This one is for posterior mesials (and molar buccal/lingual surfaces), not distals.
This one is made for anterior teeth, not the distal surfaces of posteriors.
This one is an alternative to the 11/12 for posterior mesials, not the distal Gracey.

q4-04.stem: Subgingival calculus is spread over the mesial, distal, facial and lingual surfaces of the lower incisors. Which Gracey handles all of them?
choices: The Gracey 3/4
The Gracey 11/12
The Gracey 13/14
The Columbia 13/14
why: This is the anterior Gracey: it works every surface of anterior teeth below the margin.
This one is for posterior mesial surfaces and molar buccal/lingual surfaces.
This one is for the distal surfaces of posterior teeth.
This is the universal curette, not the area-specific Gracey for anteriors.

q4-05.stem: Which of these curettes can be used on any tooth surface, instead of being made for one area of the mouth?
choices: The Columbia 13/14
The Gracey 11/12 curette
The Gracey 15/16
The Gracey 3/4
why: It is the universal curette: with two cutting edges it can work any surface.
This Gracey is made for one area: posterior mesials and molar buccal/lingual surfaces.
This Gracey is made for one area, as an alternative instrument for posterior mesials.
This Gracey is made for one area, the anterior teeth.

q4-06.stem: Supragingival calculus is packed between two lower molars. Which scaler is designed for that spot?
choices: The S204SD9 sickle
The H6/7 anterior sickle
The Gracey 13/14
The Gracey 11/12
why: Its right-angled shank is built for supragingival work on posterior interproximal surfaces.
This straight-shank anterior sickle is for anteriors and molar buccal/lingual surfaces, not posterior interproximals.
This is a subgingival curette for posterior distals, not a supragingival scaler.
This is a subgingival curette for posterior mesials and molar buccal/lingual surfaces, not a supragingival scaler.

q4-07.stem: Where in the mouth is the H6/7, the straight-shank anterior sickle, meant to be used above the gingival margin?
choices: The anterior teeth, plus the buccal and lingual of molars
The interproximal surfaces of all the premolars and molars
The distal surfaces of the premolars and the molars
The furcation entrances and root concavities of molars
why: That is the H6/7's territory: anteriors and the molar buccal/lingual surfaces, supragingivally.
Posterior interproximals are covered by the right-angled S204SD9 posterior sickle.
Posterior distals are worked below the margin with the Gracey 13/14, not this sickle.
Furcations and root concavities are subgingival areas for curettes or ultrasonics, not a supragingival sickle.

q4-10.stem: At one site the probe reads 2 mm and the margin has receded 5 mm. What clinical attachment level do you chart?
choices: 7 mm
3 mm
2 mm
5 mm
why: Add the two: 2 mm of probing depth plus 5 mm of recession gives 7 mm.
This subtracts the numbers; CAL is the sum of probing depth and recession.
This is the probing depth alone and leaves out the 5 mm of recession.
This is the recession alone and leaves out the 2 mm pocket.

q4-12.stem: Which two landmarks bound the measurement you record as gingival recession?
choices: From the CEJ to the gingival margin
From the gingival margin to the pocket base
From the CEJ to the base of the pocket
From the alveolar crest to the CEJ
why: Recession is the distance between the CEJ and the gingival margin.
That distance is the probing depth.
That distance is the clinical attachment level (PD plus recession).
That is a radiographic bone-level distance, not recession.

q4-13.stem: When you chart probing depths, how many numbers go down for each tooth, and which value is kept at each site?
choices: Six (DB, B, MB, DL, L, ML), keeping the deepest reading at each
Four sites (M, D, B, L), keeping the average of the readings at each surface
Three sites on the buccal only, adding lingual sites only when there is bleeding
One number, the deepest site anywhere on the tooth, as its only probing depth
why: Each tooth is probed at six sites, and the deepest reading at each site is the one recorded.
Six sites are probed, not four, and the deepest reading is kept, never an average.
Lingual sites are probed every time; all six are recorded, bleeding or not.
A single number per tooth would miss most disease; six sites are charted.

q4-14.stem: You are probing the mesial of a premolar and reach the line angle. What should the probe do next?
choices: Go past the line angle, tilted slightly toward the area apical to the contact
Stay vertical and stop there, since the line angle is where the reading is taken
Be pushed straight through the contact horizontally
Tilt away from the contact and toward the facial surface of the tooth
why: Interproximal probing carries the probe past the line angle and under the contact, tilted slightly toward the area apical to it.
Stopping at the line angle is line-angle probing and misses the site under the contact.
A probe can't be forced horizontally through a contact; it goes under it with a slight tilt.
Tilting away from the contact misses the interproximal area; the tilt goes toward the area apical to the contact.

q4-15.stem: Between two instrument handles a tooth shifts about 1.5 mm, and it can't be pushed down into its socket. How do you grade it on the Miller scale?
choices: Class 2
Class 1
Class 3
Class 0
why: Movement over 1 mm but under 2 mm, with no vertical displacement, is Class 2.
Class 1 is under 1 mm, and this tooth moves more than that.
Class 3 needs vertical displacement (a depressible tooth), and this tooth has none.
Class 0 is physiologic mobility only, not movement over 1 mm.

q4-16.stem: What finding puts a mobile tooth into Miller Class 3?
choices: Severe faciolingual and/or mesiodistal movement, and the tooth is also depressible
Horizontal movement of less than 1 mm, felt between the two rigid instrument handles
Movement in the mesiodistal direction only, with none faciolingually at all
A widened PDL space on the radiograph, with no movement felt clinically
why: Class 3 is the only class with vertical displacement, added to severe horizontal movement.
Under 1 mm of horizontal movement is Class 1.
The classes grade how much the tooth moves and add vertical displacement for Class 3; mesiodistal-only movement isn't the definition.
Mobility is graded clinically; a widened PDL on a film alone isn't a Miller class.

q4-17.stem: You want to grade a tooth's static mobility. What do you use to move it?
choices: Two rigid instruments, one placed on each side
A finger on the root as the patient bites together
The tip of the probe pressed against the crown
The PDL width seen on a periapical radiograph
why: Static mobility is tested by moving the tooth between two rigid (blunt) instruments, one on either side.
A finger on the root during occlusion feels fremitus, which is mobility in function.
The probe is for pocket depth; static mobility needs two rigid instruments.
A widened PDL shows on a film, but a radiograph can't show how far a tooth moves.

q4-18.stem: A new patient's calculus is so heavy you can't chart the margins. What is the purpose of the full-mouth debridement (D4355) you schedule?
choices: To grossly remove plaque and calculus so the full evaluation and diagnosis can follow at a later visit
To finish definitive periodontal treatment in a single visit, in place of SRP for heavy calculus
To maintain a treated periodontitis patient who has fallen behind on recall appointments
To polish and remove stain once SRP is finished, billed after the root planing visits are done
why: D4355 is gross removal that makes the margins visible and chartable, so evaluation and diagnosis come later.
Debridement isn't definitive treatment, and it never replaces or is combined with SRP.
A treated periodontitis patient is seen under periodontal maintenance, not debridement.
Post-SRP polishing isn't what D4355 is for; debridement is gross removal before a diagnosis.

q4-19.stem: Which patient is the right fit for scaling in the presence of gingival inflammation (D4346)?
choices: No periodontitis, but swollen inflamed gingiva, generalized suprabony pockets and moderate-to-severe BOP
Active periodontitis with attachment loss, bone loss on the films and bleeding pockets on several teeth
A healthy patient here for a routine 6-month recall with very little or no calculus at all
A patient needing implant maintenance only, with cleaning around abutments and not natural teeth
why: D4346 is for inflamed, swollen gingiva with suprabony pockets and moderate-to-severe BOP, in a patient without periodontitis.
Periodontitis with attachment and bone loss calls for scaling and root planing.
A healthy patient with little calculus gets a routine prophylaxis.
D4346 is scaling of natural teeth with gingival inflammation, not an implant-maintenance code.

q4-21.stem: What does root planing actually do?
choices: Taking off rough, calculus-impregnated or contaminated cementum or surface dentin from the root
Taking supragingival stain and plaque off the enamel, finished with a rubber cup and paste
Smoothing the enamel and exposed root with pumice so plaque has less to hold on to later
Taking out the inflamed soft-tissue pocket lining so a new connective-tissue attachment forms
why: That is root planing: definitive removal of rough, calculus-impregnated or contaminated cementum or surface dentin.
Removing supragingival stain and plaque with a rubber cup is coronal polishing.
Smoothing enamel and root with pumice is polishing, not root planing.
That is gingival curettage, done on the soft-tissue pocket wall; root planing works on the root.

q4-23.stem: A patient asks whether splitting their scaling and root planing into several visits works better than doing it all in one. What does the evidence say?
choices: Several sessions offer no considerable advantage
Several sessions double the patient's gain in attachment
Doing it all in one session is contraindicated
Several sessions remove all residual calculus
why: The studies found no considerable advantage to spreading instrumentation across several sessions.
Attachment gain is not doubled; results are similar to one session.
One-session therapy isn't contraindicated; it works about as well as several.
Calculus left behind after several sessions stays for the same reasons it stays after one.

q4-24.stem: Comparing hand instruments with ultrasonic (mechanically driven) instrumentation, what did the studies find?
choices: No statistical difference in PD reduction or in CAL gain
Ultrasonic scaling produced significantly more CAL gain
Hand scaling produced significantly more PD reduction
Subgingival calculus came off only with the ultrasonic scaler
why: Hand and ultrasonic instrumentation showed no statistical difference in either PD reduction or CAL gain.
Ultrasonics didn't give significantly more CAL gain; the results were statistically similar.
Hand instruments didn't give significantly more PD reduction; the results were statistically similar.
Both hand and ultrasonic instruments remove subgingival calculus.

q4-25.stem: Researchers added subgingival irrigation with chlorhexidine, saline or peroxide to mechanical instrumentation. What was the result?
choices: It gave no extra improvement
It doubled the PD reduction
It was needed to suppress A.a.
It made root planing unneeded
why: The irrigants added no further benefit; the instrumentation does the work.
PD reduction wasn't doubled; irrigation added nothing measurable.
Irrigation isn't required to suppress A.a.; it added nothing beyond instrumentation.
Irrigation can't take the place of root planing; it added nothing to it.

q4-26.stem: After root debridement of a pocket 5 mm or deeper, what is the chance the debridement was inadequate?
choices: Roughly 65%
Roughly 5%
Roughly 25%
Roughly 90%
why: Greenstein (2000) puts inadequate debridement at about 65% in pockets of 5 mm or more.
This badly underestimates it; leftover calculus is the rule in deep pockets.
This is too low; the cited figure for pockets of 5 mm or more is about 65%.
This overstates it: a 5 mm pocket doesn't mean calculus is left every time.

q4-28.stem: A deep pocket probes shallower once SRP has healed. What accounts for most of that drop?
choices: Inflammation and edema subsiding, seen as recession
New bone forming at the base of the periodontal defect
New connective-tissue attachment on the freshly planed root
The tooth extruding as the inflamed tissue shrinks back
why: Most of the reduction is inflammation and edema going away (showing as recession), with some reattachment at the base.
Non-surgical therapy doesn't regenerate bone at the base of the defect.
Connective tissue does reattach at the pocket base by about 4-6 weeks, but that is the smaller share; most of the drop is inflammation and edema resolving at the margin.
Teeth don't extrude after SRP; the gingiva shrinks as inflammation settles.

q4-29.stem: You finished SRP today. Roughly when will the dentogingival junction be back in place?
choices: In 2-4 weeks
In 24 hours
In 9-12 months
In 6 months
why: The dentogingival junction is re-established about 2-4 weeks after SRP.
One day is far too soon for any epithelial or connective-tissue reattachment.
9-12 months is how long repair and maturation can go on, not when the junction is re-established.
Six months is too long; the junction is back in 2-4 weeks, with collagen maturing over 3-6 months.

q4-30.stem: At re-evaluation the tissues haven't responded to Phase I therapy. Each of these is a recommended next step EXCEPT:
choices: Moving to routine 6-month prophylaxis
Using antibiotics or antimicrobials
Repeating the non-surgical therapy
Referring for Phase II periodontal surgery
why: This is the exception: a patient whose Phase I failed needs more treatment, not a step down to routine 6-month prophys.
Antibiotics or antimicrobials are one of the listed next steps when Phase I fails.
Repeating non-surgical therapy is one of the listed options after a failure.
Phase II periodontal surgery is one of the listed options after a failure.

q4-31.stem: Looking at the working end, which feature tells you the instrument is a sickle scaler and not a curette?
choices: A pointed tip and a triangular cross-section
A rounded tip and a half-circle cross-section
A single cutting edge with a rounded back
A design made for deep subgingival work
why: The sickle design is a pointed tip with a triangular cross-section (and two cutting edges).
A rounded tip and half-circle cross-section are the curette design.
One cutting edge and a rounded back describe a Gracey curette, which spares the soft tissue.
Deep subgingival work belongs to curettes; a sickle reaches only a little below the margin.

q4-32.stem: Which set of features belongs to a Gracey curette?
choices: 70° blade angle, a single cutting edge, rounded back, lower shank parallel to the tooth's long axis
Two cutting edges and a pointed tip, used both above and below the gingival margin
Triangular cross-section, one cutting edge and pointed tip, used only above the margin on anteriors
90° blade angle, two cutting edges and a straight shank, used with a push stroke on any surface
why: That is the Gracey: 70° blade offset, one cutting edge, rounded back, lower shank parallel to the long axis.
Two cutting edges and a pointed tip are the sickle scaler.
A triangular cross-section and pointed tip are a sickle; a Gracey has a rounded back and toe.
A Gracey's blade sits at 70° with one cutting edge; two cutting edges for any surface describe a universal curette like the Columbia 13/14.

q4-33.stem: What blade angles do you use to slide a Gracey under the tissue and then work the root?
choices: Closed to insert into the sulcus or pocket, then opened to 70-80° against the root
90° to the root on insertion, and held at that same angle through the whole stroke
Open at 80° on insertion to clear the tissue, then closed to 0° against the root to work
45° on insertion, then worked with a push stroke down toward the base of the pocket
why: The blade goes in closed (near 0°) to slip under the tissue, then opens to a 70-80° working angle to engage deposits.
90° is too open to insert safely and too open to work the root well.
This reverses it: you insert closed and work open at 70-80°.
Curettes go in closed and work with a pull stroke, not a push stroke at 45°.

q4-34.stem: Per the deck, a sickle scaler can reach calculus to what depth below the gingival margin?
choices: About 1-2 mm
About 5-6 mm
To the base of any pocket
Not below it at all
why: The deck says 1-2 mm below the margin (Dr. Kaur said about 2-3 mm in class).
5-6 mm is deep subgingival work that needs curettes, not a sickle.
A sickle can't safely reach the bottom of a deep pocket; it is mainly supragingival.
A sickle can take calculus slightly below the margin, about 1-2 mm.

q4-37.stem: Once the calculus is off, you switch from scaling to root planing. How should your strokes change?
choices: They get longer and shaving, with lighter pressure
They get short and overlapping, with more pressure
They get shorter, with the same heavy pressure
They become light exploring strokes with no pressure
why: Root planing uses longer, shaving strokes and lighter pressure to leave the root smooth.
Short, overlapping, powerful strokes are scaling strokes that break calculus off.
Root planing strokes are longer and lighter, not shorter and heavy.
Light exploratory strokes map the pocket and find calculus; root planing is a working stroke.

q4-38.stem: Before working, you run the instrument through the pocket to learn its depth, shape and where the calculus is. What does that stroke look like?
choices: Light force with the instrument adapted, mapping depth, topography and calculus
A tight grasp and firm lateral pressure on the tooth to break the calculus loose
A rubber cup held at 90° with light, intermittent pressure on the enamel
A short pull with the lower third of a sickle blade under the ledge of calculus
why: That is the exploratory stroke: light force, instrument adapted, used to map depth, topography and calculus.
A tight grasp with firm lateral pressure is a working (scaling) stroke.
A rubber cup at 90° with light, intermittent pressure is polishing.
A short, powerful pull with the lower third of a sickle blade under the calculus ledge is a working scaling stroke.

q4-41.stem: At re-evaluation, residual calculus is found. Where is it most likely to have been left behind during SRP?
choices: At the CEJ, furcation entrances, line angles and the distals of posterior teeth
On the facials of the anterior teeth, where the gingiva is thin and roots show
On the occlusal surfaces of the molars, where calculus builds up the fastest
Only on the palatal surfaces of the upper incisors and nowhere else at all
why: These sites are hard to see and reach, so they are the ones most often missed.
Anterior facials are easy to see and reach, so they aren't the usual misses.
SRP is done on root surfaces, not occlusal surfaces.
Upper incisor palatals aren't the classic missed sites; distals, line angles, furcations and the CEJ are.

q4-43.stem: An instrument tray lists a UNC-15. What kind of instrument is that?
choices: A 15 mm periodontal probe
A curved furcation probe
A root-roughness explorer
A universal root curette
why: The UNC-15 is the periodontal probe, 15 mm long, used for probing depth and CAL on every tooth.
The curved furcation probe is the Nabers, with light and dark bands 3 mm apart.
Root roughness is checked with an explorer such as the ODU 11/12.
The universal curette is the Columbia 13/14; the UNC-15 is a probe.

q4-44.stem: A tooth is polished with pumice paste for 30 seconds. At most, how much enamel could that take off?
choices: About 4 µm
About 40 µm
About 0.4 mm
No enamel
why: Thirty seconds of pumice can remove up to 4 µm, the fluoride-rich outer layer.
This is ten times the cited 4 µm.
0.4 mm (400 µm) is a hundred times the cited figure.
Pumice is abrasive and does remove enamel, up to 4 µm in 30 seconds.

q4-46.stem: You want to polish while losing as little enamel and soft tissue as possible. Which approach is taught?
choices: Low-abrasion paste, slow speed, little heat, cup at 90° with light intermittent pressure
Coarse paste at high speed with steady heavy pressure so stain comes off in one pass
Pumice for a full 2 minutes per tooth with the cup held flat and pressed firmly on
Polishing below the margin to the base of the pocket with a pointed rubber cup
why: Low-abrasion paste, slow speed, minimal heat and a cup at 90° with light, intermittent pressure limit enamel and tissue loss.
Coarse paste, high speed and heavy pressure take off more enamel and build heat, the opposite of what's taught.
Two minutes of pumice per tooth under heavy pressure can strip sulcular epithelium and remove enamel.
Polishing isn't carried subgingivally to the pocket base; it is selective and coronal.

q4-47.stem: Polishing has costs, but which of these is a reason that justifies doing it?
choices: Clearing extrinsic stain before sealants or fluoride, and patient satisfaction
Taking off subgingival calculus that was left on the root after the curette
Lowering probing depth by smoothing the soft-tissue side of the pocket wall
Taking off the endotoxin that is bound to the cementum on the root surface
why: Clearing extrinsic stain before sealants or fluoride, and pleasing the patient, are the valid reasons to polish.
Polishing can't remove subgingival calculus; curettes or ultrasonics do that.
Polishing has no effect on the soft-tissue pocket wall or on probing depth.
Polishing doesn't deal with root-bound endotoxin; root instrumentation does.

q4-52.stem: How do you find out whether your scaling and root planing in Phase I was done well?
choices: Explore the root as you work; at re-evaluation, look for less erythema, edema and BOP
Take a same-day radiograph and compare interproximal calculus with the pre-op film
Look for new bone fill at one week, since good root planing shows bone gain by then
Ask about sensitivity afterward, because smooth, clean roots are always sensitive
why: Explore the root during the session, then judge the tissue response (less erythema, edema and BOP) at re-evaluation.
Radiographs show small deposits poorly and can't confirm clean roots on the same day.
SRP doesn't produce radiographic bone fill, and certainly not in a week.
Sensitivity is a possible side effect, not a measure of how well you root planed.

q4-L01.stem: Which of these diagnoses can never be made, because the terms contradict each other?
choices: Periodontitis on an intact periodontium
Gingivitis on a reduced periodontium
Health on a reduced periodontium
Gingivitis on an intact periodontium
why: Periodontitis always includes bone loss, so the periodontium can't be intact.
This is a real diagnosis, as in the post-ortho extraction case.
This is a real diagnosis, for example a stable treated patient.
This is ordinary gingivitis, a real diagnosis.

q4-L02.stem: For a plaque score, you sweep the probe about 1 mm into each sulcus, marking 1 if plaque comes out and 0 if not. What information does that give you?
choices: Only whether plaque is present or absent
How much plaque sits at each site
How thick the plaque is in the gingival third
The probing depth at each of the sites
why: A 1-or-0 score at each site tells you only whether plaque is there.
A 1 or 0 doesn't measure amount; quantifying every site would take too much chair time.
Thickness in the gingival third comes from a quantified index, which this method isn't.
Probing depth is read at the pocket base, not from a 1 mm sweep into the sulcus.

q4-L03.stem: While charting the upper left, you notice bleeding at some upper-right sites that looked dry when you probed them. What do you record for those sites?
choices: Bleeding (1)
No bleeding (0), since bleeding must be immediate
Nothing yet; re-probe them next visit
Suppuration
why: Bleeding that shows up late still counts as BOP, so they're scored 1.
BOP doesn't have to appear right away; delayed bleeding counts.
No need to wait for the next visit; the delayed bleeding is recorded now.
Suppuration means pus, a different finding; these sites are bleeding.

q4-L04.stem: Two patients have similar periodontitis, but one smokes heavily. What difference would you expect in the smoker's gingiva?
choices: Paler and more cyanotic, with inflammation masked by nicotine's vasoconstriction
More edema and bleeding, since nicotine raises blood flow to the gingiva
Bulbous interdental overgrowth, like that seen with calcium channel blockers
No difference, since smoking alters bone levels but not how gingiva looks
why: Nicotine constricts vessels and masks inflammation, so the smoker's gingiva looks less inflamed and more cyanotic.
Nicotine lowers blood flow, so the tissue looks less edematous and hemorrhagic, not more.
Bulbous interdental overgrowth is drug-induced (calcium channel blockers), not a smoker's look.
Smoking does change the gingiva's appearance: it hides the signs of inflammation.

q4-L05.stem: A patient on blood pressure medication shows bulbous, mostly interdental gingival enlargement, worse on the buccal/labial than the lingual/palatal. Which drug on their list is the likely cause?
choices: Amlodipine
Metformin
Atorvastatin
Lisinopril
why: This calcium channel blocker is a classic cause of drug-induced gingival overgrowth.
This diabetes drug isn't linked to gingival overgrowth.
This statin doesn't cause gingival overgrowth.
This is an ACE inhibitor; the antihypertensives classically behind overgrowth are calcium channel blockers.

q4-L06.stem: The probe reads 5 mm at a site where the margin covers the CEJ by 3 mm (recession of −3 mm). What attachment level do you chart?
choices: 2 mm
5 mm
8 mm
3 mm
why: PD plus GR: 5 + (−3) = 2 mm.
This is only the probing depth; it ignores the negative recession and over-diagnoses.
This adds the 3 as positive recession, but the margin is coronal to the CEJ, so it is −3.
This is only the recession value, not the attachment level.

q4-L07.stem: On a healthy, intact periodontium, what is the relationship between a site's probing depth and its CAL?
choices: They differ, since the gingival margin lies coronal to the CEJ
They match, since the margin and the CEJ sit at the same level
CAL always exceeds PD, because some attachment loss is normal
CAL can't be recorded, since the covered CEJ can't be located
why: In health the margin sits coronal to the CEJ, so recession is negative and PD isn't equal to CAL.
In health the margin is coronal to the CEJ, not level with it, so they don't match.
Attachment loss isn't part of health; in health CAL is smaller than PD.
CAL can be measured in health by feeling for the CEJ with the probe.

q4-L08.stem: At a site where the margin covers the CEJ, a student leaves recession empty in Salud, or enters 0 without checking. What does Salud do with that site?
choices: Sets CAL equal to PD, so it over-diagnoses
Estimates recession from the radiograph
Flags the site and refuses to save the chart
Records the CAL at that site as zero
why: An empty field or a reflexive 0 makes Salud set CAL = PD, so the site shows more attachment loss than it has.
Salud isn't linked to the radiograph; it uses only what you type in.
Salud doesn't block saving; it silently records CAL as PD.
Salud treats the recession as zero, not the CAL, so CAL comes out equal to PD.

q4-L09.stem: The gingival margin hides the CEJ. How do you get the negative recession value for that site?
choices: Probe to the base, slowly withdraw until the CEJ is felt, and read what is still under the margin
Find the bone crest on a bitewing, then subtract the probing depth from that bone-level reading
Run a Nabers probe horizontally along the margin and note the first spot where it catches
Chart recession as zero, because a CEJ you can't see means the margin still sits coronal to it
why: Go to the pocket base, withdraw slowly until the CEJ is felt, and the millimeters still under the margin are the negative recession.
