A bitewing shows the bone crest, not the clinical CEJ-to-margin distance, so it can't give recession.
The Nabers probe is for furcations, not for locating the CEJ under the margin.
A hidden CEJ means negative recession, not zero; charting 0 makes CAL equal PD and over-diagnoses.

q4-L10.stem: Several things can hide the CEJ when you try to read negative recession. Which one is a physiologic variant, not a disease process?
choices: Altered passive eruption
Drug-induced gingival overgrowth
Gingival inflammation
Subgingival calculus
why: It keeps the margin coronal to the CEJ, but it is physiologic, not disease.
Drug-induced overgrowth also hides the CEJ, but it is pathologic.
Inflammation also hides the CEJ, but it is pathologic.
Calculus can feel like a CEJ, but it is a pathologic deposit, not a physiologic variant.

q4-L12.stem: Full-mouth debridement has a single indication. Which situation is it?
choices: Deposits so heavy the gingival margin can't be seen or explored for charting
Moderate periodontitis that you'd like to finish completely in one appointment
A maintenance patient with heavy stain and plaque that needs polishing first
Some subgingival calculus that turned up during a routine adult prophylaxis
why: This is the one indication: calculus hides the margin so fully that it can't be seen or explored, and no numbers can be recorded.
Debridement isn't therapeutic, and it never stands in for SRP or gets combined with it to treat periodontitis.
A maintenance visit handles stain and plaque; debridement is reserved for margins you can't chart.
Shallow subgingival calculus comes off during a prophylaxis; only calculus that hides the margin calls for debridement.

choices: It has a full-mouth code and nothing else
Each quadrant has its own debridement code
A half-mouth version can be billed with SRP
It's billed at the same visit as the perio exam
why: Correct: the only debridement code is the full-mouth one (D4355).
Quadrant codes exist for SRP, not for debridement.
Debridement is never billed together with SRP, and there is no half-mouth code.
Insurance won't cover debridement and a periodontal exam on the same visit.

q4-L15.stem: Which Glickman furcation class has the best outlook for regeneration?
choices: Class II
Class I
Class III
Class IV
why: The Class II cul-de-sac has depth plus a bony wall on the far side, so it can contain a graft.
A Class I is only a catch at the entrance and usually doesn't need regeneration.
A Class III goes all the way through, leaving no wall to hold a graft.
A Class IV is through-and-through and visible, so nothing contains a graft.

q4-L16.stem: A molar has a Class IV furcation. What makes close monitoring at each maintenance appointment necessary?
choices: Its exposed root can get root caries, and furcation caries leaves the tooth hopeless
It reverts to Class II as the tissue heals, so its class must be rechecked every visit
It is the class that regenerates best, so you watch for the right moment to place a graft
No hygiene aid can reach it, so it needs professional debridement at every visit
why: The exposed root surfaces of a Class IV are at risk for root caries, and caries in the furcation makes the tooth hopeless.
A Class IV doesn't revert to Class II when tissue heals.
Class II is the class most amenable to regeneration; a Class IV has no wall to contain a graft.
The patient can clean a Class IV with interdental aids or a water flosser.

q4-L17.stem: You are using a Nabers probe, whose light and dark bands are 3 mm apart. Which finding makes a furcation Glickman Class I?
choices: The tip only catches at the furcation entrance
The tip goes in no more than 3 mm
The tip goes in and stops against bone on the far side
The tip passes all the way through between the roots
why: An incipient Class I is just a catch; Glickman grades by how far the probe goes, not by a millimeter value.
The bands are a visual aid, but Glickman isn't a millimeter scale, so Class I isn't '3 mm or less'.
Going in and meeting a bony wall on the other side is Class II, the cul-de-sac.
Passing through between the roots is Class III, through-and-through.

q4-L18.stem: During the periodontal exam, what does the rolling technique help you find?
choices: Where the mucogingival junction is, giving keratinized tissue width
Where a furcation entrance is, as the probe rolls around the root
Whether disclosing solution has spread evenly over all the teeth
How mobile the tooth is when it's rolled between two handles
why: The mucosa stops rolling at the mucogingival junction, which marks the width of keratinized tissue.
Furcation entrances are located with the Nabers probe, not the rolling technique.
Disclosing solution comes from a chewed tablet and a brief rinse and has nothing to do with the mucogingival exam.
Mobility is checked between two rigid instruments; the tooth isn't rolled.

choices: A vibration felt by a finger on the tooth as the patient bites together
Static movement tested by pushing between two rigid instrument handles
A widened PDL space that shows up on a periapical radiograph
A tooth that can be pushed down into its socket under pressure
why: Fremitus is mobility in function: a finger on the root feels for vibration as the patient brings the teeth together.
Static mobility between two rigid instruments is the Miller mobility test, not fremitus.
A widened PDL space is a radiographic finding; fremitus is palpated.
A tooth depressible in its socket is Miller Class 3, ready for extraction, not fremitus.

q4-L20.stem: A patient has lost the posterior teeth, and the maxillary premolars test positive for fremitus. What best explains it?
choices: With no posterior support, the premolars carry the load meant for molars
Drug-induced gingival overgrowth has pushed the premolars out of their usual contacts
Altered passive eruption left short clinical crowns that take up the extra occlusal load
Root caries has weakened the premolar roots, so normal chewing produces fremitus
why: Without posterior support the premolars take molar loads, which causes occlusal trauma felt as fremitus.
Overgrowth changes the tissue, not the occlusal load, so it doesn't cause fremitus.
Altered passive eruption affects where the tissue sits, not the occlusal forces behind fremitus.
Root caries isn't the cause here; the premolars are overloaded by the missing posterior support.

q4-L21.stem: You notice erosion, a wear pattern and signs of clenching during the perio exam. Where do these findings go?
choices: In the notes section; the perio chart has nowhere to put them
In the mobility row, written beside each tooth's Miller class
In the furcation column, written beside each molar's Glickman class
Nowhere in the perio exam; they belong only on the restorative chart
why: The perio chart has no field for wear, erosion or parafunction, so they're written in the notes.
The mobility row is for Miller classes only.
The furcation column is for furcation classes only.
Occlusal findings belong in the perio exam's notes because they affect perio treatment.

q4-L22.stem: Before starting scaling and root planing, which record is most useful to keep on the screen?
choices: The radiographs, not the probing chart
The probing chart, to find the deepest pockets
Only the patient's medical history
None; rely on touch alone
why: The radiographs show the calculus, PA lesions and root anatomy you'll encounter.
The instrument finds the pocket and its base is your limit, so you don't need the chart to locate deep pockets.
The medical history matters, but it doesn't guide your instrument the way the radiographs do.
Working by touch alone throws away the radiographic map of calculus and root anatomy.

q4-L23.stem: About how much of the tissue destruction in periodontitis comes from the host's own response?
choices: About 75%
About 25%
About 50%
Nearly 100%
why: About 75% of the destruction comes from the host's inflammatory mediators and osteoclasts.
About 25% is the bacteria's share, not the host's.
An even split isn't the class figure, which is about 75% host and 25% bacteria.
Bacteria account for about 25%, so the host isn't responsible for nearly all of it.

q4-L24.stem: According to the host-bacteria model, which pairing correctly names what starts periodontitis and what makes it progress?
choices: Started by plaque bacteria; progressed by the host response
Started by the host response; progressed by plaque bacteria
Started by calculus; progressed by the patient's smoking
Started by genetics; progressed by the plaque bacteria
why: Plaque bacteria initiate the disease, and the host's immune response drives its progression.
This flips the model: the bacteria initiate it and the host response drives progression.
Calculus retains plaque and smoking is a risk factor; neither is the initiator or the driver in this model.
Genetics adds risk, but bacteria initiate and the host response drives progression.

q4-L28.stem: Phase I re-evaluation is scheduled 4-6 weeks after SRP rather than at 3 months. What justifies the shorter wait?
choices: PD reduction peaks by 4-6 weeks, so a longer wait gains nothing
Collagen matures only at 3 months, so earlier probing tears new attachment
Insurance demands it at 4-6 weeks, though healing goes on for months
Calculus re-forms after about 6 weeks, so pockets would look deeper later
why: The maximum probing-depth reduction has happened by 4-6 weeks; waiting 3 months adds nothing and delays decisions.
Probing at 4-6 weeks doesn't tear the new attachment; re-evaluation is done routinely then.
The reason is biologic, the maximum reduction by 4-6 weeks, not an insurance rule.
Calculus re-forming isn't the reason; the PD reduction has simply leveled off by 4-6 weeks.

q4-L29.stem: Relative to the gingival margin, where does scaling work?
choices: Both above and below it
Above it only; root planing covers below
Below it only, on the root surfaces
Above it, unless the pocket is over 3 mm
why: Scaling removes deposits from tooth and root surfaces both supragingivally and subgingivally.
Scaling isn't limited to above the margin; it works both above and below, and root planing is done alongside it.
Working only below the margin, on root surfaces, describes root planing, not scaling.
No pocket depth limits scaling to above the margin; it works on surfaces above and below.

q4-L30.stem: A patient with no history of periodontitis has normal sulci, but you find 1-2 mm of calculus under the margin. Which procedure fits?
choices: Prophylaxis
Periodontal maintenance
Scaling and root planing
Full-mouth debridement
why: With no periodontitis and normal sulci, a prophylaxis is right, even with some subgingival calculus.
Periodontal maintenance is only for patients who have already been treated for periodontitis.
SRP treats periodontitis, and subgingival calculus alone doesn't mean periodontitis.
Debridement is only for when the margin can't be seen or charted.

q4-L31.stem: At recall, a patient previously treated for periodontitis has mostly 1-3 mm sites, a few 4 mm sites that don't bleed, one 5 mm site, good home care and no radiographic progression. What is the right plan?
choices: Keep up periodontal maintenance, with localized SRP on the non-responding site as part of it
Redo full-mouth SRP, because any 4-5 mm site left over means Phase I failed and must be repeated
Move to a routine prophylaxis, since most sites are 1-3 mm and none bleed on probing anymore
Refer for flap surgery right away, since the single 5 mm site shows the disease is progressing
why: The patient is stable, so maintenance continues, and maintenance includes localized SRP on the one non-responding site.
A few non-bleeding 4s and one 5 mm site don't mean Phase I failed; repeating full-mouth SRP is overtreatment.
A patient treated for periodontitis is never moved back down to a prophylaxis.
One 5 mm site with no bleeding and no radiographic progression doesn't call for flap surgery.

q4-L32.stem: A young patient with no periodontitis history had premolars removed for orthodontics, leaving some bone loss and tipping. Heavy plaque and calculus now cause generalized inflammation. How should this be diagnosed?
choices: Generalized gingival inflammation on a reduced periodontium (non-periodontitis patient)
Stage 2 periodontitis, since the extraction sites already show radiographic bone loss
Gingival health on an intact periodontium, because periodontitis was never present
Necrotizing periodontitis, given widespread inflammation in a young, healthy patient
why: No periodontitis history and bone loss from the extractions: this is gingival inflammation on a reduced periodontium in a non-periodontitis patient.
Bone loss from orthodontic extractions isn't periodontitis, so it can't be staged.
There is generalized inflammation and some bone loss, so it is neither health nor an intact periodontium.
Necrotizing disease needs necrotic, painful papillae; inflammation from heavy plaque isn't that.

q4-L33.stem: You know you removed every deposit during SRP, yet at the Phase I evaluation the pockets and inflammation remain. What is most likely to make a difference now?
choices: Better home care by the patient
Another round of full-mouth SRP
A second session of irrigation
Extracting the teeth right away
why: The roots are already clean, so persistent disease points to home care; improving oral hygiene helps most.
Repeating SRP on roots that are already clean won't accomplish anything more.
Irrigation adds nothing to instrumentation, so another round won't help.
Extraction isn't the answer to persistent inflammation after thorough SRP.

q4-L34.stem: The clinic's piezoelectric ultrasonic can do all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Plane the root
Remove subgingival deposits
Remove gross calculus
Lavage the pocket
why: This is the exception: the piezo can't leave a planed, smooth root; hand instruments do that.
The ultrasonic can remove deposits below the gingival margin.
The ultrasonic can remove gross calculus.
The ultrasonic's water flushes (lavages) the pocket.

q4-L36.stem: What design feature makes a Gracey curette the safer choice below the gum line compared with a scaler?
choices: Only one side of its blade cuts, so the side against soft tissue stays safe
It is shorter, so it can't reach the pocket base and harm the attachment there
Its pointed tip slides more easily under the tissue without tearing it apart
It is used with a push stroke, which moves calculus away from the soft tissue
why: A Gracey has a single cutting edge, so the side facing the soft tissue doesn't cut it.
Curettes are designed to reach the pocket base; length isn't what makes them safe.
Curettes have a rounded toe; the pointed tip belongs to the sickle, which is less safe subgingivally.
Curettes are used with a pull stroke, not a push stroke.

q4-L37.stem: Instruments on your kit are marked either 'SG' or 'SC'. Which instrument does SC mark?
choices: The kit's one universal curette, with cutting edges on both sides
An area-specific Gracey curette that cuts on only one side of the blade
A sickle scaler with a pointed tip, used only above the gingival margin
A probe marked in millimeters, used to chart probing depth around each tooth
why: SC marks the single universal curette, which has a blade on both sides.
The site-specific Gracey curettes are the ones marked SG, not SC.
SC isn't a sickle scaler; it marks the universal curette.
SC marks a curette, not a calibrated probe.

q4-L38.stem: What do you check with the periodontal explorer in your exam kit?
choices: Whether roots are smooth after therapy, with no catch or roughness
Whether pits and fissures have occlusal caries before restorative planning
How deep the pockets are when no calibrated probe is in the exam kit
How far the tip passes between molar roots, to classify the furcation
why: The periodontal explorer is a tactile check for smooth roots; a catch or roughness means calculus is still there.
Checking pits and fissures for caries is the caries explorer's job.
Probing depth is measured with the calibrated probe, not an explorer.
Furcations are classified with the Nabers probe.

q4-L39.stem: To get a correct mesiobuccal probing reading on a molar, where should the probe go?
choices: Beyond the line angle, under the contact area
Right at the mesiobuccal line angle
At the middle of the buccal surface
Pressed firmly through the contact
why: Interproximal readings are taken past the line angle, under the contact area.
Stopping at the line angle is line-angle probing and misses the interproximal site.
Mid-buccal is a separate probing site from the mesiobuccal.
The probe goes under the contact, not forced through it.

q4-L42.stem: Smokers and patients with uncontrolled diabetes are more likely to show 'failure of therapy' even after thorough SRP. Why?
choices: The host response governs healing too, so short- and long-term results are worse
They build calculus more quickly, so deposits come back before the tissue has time to heal
Ultrasonic tips work poorly on their roots, so far less calculus comes off during SRP
Their pockets are always shallower, leaving less probing-depth reduction to be gained
why: The host response shapes healing as well as disease, so smokers and diabetics heal more poorly after SRP.
Faster calculus formation isn't the reason taught; the impaired host response is.
Ultrasonic tips work the same on their roots; what differs is the host response.
Their pockets aren't shallower; the problem is poorer healing, not less to gain.

q1-P01.stem: Using the findings in the box, how should this patient's periodontal condition be classified?
choices: Localized Stage 2 Grade B periodontitis
Localized Stage 2 Grade A periodontitis
Localized Stage 3 Grade B periodontitis
Generalized gingivitis
why: 4 mm of CAL with bone loss in the coronal third is Stage 2; 25 / 45 is about 0.56, Grade B; two sites make it localized.
Grade A would need a ratio below 0.25, and hers is about 0.56, which is Grade B.
Stage 3 would need 5 mm or more of CAL, middle-third bone loss or a complexity trigger, and she has none of them.
She has lost attachment and bone, so this is periodontitis rather than gingivitis.

q1-P05.stem: Looking at each finding in the box separately, which ones would be enough by themselves to put this case in Stage 3 or 4? Select all that apply.
choices: The 4 mm angular defect at #19 mesial
The Class II furcation at #30
The loss of #3 to periodontitis
The 5 mm pocket at #14 mesial
Bleeding on probing at 40%
Having smoked until 10 years ago
why: An angular (vertical) defect of 3 mm or more automatically puts a case in Stage 3 or 4.
A Class II or III furcation automatically puts a case in Stage 3 or 4.
Any tooth lost because of periodontitis automatically puts a case in Stage 3 or 4.
A pocket depth on its own doesn't set a stage; CAL and the complexity factors do.
Bleeding shows inflammation but has no role in staging.
A former smoker gets no modifier, and smoking acts on the grade, not the stage.

q2-P01.stem: For the surgery planned in the patient box, which of these choices are appropriate? Select all that apply.
choices: Raising a full-thickness (mucoperiosteal) flap
A trapezoidal outline, with a vertical release on each side
Closing over the graft with slow-resorbing poly-glycolic acid (PGA)
Raising a split-thickness flap
Closing over the graft with chromic gut
why: Belongs: a bone graft needs the bone exposed, so the flap is full thickness.
Belongs: a major augmentation needs two vertical releases so the flap can advance passively and close without tension.
Belongs: PGA lasts the longest of the resorbables (55-70 days), and the chart lists it for ridge and sinus augmentation (non-resorbable PTFE would also work).
Doesn't belong: split thickness leaves the periosteum on the bone, so there is no exposed bone to graft on.
Doesn't belong: chromic gut is weak and gone in 7-10 days, too early for a graft closure.

q3-P01.stem: Based on this patient's history and today's findings, how often should he return for periodontal maintenance?
choices: About every 3 months
About every 6 months
About every 12 months
Not at all, now that pockets are ≤4 mm
why: Right: a treated Stage 3 Grade C patient who still smokes a pack a day is high risk, and pathogens repopulate in about 9-11 weeks.
Six months suits low-risk patients; pathogens come back in about 9-11 weeks, long before 6 months.
A 12-month gap would leave a high-risk patient unsupervised far too long.
Once periodontitis, always at risk; a treated patient needs maintenance for life.

q3-P02.stem: Dr. Geisinger walked the class through this case. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Stage 3 Grade C, localized, molar-incisor pattern
Stage 2 Grade B, generalized, mostly horizontal loss
Stage 2 Grade A, localized, molar-incisor pattern
Stage 4 Grade C, localized, molar-incisor pattern
why: Right: 8-11 mm pockets over deep vertical defects are Stage 3; only the first molars and #14 are involved, a localized molar-incisor pattern; and this much loss at 13 is rapid, Grade C.
Only the first molars and #14 are affected, so it's localized; the films show deep vertical defects, not mostly horizontal loss; and loss this fast at 13 is Grade C.
8-11 mm pockets over deep vertical defects go beyond Stage 2, and so much loss with little plaque at 13 means rapid progression, Grade C, not A.
Nothing here adds Stage 4's complexity, such as teeth lost to periodontitis or a need for complex rehabilitation, so it stays Stage 3.

q4-P04.stem: Given today's findings, how should you proceed?
choices: Remove the residual calculus; recheck in 2 weeks
Send her for osseous surgery today
Do full-mouth SRP again
Wait another 3 months for more pocket reduction
why: The residual calculus explains the two persistent sites, so remove it and re-evaluate in two weeks.
Surgery comes up only after the cause, the residual calculus, is removed and the sites are re-evaluated.
Most sites responded; only two need attention, so a full-mouth repeat isn't needed.
The maximum PD reduction is reached by 4-6 weeks; a longer wait adds nothing.

q4-P05.stem: Select every statement that is true for this patient.
choices: Vasoconstriction from nicotine can hide inflammation, so the tissue looks paler and cyanotic
Even with excellent SRP, his short- and long-term outcome may be worse
His uncontrolled diabetes tends to make inflammation look more pronounced
Because his tissue is pale, recording BOP is unnecessary
Additional rounds of SRP will compensate for his poorer healing
why: True: nicotine's vasoconstriction masks inflammation, producing the paler, cyanotic look he has.
True: the host response shapes healing too, so a smoker with uncontrolled diabetes may do worse short- and long-term even after excellent SRP.
True: uncontrolled diabetes exaggerates inflammation, the opposite of what smoking does.
False: BOP is always recorded; in a smoker, pale tissue hides inflammation rather than ruling it out.
False: once all deposits are removed, more SRP won't help; improving his oral hygiene is what does.

q1-M01.stem: Which of these would push a periodontitis case into Grade C even when the bone-loss/age ratio says otherwise? Select all that apply.
choices: Smoking at least 10 cigarettes a day
An HbA1c of 7% or more
Never having smoked
Diabetes controlled to an HbA1c of 6%
Being older than 65
why: Belongs: smoking 10 or more a day is a modifier that moves the case to Grade C.
Belongs: in a diabetic patient, an HbA1c of 7% or more is a modifier that moves the case to Grade C.
Doesn't belong: modifiers only raise a grade; not smoking never moves a case to C, or down.
Doesn't belong: an HbA1c under 7% is below the Grade C cutoff, so this well-controlled diabetes doesn't force C.
Doesn't belong: age is part of the bone-loss/age ratio itself, not a separate modifier.

q1-M02.stem: A patient has plaque-induced gingivitis. Which of these would you expect to be true? Select all that apply.
choices: Pockets may probe 4-5 mm deep
The gingiva bleeds on probing
No attachment or bone has been lost
Controlling plaque reverses it
Any bone loss stays in the coronal third
why: Belongs: swollen gingiva can make 4-5 mm pseudopockets without any attachment loss.
Belongs: bleeding on probing is the hallmark of plaque-induced gingivitis (the course uses a 10% full-mouth threshold).
Belongs: gingivitis stays within the gingiva, so attachment and bone are not lost.
Belongs: gingivitis goes away once plaque is controlled, which is what separates it from periodontitis.
Doesn't belong: any bone loss at all, even in the coronal third, makes the case periodontitis instead.

q1-M03.stem: Which of these steps are part of the non-surgical phase (Phase I) of treatment? Select all that apply.
choices: Coaching the patient on oral hygiene
Treating carious lesions
Fixing restoration margins that trap plaque
Resective osseous surgery
Seating the definitive crowns
why: Belongs: hygiene instruction is the heart of Phase I, which removes the causes of disease.
Belongs: caries control is part of Phase I, the item the lecture said never to forget.
Belongs: a margin that holds plaque is a local cause, so correcting it is Phase I.
Doesn't belong: resective osseous surgery is Phase II, the surgical phase.
Doesn't belong: final crowns are Phase III (restorative) and wait until periodontal therapy is complete.

q2-M01.stem: Which of these suture materials dissolve in the body on their own, with no removal needed? Select all that apply.
choices: Chromic gut
PGA, poly-glycolic acid
PGCL, poly(glycolide-co-caprolactone)
Silk
PTFE
Polypropylene
why: Belongs: chromic gut resorbs, in about 7-10 days.
Belongs: PGA resorbs, over about 55-70 days.
Belongs: PGCL resorbs, over about 22-55 days.
Doesn't belong: silk never resorbs and must be taken out (its braid also wicks plaque).
Doesn't belong: PTFE is a non-resorbable monofilament that has to come out.
Doesn't belong: polypropylene is a non-resorbable monofilament that has to come out.

q2-M02.stem: A student is planning incisions for a flap. Which of these plans agree with the surgical principles from the course? Select all that apply.
choices: Cut with one firm, continuous stroke
Put each vertical incision at the tooth's line angle
Keep the incision at a distance from the bony defect
Run the vertical incision through the center of the papilla
Run the vertical incision down the center of the facial surface
why: Belongs: one firm, continuous stroke rather than several tentative passes is the first principle.
Belongs: verticals are placed at the line angle of the tooth.
Belongs: the incision stays away from the lesion or defect, not right over it.
Doesn't belong: cutting through the middle of the papilla can kill it and leave a black triangle.
Doesn't belong: a vertical in the middle of the facial surface leads to recession.

q2-M03.stem: For which of these procedures is the periosteum lifted with the flap? Select all that apply.
choices: Placing an implant
Augmenting bone, a ridge or a sinus
Crown lengthening or osseous surgery
Grafting soft tissue
why: Belongs: an implant needs the bone exposed, so the flap is full thickness.
Belongs: bone, ridge and sinus augmentation all need bare bone, so the flap is full thickness.
Belongs: crown lengthening and osseous surgery reshape bone, so the periosteum comes up with the flap.
Doesn't belong: soft-tissue grafting is split thickness, leaving the periosteum as a vascular bed for the graft.

q3-M01.stem: A clinician is filling out a UniFe risk score. Which of these items will she score? Select all that apply.
choices: Cigarettes smoked per day
HbA1c, for diabetic status
Bone loss relative to age
The plaque index
How many furcations there are
why: Scored: cigarettes a day is one of UniFe's five inputs.
Scored: HbA1c (diabetic status) is one of UniFe's five inputs.
Scored: the bone-loss/age ratio is one of UniFe's five inputs.
Not scored: UniFe counts bleeding (BOP %), not plaque; the plaque index is the most common wrong pick.
Not scored: furcations aren't an input; UniFe counts pockets of 5 mm or more instead.

q3-M02.stem: Which of these are true of the Kwok & Caton prognosis system? Select all that apply.
choices: Its question is whether periodontal stability is achievable
It can only be used as a therapeutic prognosis
Its questionable category is the middle of the scale
It suits patients with complex medical histories
It is used for molars and nothing else
It gives a number computed from smoking and A1c
why: True: Kwok & Caton bases its prognosis on whether periodontal stability can be achieved.
True: it judges the outcome of treatment, so it is therapeutic only.
True: questionable sits in the middle, between favorable and unfavorable.
True: quitting smoking or vaping and controlling the A1c become part of the treatment it judges, so it suits medically complex patients.
False: molars only describes Miller & McEntire, not Kwok & Caton.
False: numeric scoring from factors like smoking describes Miller & McEntire, not Kwok & Caton.

q3-M03.stem: P4 medicine is named for four words starting with P. Which of these are among them? Select all that apply.
choices: Personalized care
Preventive care
Predictive care
Participatory care
Palliative care
Prescriptive care
why: One of them: personalized is one of the four P's.
One of them: preventive is one of the four P's.
One of them: predictive is one of the four P's.
One of them: participatory is one of the four P's; the patient takes part in their own care.
Not one of them: palliative care isn't a P of P4 medicine.
Not one of them: prescriptive sounds like it fits but isn't a P; P4 is set against one-size-fits-all medicine.

q4-M01.stem: You are trying to locate the CEJ to measure negative recession. Which of these can get in the way? Select all that apply.
choices: Severe gingival inflammation
Gingival overgrowth caused by a drug
Altered passive eruption
Calculus or a restoration margin
True (positive) recession
Healthy tissue where the CEJ is visible
why: Yes: swollen, inflamed tissue covers the CEJ and makes it hard to feel (a pathologic cause).
Yes: drug-induced overgrowth covers the CEJ with extra tissue (a pathologic cause).
Yes: in altered passive eruption the gingiva stays over the CEJ (a physiologic cause).
Yes: calculus or a restorative margin can feel like the CEJ and mislead the probe.
No: with true recession the margin sits apical to the CEJ, so the CEJ is exposed rather than hidden.
No: when healthy tissue leaves the CEJ visible, it is easy to find.

q4-M02.stem: What is scaling and root planing meant to achieve? Select all that apply.
choices: Less inflammation
A flora shift from gram-negative toward gram-positive
Halting disease progression
Regaining lost bone and attachment
Getting rid of the pocket (its main rationale)
why: Yes: removing plaque and calculus reduces inflammation.
Yes: SRP shifts the flora away from gram-negative anaerobes toward a gram-positive, health-associated flora.
Yes: SRP aims to arrest disease progression.
No: SRP doesn't restore lost bone or attachment; it stops further loss.
No: pocket elimination isn't the rationale for SRP, even though probing depth does decrease.

q4-M03.stem: Probing depths drop after SRP. Which changes account for that drop? Select all that apply.
choices: The margin receding as swelling goes down
Reattachment of the junctional epithelium
Reattachment of connective tissue
Bone regrowing into the defect
The tooth extruding
why: Yes: as edema resolves the margin moves apically, and that extra recession is part of the PD drop.
Yes: the junctional epithelium reattaches to the clean root at the pocket base in about 7-10 days.
Yes: connective tissue reattaches to the root in about 4-6 weeks, adding to the reduction.
No: SRP doesn't regrow bone; bone fill needs regenerative therapy.
No: the tooth doesn't extrude after SRP; the PD drops from recession and reattachment.

q4-M04.stem: Select every correct statement about full-mouth debridement.
choices: It does not treat the disease
Its only indication is a gingival margin you can't see or explore
It has a full-mouth code and no other
It is never done together with SRP
Each quadrant can be billed separately
Insurance covers it along with a periodontal exam on the same visit
why: Correct: debridement isn't therapeutic; it clears heavy deposits so a proper exam can follow.
Correct: it's indicated when deposits keep you from seeing or exploring the gingival margin.
Correct: only a full-mouth code exists, with no quadrant or half-mouth version.
Correct: it is never combined with SRP; definitive therapy comes after the exam.
Incorrect: debridement has no quadrant code; it's billed full mouth only.
Incorrect: insurance won't pay for debridement and an exam the same day, so the exam is usually about 2 weeks later.

q4-M05.stem: Select every item that is a limitation of scaling and root planing.
choices: You work blind, guided by touch
Motile bacteria get into the pocket's soft-tissue lining
Restorations with overhanging or subgingival margins
Taking off too much cementum, leading to hypersensitivity
Pockets of 5 mm or more always have calculus left in them
Ultrasonic tips can't work below the gingival margin
why: Yes: SRP is a blinded procedure, so tactile sensation and proprioception guide you in the pocket.
Yes: motile bacteria invade the soft-tissue lining, while SRP reaches only the pocket itself.
Yes: overhanging, subgingival, open or rough margins collect plaque and resist cleaning.
Yes: chasing a smooth root can remove too much cementum and cause hypersensitivity.
No: deeper pockets are harder to reach, but a 5 mm pocket doesn't mean calculus is left every time.
No: the clinic's piezoelectric ultrasonic works subgingivally; what it can't do is root plane.

q4-M06.stem: Before you pick up a probe, which of these can the radiographs already show you? Select all that apply.
choices: Whether the bone loss is localized or generalized
Whether the bone loss is horizontal or vertical
Roots that are close together or fused
Calculus and periapical lesions
Bleeding on probing
How wide the keratinized gingiva is
why: Yes: the film shows whether bone loss is localized or generalized.
Yes: the film shows the pattern of bone loss, horizontal, vertical or both.
Yes: root proximity and fused roots show on the film, and root proximity matters for surgical and non-surgical therapy.
Yes: calculus and periapical lesions both show, so you know what to expect before touching the patient.
No: bleeding on probing is a clinical finding that only probing can reveal.
No: keratinized tissue width is measured clinically, directly or with the rolling technique.

q5-02.stem: You probe the distopalatal furcation of a maxillary first molar. Roughly how many millimeters apical to the CEJ should you expect its entrance?
choices: About 5 mm
About 3 mm
About 3.5 mm
About 8 mm
why: Of the three entrances, the distal (distopalatal) one lies deepest: the exam-review guide rounds it to about 5 mm (4.8 mm as taught).
The guide's 3 mm belongs to the mesial entrance, which sits nearest the CEJ.
The guide gives about 3.5 mm for the buccal entrance, not the distal one.
Around 8 mm is where a maxillary premolar's furcation sits, not a molar's.

q5-03.stem: Comparing maxillary first and second molars, which one has its furcation closer to the CEJ because of a shorter root trunk?
choices: The first molar
The second molar
Neither; their trunks match
Neither; molars lack a measurable trunk
why: The first molar's trunk is the shorter one, so its furcation is reached with less attachment loss.
The second molar has the longer trunk, which places its furcation farther from the CEJ.
Their trunks aren't the same length; the first molar's is shorter.
Each molar has a measurable trunk running from the CEJ to the furcation.

q5-05.stem: A maxillary premolar can have a furcation only when it has two root cones. About how often is that the case?
choices: About 40% of the time
About 10% of the time
About 75% of the time
About 5% of the time
why: Roughly 40% of maxillary premolars are two-rooted, which is why a furcation is possible on them.
10% underestimates it; the figure is about 40%.
75% overestimates it; the figure is about 40%.
5% underestimates it; about 40% have two roots.

q5-06.stem: A molar shows an incipient Class I furcation. What treatment fits it best?
choices: SRP plus furcation plasty
Extracting the tooth
Resecting a root
A GTR membrane over the furcation
why: An incipient Class I lesion needs only SRP with furcation plasty, smoothing the entrance so it can be kept clean.
Removing the tooth is far too much for an incipient lesion; extraction is considered for advanced Class II-III.
Root resection is reserved for deep Class II and Class III furcations.
Regeneration with GTR is a Class II option and isn't needed at Class I.

q5-07.stem: For a Class II furcation, which teeth does the exam-review guide name as candidates for GTR?
choices: Mandibular molars
Maxillary premolars
The mesial and distal furcations of maxillary molars
Mandibular premolars
why: The guide names Class II mandibular molars for GTR; the lecture also adds the buccal furcation of maxillary molars.
Maxillary premolar furcations aren't on the GTR list; they're narrow and difficult to reach.
Interproximal (mesial and distal) degree II furcations on maxillary molars are much less suited because access is limited.
Mandibular premolars usually have a single root, so there's no furcation to regenerate.

q5-08.stem: The bone between the teeth has dropped below the level of the bone over the facial and lingual root surfaces, forming craters. What is this pattern called?
choices: Reverse architecture
Positive architecture
Flat architecture
It has no name
why: Reverse (negative) architecture is interdental bone lying apical to the facial and lingual bone, which forms craters.
Positive architecture, the healthy form, has interdental bone coronal to the facial and lingual bone.
Flat architecture has interdental and radicular bone at roughly one level.
The pattern does have a name: reverse (negative) architecture.

q5-09.stem: A healthy periodontium has positive bone architecture. Compared with the bone at the midfacial and midlingual, the interdental bone is:
choices: Coronal to it
Apical to it
At the same height
Not related to it
why: Positive architecture has the interdental bone peaking coronal to the midfacial and midlingual bone, tracking the CEJ's scallop.
Interdental bone apical to the radicular bone is the reverse (negative) pattern.
Interdental bone level with the radicular bone describes flat architecture.
They are related: architecture is defined by where interdental bone sits compared with them.

q5-R01.stem: Osseous surgery shapes the bone to match the gingiva over it. What is the reason?
choices: The gingiva regains its scallop, so pockets recur over unmatched bone
Bone always regrows to its earlier height within about a year
The gingiva simply copies whatever contour the bone is given
Flat bone keeps the teeth from loosening once the surgery is done
why: This was his most important slide: bone that doesn't follow the gingival architecture over it lets pockets come back.
Bone that is resected doesn't regrow, which is why removal stays conservative.
It works the other way: the gingiva holds its scalloped shape even when the bone doesn't.
Mobility rises after osseous surgery whatever the bone's shape, so that isn't why bone is reshaped.

q5-R02.stem: After scaling and root planing are finished, how long should you wait before the Phase I re-evaluation?
choices: Roughly 4 to 6 weeks
No wait; same day as the last SRP
Roughly 6 months
Until after periodontal surgery
why: At about 4-6 weeks, SRP has had its full effect, the flora is most favorable and hygiene is at its best.
On the same day, no healing has taken place yet.
Six months is a maintenance interval, much too late for deciding on surgery.
The re-evaluation is what decides whether surgery is needed, so it has to come before it.

q5-R03.stem: A patient returns for re-evaluation with clean teeth, but probing still finds 6-7 mm pockets. What comes next?
choices: Considering Phase II surgery
Going through Phase I again
Periodontal maintenance alone
Extracting the affected teeth
why: Good hygiene with pockets too deep to keep clean makes the patient a surgical candidate.
Phase I is repeated when the patient's hygiene has failed, which it hasn't here.
Maintenance suits shallow pockets with good hygiene.
Deep pockets by themselves don't make teeth hopeless.

q5-R04.stem: At the re-evaluation, every tooth has plaque, the gums bleed and the pockets are still there. What should happen now?
choices: Phase I again: go over home care and debride once more
Osseous surgery to remove what's left of the pockets
Periodontal maintenance visits every 3 months
Regenerative surgery at the deepest sites
why: Something was missed; review home care and repeat the debridement.
Poor plaque control is the first contraindication to surgery.
Maintenance is for a mouth that is clean and stable.
Regeneration also depends on good plaque control first.

q5-R05.stem: Dr. Litz's slides list the goals of Phase I therapy. Which one is NOT among them?
choices: Getting rid of bony craters
Lowering gingival inflammation
Leaving tissue that handles well in surgery
Giving the patient a mouth they can keep clean
why: Bony craters are corrected surgically, in Phase II, not by Phase I.
Reducing or eliminating inflammation is a Phase I goal.
Firm tissue that bleeds little is a Phase I goal.
A cleanable environment is the goal he repeats "ad nauseam".

q5-R06.stem: A patient obviously headed for surgery asks to skip Phase I. What is the main reason not to?
choices: Flaps in inflamed gingiva bleed heavily and tear apart
Insurance demands two cleanings before any surgery
Phase I by itself always removes the need for surgery
Root planing softens bone so it reshapes more easily
why: Like clearing an infected laceration before fixing the fracture: inflamed gingiva bleeds heavily and shreds.
His reasons were biological, not insurance rules.
Phase I doesn't always prevent surgery; many patients still need it.
SRP acts on the root and soft tissue, not on bone.

q5-R07.stem: The 1981 root planing study looked at pockets over 5 mm deep. What did it report about root planing at that depth?
choices: Incomplete calculus removal is the usual result
Calculus is removed as completely as in shallow pockets
Incomplete removal can happen but is uncommon
Too much cementum is taken off
why: Beyond 5 mm, the chance of failing to remove all the calculus dominates.
Residual calculus goes up as pockets get deeper, so removal is less complete, not equal.
That fits 3-5 mm pockets, where the chance of failure becomes greater; over 5 mm it dominates.
The study measured calculus left behind, not overinstrumentation.

q5-R08.stem: The study gave three reasons why more calculus is left behind as pockets get deeper. Which is NOT one of them?
choices: Deep pockets hold more motile bacteria
The root surface to scale is larger
More irregularities, like furcations, are in the way
The apical part tapers and is hard to reach
why: The types of bacteria weren't among the study's three reasons.
A larger surface area is the first reason.
More irregularities (furcations at 3.6-4.8 mm) is the second reason.
A narrow, hard-to-reach apical portion is the third reason.

q5-R10.stem: Looking at a radiograph of a healthy periodontium, how far apical to the neighboring CEJs would you expect the interproximal bone crest?
choices: Roughly 1 to 2 mm
Roughly 4 to 5 mm
At the CEJ itself
Around half the root's length
why: In health the crest lies within about 1-2 mm of the CEJs.
A 4-5 mm distance would mean bone has been lost.
The crest is slightly apical to the CEJ, not level with it.
Half the root length would be advanced bone loss.

q5-R11.stem: When osseous surgery is done properly, about how much supporting bone height does the tooth lose on average?
choices: Roughly 0.6 mm
Roughly 2 mm
Roughly 3 mm
No bone height
why: About 0.6 mm is lost around the tooth's circumference.
That is too much; removal is kept conservative.
Far too much; that would weaken the tooth.
Ostectomy does take away some supporting bone.

q5-R12.stem: During osseous surgery, bone is taken from the facial and lingual surfaces instead of interproximally. Why?
choices: Those surfaces hold less of the tooth's support
Facial bone reliably regrows afterward
A bur can't reach interproximal bone
Facial bone has no attachment to the root at all
why: The facial and lingual surfaces are smaller, so taking bone there costs less support.
Bone that's resected doesn't regrow.
Interproximal bone can be reached; vertical grooving is done there.
Facial bone over the root is supporting bone; removing it is ostectomy.

q5-R13.stem: A patient asks whether their teeth will feel looser after osseous resection. What is the accurate answer?
choices: Yes, at first; back to pre-op levels in about a year
No, mobility drops right away and stays lower once healed
Yes, for good, so the teeth will need a splint afterward
No change, since the interproximal bone is kept
why: Selipsky: the increase in mobility returns to pre-op levels after about a year, so warn the patient.
Taking bone away doesn't firm teeth up; mobility goes up first.
The increase is temporary, so splinting isn't planned; the patient is warned instead.
Mobility still rises at first, even with the interproximal bone preserved.

q5-R14.stem: Which choice correctly separates ostectomy from osteoplasty?
choices: Ostectomy removes supporting bone; osteoplasty reshapes unattached bone
Ostectomy reshapes bone; osteoplasty takes away the entire alveolar process
Ostectomy works on soft tissue; osteoplasty works on bone
No difference; the two terms name one procedure
why: Ostectomy removes tooth-supporting bone; osteoplasty reshapes bone not attached to the tooth, without removing supporting bone.
This reverses them, and neither removes the whole process.
Both are procedures on bone.
They differ in whether supporting bone is removed (Friedman 1955).

q5-R15.stem: A thick buccal ledge of bone sits away from the root, not touching it, and the surgeon thins it. Which procedure is this?
choices: Osteoplasty
Ostectomy
Gingivectomy
Hemisection
why: Reshaping bone that isn't attached to the tooth is osteoplasty, even on the facial.
Ostectomy is removing bone that supports the tooth.
A gingivectomy removes soft tissue, not bone.
A hemisection takes off a root with its part of the crown.

q5-R16.stem: As taught, which step comes first in osseous surgery?
choices: Grooving the bone vertically
Gradualizing the marginal bone
Flattening interproximal bone
Blending the radicular bone
why: Step 1 is vertical grooving interproximally (osteoplasty).
Gradualizing the marginal bone is the fourth step.
Flattening the interproximal bone is the third step.
Radicular blending is the second step.

q5-R17.stem: Dr. Litz singled out one step as the most important in any periodontal surgery. Which?
choices: Debriding the root surfaces thoroughly
Taking enough bone to flatten each defect
Grafting bone into every defect
Closing the flap with silk sutures
why: "If these are not clean root surfaces, nothing is going to work."
Bone removal is kept conservative and ranks behind clean roots.
Grafting fails too if the roots aren't clean.
Silk sutures close the flap, but closing isn't the key step.

q5-R18.stem: You're doing osseous surgery around a maxillary molar. What is done with the buccal furcation?
choices: Each buccal root is treated like its own tooth; furcation bone stays
The furcation bone is taken down so the patient can clean it
The furcation is opened into a tunnel a brush fits through
The mesiobuccal root is resected to open the furcation for cleaning
why: Bone comes off each root's facial, never from the furcation: exposing it lowers the prognosis, and that bone is hard to regain.
Taking furcation bone exposes the furcation, which is exactly what's avoided.
Tunneling is a separate procedure, limited to mandibular molars with long, divergent roots.
Root resection is a different procedure, not part of routine osseous surgery.

q5-R19.stem: "Every periodontist knows" the first contraindication to periodontal surgery. What is it?
choices: Plaque control that isn't working
A two-wall crater defect
Mild horizontal bone loss
Exostoses on the buccal bone
why: Surgery only creates a cleanable environment; if the patient doesn't clean, it fails.
Crater defects are an indication for resective surgery.
Mild to moderate horizontal bone loss is an indication.
Removing ledges and exostoses is an indication.

q5-R20.stem: A deep intrabony defect is a good candidate for regeneration. What does that mean for resective surgery at that site?
choices: It argues against resection: regenerate instead
It argues for resection: take down its walls
It doesn't change which surgery is chosen
Resect now and regenerate afterward
why: A hard-tissue defect amenable to regeneration is a contraindication to resective surgery.
Taking down the walls of a regenerable defect destroys what regeneration relies on.
It does change the decision: regeneration is preferred.
Once the walls are resected, nothing is left to regenerate.

q5-R21.stem: A patient with a high smile line has defects in the maxillary anterior. Why is resective surgery a poor fit there?
choices: The teeth end up longer, and that look is unacceptable
There's no interproximal bone on anterior teeth to reshape
Osseous surgery can't get to bone around anterior teeth
Defects in the anterior must always be regenerated
why: An expected unacceptable cosmetic result is a contraindication.
Anterior teeth have interproximal bone like any other teeth.
Anterior bone is reachable through a flap; the concern is appearance.
Whether to regenerate depends on the defect, not where it is.

q5-R22.stem: Getting to positive architecture would mean taking too much bone from the facial and lingual. What end result does Dr. Litz settle for?
choices: Flat architecture
Reverse architecture
Grafting instead
Removing the tooth
why: Flat isn't ideal, but it limits bone removal and protects the tooth's support.
Reverse architecture is what produces the pockets.
Grafting changes the procedure; his point was about limiting how much is resected.
The tooth is kept; only the amount of bone removed is limited.

q5-R23.stem: After osseous surgery, how should the bone ideally meet the root?
choices: As a thin knife-edge with convex contours
As a thick buttress meeting the tooth at a right angle
As a ledge shielding the gingival margin
As a concavity holding the gingiva in place
why: A knife-edge approximation with convex contours leaves an area that can be cleaned.
A thick buttress meeting at a right angle is what makes cleaning hard.
Ledges are trimmed back, never created.
Concave areas are harder to clean than convex ones.

q5-R24.stem: The 1981 study showed that more calculus is left behind as pockets deepen. Which surgical indication does that finding back most directly?
choices: Access for root debridement
Regrowing lost attachment
Fixing mucogingival defects
Better esthetics
why: Closed root planing leaves more calculus as pockets deepen; a flap lets you see the root and clean it, like doing a filling with your eyes open.
Regeneration aims to regrow lost support; the study concerns calculus closed instrumentation can't reach.
Mucogingival work treats recession and thin tissue, not calculus left in deep pockets.
Esthetics is on his list of indications, but the study is about calculus left in deep pockets.

q5-RS1.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. After surgery, the gingiva tends to go back to a scalloped shape, whether or not the bone underneath is scalloped.
2. Resective surgery is indicated when the pockets are shallow.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 2 is false: shallow pockets are a contraindication, not an indication.
Statement 1 is true: the gingiva goes back to its scalloped form.
The gingiva returns to its scallop, and operating on shallow pockets causes attachment loss, so 2 is false.
Statement 1 is true: the gingiva regains its scallop even if the bone doesn't. Statement 2 is false: shallow pockets contraindicate surgery, because surgery there causes attachment loss.

q5-RS2.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. When osseous surgery is done on a maxillary molar, the furcation bone is taken down so the patient can keep it clean.
2. Phase I is re-evaluated roughly 4 to 6 weeks after it ends.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is false: furcation bone is never taken down, because exposing the furcation lowers the prognosis.
Statement 2 is true: the re-evaluation comes about 4-6 weeks after Phase I.
Only statement 2 is true: furcation bone is preserved, and the re-evaluation is at 4-6 weeks.
Bone comes off each root's facial, never from the furcation, and the re-evaluation is about 4-6 weeks after Phase I.

q5-RM1.stem: Select every finding that would argue against doing resective periodontal surgery.
choices: Plaque control that isn't effective
Systemic disease that isn't controlled
Pockets that are shallow
Two-wall crater defects
Exostoses on the buccal
why: Counts: it's the first contraindication.
Counts: uncontrolled systemic disease is a contraindication.
Counts: operating on shallow pockets causes attachment loss.
Doesn't count: two-wall craters are an indication.
Doesn't count: taking off ledges and exostoses is an indication.

q5-RM2.stem: Dr. Litz listed what goes into Phase I periodontal therapy. Select every item that is part of it.
choices: Teaching oral hygiene
Scaling and root planing
Fixing overhanging restoration margins
Recontouring the bone
Periodontal maintenance
why: Part of it: OHI always comes first.
Part of it: SRP is the center of Phase I.
Part of it: controlling plaque-retentive features belongs to Phase I.
Not part of it: bone surgery is Phase II.
Not part of it: maintenance comes after active therapy.

q5-RP1.stem: Given this patient's re-evaluation findings, which treatment should come next?
choices: Resective osseous surgery
Another round of Phase I
Maintenance alone
Extraction of #2-#4
why: Hygiene is good, deep pockets persist, and the bone shows reverse architecture with ledges: an ideal resective case.
His hygiene is already good, and repeating Phase I won't shrink the craters.
Pockets of 6 mm can't be kept clean at home.
These teeth have defects that can be treated.

q5-RP2.stem: How should you answer this patient?
choices: Redo Phase I and improve home care before any surgery
Book osseous surgery, because the pockets are deep
Regenerate the deepest sites rather than resect
Put her on 3-month periodontal maintenance only
why: Poor plaque control is the first contraindication; go over hygiene and debride again.
Surgery on a patient who doesn't clean will look like it was never done.
Regeneration depends on good plaque control as well.
Maintenance alone ignores the active disease and the deep pockets.

q5-L01.stem: A furcation and a furcation defect are not the same thing. Which choice draws the line correctly?
choices: The furcation is normal anatomy; the defect is periodontal loss of tissue and bone there
The furcation appears only after attachment loss; the defect is that site once it bleeds
The furcation shows only on radiographs; the defect is what a Nabers probe finds clinically
The furcation exists only on molars; on premolars that area is always termed a defect
why: A furcation is the normal place where roots divide; the defect is the bone and tissue destroyed there by periodontal disease.
Every multi-rooted tooth has a furcation from development; attachment loss creates the defect, not the furcation.
A furcation is anatomy whether or not a film shows it, and defects are found both clinically and on radiographs.
Two-rooted premolars have furcations too, and a defect means destruction, not a kind of tooth.

q5-L02.stem: In the furcation lecture, which point did Dr. Litz describe as arguably the most important?
choices: Attachment loss into the furcation sharply lowers prognosis
Only a radiograph can diagnose furcation involvement
Any furcation defect should go to surgery as soon as it's found
Only mandibular molars have furcations
why: His key point: once attachment loss reaches the furcation, the prognosis drops sharply, since the area is so hard to clean.
Furcations are diagnosed clinically with a Nabers probe first; radiographs confirm them and often miss them.
Furcation involvement alone isn't an indication for treatment; early involvement often needs none.
Maxillary molars and two-rooted premolars have furcations too; maxillary molars are affected most often.

q5-L03.stem: Where does the root trunk begin and end?
choices: From the CEJ to the furcation entrance
From the furcation fornix to the apex
From the CEJ all the way to the apex
From the alveolar crest to the fornix
why: The trunk spans the CEJ to the furcation entrance, where the roots first split.
Fornix to apex is the individual root cones, not the trunk.
CEJ to apex is the whole root complex (trunk plus cones).
The trunk is measured from the CEJ, not from the alveolar crest.

q5-L04.stem: Which structure is the furcation fornix?
choices: The furcation's roof, where the trunk stops
The space separating two diverging roots
A single root lying below the trunk
The radiographic triangle aimed at a furcation
why: The fornix is the roof of the furcation, where the root trunk ends and the roots separate.
The space between diverging roots is the divergence (interradicular dimension).
A single root below the trunk is a root cone.
The radiographic triangle aimed at a furcation is a furcation arrow.

q5-L05.stem: What share of a molar's periodontal attachment sits on the root trunk, on average?
choices: Roughly 30%
Roughly 10%
Roughly 50%
Roughly 70%
why: About 30% of the attachment is on the trunk, depending on trunk length.
10% is too low; about 30% is on the trunk.
50% is too high; about 30% is on the trunk and 70% on the roots.
70% is the share on the individual roots, not on the trunk.

q5-L06.stem: A molar with a long root trunk starts out protected but becomes harder to treat later. Which choice accounts for both?
choices: Reaching the furcation takes more attachment loss, but once it's reached, the short roots left make resection a poor choice
At first it conceals Grade 3 cervical enamel projections, which later lead plaque straight into the furcation
The entrance begins narrow and sheltered, then widens as bone is lost so plaque enters more easily than with a short trunk
It shields mandibular molars early, but they regenerate poorly once involved, unlike maxillary teeth
why: Both follow from trunk length: the furcation is far from the CEJ, so more loss is needed to reach it; but roots are only so long, so a long trunk leaves short roots and little support for resection.
Trunk length doesn't set the CEP grade; a Grade 3 CEP is defined by reaching into the furcation, whatever the trunk.
A long trunk places the entrance farther from the CEJ; it doesn't make the entrance narrow at first and wider later.
Long trunks occur on maxillary teeth too (premolars, second molars), and the later problem is short roots, not the arch.

q5-L07.stem: Which teeth would show furcation involvement after the least attachment loss?
choices: Multi-rooted teeth whose root trunks are short
Multi-rooted teeth whose root trunks are quite long
Single-rooted teeth with long roots
Teeth whose roots diverge widely
why: With a short trunk (say 2 mm), just 2 mm of attachment loss reaches the furcation.
A long trunk needs more attachment loss before the furcation is involved.
A single-rooted tooth has no furcation to involve.
Widely divergent roots make treatment easier; they don't bring involvement sooner.

q5-L08.stem: Order the furcation entrances of a maxillary first molar by distance from the CEJ, starting with the closest.
choices: Mesiopalatal, then buccal, then distopalatal
Buccal, then mesiopalatal, then distopalatal
Distopalatal, then buccal, then mesiopalatal
All three at one depth
why: As taught (Bower): mesiopalatal about 3.6 mm, buccal about 4.2 mm, distopalatal about 4.8 mm.
The buccal is the narrowest entrance, not the closest; the mesiopalatal lies nearer the CEJ.
This reverses the order: the distopalatal is the deepest, not the closest.
The entrances lie at different depths, from 3.6 to 4.8 mm.

q5-L09.stem: As taught, roughly how many millimeters below the CEJ are a mandibular first molar's furcation entrances?
choices: About 2.4-2.5 mm, shallower than on a maxillary molar
About 4-5 mm, a bit deeper than on a maxillary molar
About 8 mm, the same as a maxillary premolar
About 3.6 mm on the buccal and 4.8 mm on the lingual
why: Buccal about 2.4 mm and lingual about 2.5 mm, shallower than the maxillary molar's 3.6-4.8 mm.
Mandibular molar entrances are shallower than the maxillary molar's, not deeper.
About 8 mm is the maxillary premolar's furcation depth.
3.6 and 4.8 mm are the maxillary first molar's mesiopalatal and distopalatal depths.

q5-L10.stem: On a mandibular molar, the lingual furcation entrance usually sits slightly more apical than the buccal one. What explains this?
choices: The tooth's lingual inclination
A lingual root that is always longer
The hourglass form of the mesial root
An intermediate bifurcation ridge on the buccal
why: Mandibular molars are angled lingually, which moves the lingual furcation slightly apical.
Mandibular molars have mesial and distal roots, not a lingual root.
The mesial root's hourglass shape affects cleaning, not how deep the entrance is.
The intermediate bifurcation ridge crosses the entrance mesiodistally; it doesn't set the lingual depth.

q5-L11.stem: Which furcal root surface carries the deepest developmental depression, one found on every tooth examined?
choices: Mandibular first molar, mesial root (about 0.7 mm)
Maxillary first molar, mesiobuccal root (about 0.3 mm)
Maxillary first molar, palatal root (about 0.1 mm)
Mandibular first molar, distal root (about 0.5 mm)
why: The mesial root of the mandibular first molar has the deepest furcal depression, about 0.7 mm, in 100% of teeth.
The maxillary mesiobuccal depression is about 0.3 mm and present 94% of the time, not 100%.
The maxillary palatal depression is shallow (0.1 mm) and present only about 17% of the time.
The mandibular distal root's depression is about 0.5 mm and present 99% of the time, shallower than the mesial's.

q5-L12.stem: On a maxillary first molar, which root shows a furcal developmental depression in about 94% of teeth?
choices: The mesiobuccal root
The distobuccal root
The palatal root
No root; these roots are convex
why: The mesiobuccal root's furcal surface has a 0.3 mm depression about 94% of the time.
The distobuccal root has a shallower 0.1 mm depression only about 31% of the time.
The palatal root has a shallower 0.1 mm depression only about 17% of the time.
Maxillary molar roots do have furcal depressions, most often on the mesiobuccal root.

q5-L13.stem: Even with profound anesthesia and a brand-new sharp Gracey, most furcations can't be debrided well. Why?
choices: The blade face is wider than most furcation entrances
A curette can't be used apical to the CEJ
Enamel lines the furcation, and curettes can't scale it
Local anesthetic doesn't reach the furcation
why: 81% of entrances are under 1 mm and 58% under 0.75 mm, while a curette blade face is 0.75-1.10 mm wide.
Curettes are designed for subgingival root surfaces below the CEJ; the problem is entrance width.
Furcations are root surfaces covered with cementum, not enamel (except where a CEP or pearl exists).
Anesthesia isn't the issue; even well anesthetized, the blade is too wide for most entrances.

q5-L14.stem: What proportion of furcation entrances measure less than 1 mm across?
choices: About 81%
About 58%
About 30%
About 17%
why: Roughly 81% of furcation entrances are under 1 mm wide.
58% is the share under 0.75 mm, not under 1 mm.
30% is nearer the share of attachment on the root trunk.
17% is how often the maxillary palatal root has a furcal depression.

q5-L15.stem: On maxillary molars, which furcation becomes involved most often?
choices: The buccal
The mesiopalatal
The distopalatal
None more than the others
why: The buccal furcation of maxillary molars is involved most often, then the mesiopalatal, then the distopalatal.
The mesiopalatal is second, behind the buccal.
The distopalatal is involved least often of the three.
They differ: buccal first, then mesiopalatal, then distopalatal.

q5-L16.stem: Several factors favor furcation involvement, but which one is its primary cause?
choices: Attachment loss from inflammatory periodontal disease
Cervical enamel projections channeling plaque inward
Overhanging restorations holding plaque at the entrance
A short root trunk placing the furcation near the CEJ
why: Plaque-driven inflammatory periodontal disease causes the attachment loss that exposes the furcation.
CEPs channel plaque into the furcation, but they are contributing factors, not the primary cause.
Overhangs hold plaque and contribute, but they aren't the primary cause.
A short trunk lets involvement happen sooner but doesn't cause it; attachment loss does.

q5-L17.stem: A molar has a cervical enamel projection running toward its furcation. How does this make furcation involvement more likely?
choices: Nothing attaches to enamel, so plaque is funneled to the furcation
Enamel is softer than cementum and decays into the furcation
It makes the entrance too narrow for a curette
It shortens the root trunk by about 2 mm
why: Connective tissue doesn't attach to enamel, so the gingiva lies over a CEP unattached and plaque is channeled into the furcation.
Enamel is harder than cementum, and the problem is missing attachment, not decay.
A CEP doesn't narrow the entrance; it removes the attachment that would seal it.
A CEP doesn't change root trunk length; it's an enamel extension over the trunk.

q5-L18.stem: What developmental error leaves a wedge of enamel pointing from the CEJ toward a molar's furcation?
choices: Enamel formation doesn't stop before the root forms
Cementum gets deposited on top of enamel at the CEJ
An ameloblast rest is caught in the periodontal ligament
Root dentin is resorbed and enamel fills in the gap
why: That is how a CEP arises: amelogenesis doesn't halt before root formation, so an enamel wedge extends toward the furcation.
Cementum lying over enamel at the CEJ is an overlap variation of the junction, not a CEP.
A free ball of enamel is an enamel pearl, and epithelial rests trapped in the PDL are a different finding altogether.
A CEP is developmental; it doesn't come from resorption, and enamel can't be laid down after eruption anyway.

q5-L19.stem: Which teeth, and at roughly what rate, carry cervical enamel projections most often?
choices: Mandibular molars, roughly 30%
Maxillary molars, roughly 30%
Mandibular molars, roughly 15%
Maxillary premolars, roughly 40%
why: Right: about 30% of mandibular molars have a CEP, about twice the maxillary molar rate.
The 30% figure belongs to mandibular molars; maxillary molars sit near 15%.
The 15% figure belongs to maxillary molars; mandibular molars sit near 30%.
Forty percent is how many maxillary premolars have two roots, not a CEP rate.

q5-L20.stem: You are checking a mandibular second molar for a cervical enamel projection. Which aspect of the tooth is the likeliest place to find one?
choices: The buccal
The lingual
The mesial
The distal
why: CEPs show up most on the buccal (and more on second molars).
The lingual is a less likely site than the buccal.
The mesial isn't where CEPs typically sit; they favor the buccal.
The distal isn't where CEPs typically sit; they favor the buccal.

q5-L21.stem: An enamel projection from the CEJ reaches toward the furcation and stops short of the entrance. How is it graded?
choices: Grade 2
Grade 1
Grade 3
Grade 4
why: Grade 2 is the one that approaches the furcation without entering it.
Grade 1 is just a distinct apical change in the CEJ, pointing toward the furcation.
Grade 3 actually extends into the furcation.
CEPs have no Grade 4; Grade IV belongs to the Glickman furcation classes.

q5-L22.stem: On #30 you find a Grade 1 enamel projection, and there is no bone or attachment loss around it. What is usually done?
choices: Leave it and keep watching it
Raise a flap and remove it with a diamond
Prepare a tunnel through the furcation
Amputate the mesial root
why: Without bone or attachment loss, a Grade 1 CEP usually needs no treatment; it is monitored.
Removal through a flap is saved for a CEP that already has attachment loss with it.
A tunnel is for deep Class II-III furcations with long, divergent roots, not a harmless CEP.
Root resection is for deep Class II-III furcations, far more than a Grade 1 CEP calls for.

q5-L23.stem: You plan to take off a thick enamel projection on a tooth with a vital pulp. What do you warn the patient may follow?
choices: Sensitivity to hot and cold
A root canal that will certainly be needed
Losing the neighboring papilla
A lasting color change of the tooth
why: Taking off thick enamel can expose dentin, and on a vital tooth that can be sensitive to temperature.
Endodontics would only be needed if the pulp were exposed, which careful removal avoids.
Papilla loss isn't the risk of reshaping enamel at the furcation.
Removing a CEP doesn't alter the visible color of the tooth.

q5-L24.stem: Every site in a stable patient's mouth probes 2-3 mm, apart from one Class II furcation on the buccal of #19. What is the first thing to look for?
choices: An enamel projection on that tooth
Generalized Stage 3 periodontitis
Brushing abrasion on #19's buccal
A systemic disease like diabetes
why: One furcation in a stable mouth means a local cause, and a CEP, which favors the buccal, is the first suspect.
Generalized disease doesn't fit 2-3 mm depths at every other site.
Toothbrush abrasion wears root and gingiva; it doesn't create a lone furcation defect. Look for a plaque trap on that tooth, such as a CEP.
A systemic cause would show at many sites, not at one site on one tooth.

q5-L25.stem: The radiograph of #3 shows a small, round radiopacity in the furcation with bone loss around it. Which finding best explains it?
choices: An enamel pearl
A furcation arrow
A Grade 1 enamel projection
An intermediate bifurcation ridge
why: An enamel pearl is a ball of enamel in a molar furcation, and enamel is radiopaque, so it shows as a semicircle.
A furcation arrow is a radiolucent triangle, the opposite of a radiopaque semicircle.
A Grade 1 CEP is only a small change at the CEJ, not a round radiopacity in the furcation.
That ridge is a mandibular molar feature, and #3 is a maxillary molar.

q5-L26.stem: Which description fits the structure called an intermediate bifurcation ridge?
choices: Convex cementum across a mandibular molar's furcation entrance
An enamel wedge from the CEJ into a maxillary molar's furcation
A ridge of bone left between the roots after osteoplasty
A radiopaque line linking the buccal roots of a maxillary molar
why: Correct: it is a convex cementum ridge running mesiodistally across a mandibular molar's furcation entrance, with a plaque-trapping dome above it.
An enamel wedge pointing from the CEJ into the furcation is a CEP.
It is a feature of the root (cementum), not bone left behind by osteoplasty.
It belongs to mandibular molars and isn't a line seen on a radiograph.

q5-L27.stem: Where should a restoration's margin sit when it has to go below the free gingival margin?
choices: Inside the gingival sulcus
Out to the furcation fornix, for retention
Right at the alveolar crest
About 1 mm into the furcation entrance
why: A margin apical to the free gingival margin should stay within the sulcus; margins near a furcation hold plaque.
Taking a margin to the fornix puts it in the furcation, where it drives plaque, inflammation and bone loss.
A margin at the crest would invade the attachment apparatus.
A margin in the furcation entrance makes exactly the plaque trap to avoid.

q5-L29.stem: Two furcations are both through-and-through. One is Glickman Grade III and the other Grade IV. What makes the second one Grade IV?
choices: Recession lets you see through it
A probe can pass all the way through
Its vertical bone loss is 7 mm or more
Its horizontal loss is over 3 mm (Hamp)
why: In Grade IV, gingival recession has exposed the through-and-through furcation so it can be seen without a probe.
A probe passes through both Grade III and IV, so this doesn't tell them apart.
Seven millimeters or more of vertical loss is Tarnow and Fletcher subclass C, not a Glickman distinction.
Over 3 mm horizontal loss is Hamp degree 2, which doesn't separate Glickman III from IV.

q5-L30.stem: A furcation has lost 4 mm of bone horizontally, but the probe doesn't come out the other side. Where does it fall in Hamp's system?
choices: Degree 2
Degree 1
Degree 3
Subclass B
why: Hamp degree 2 is more than 3 mm of horizontal loss without a through-and-through lesion.
Degree 1 is less than 3 mm of horizontal loss.
Degree 3 is through-and-through.
Subclass B (4-6 mm) is a Tarnow and Fletcher vertical subclass, not a Hamp degree.

q5-L31.stem: What do Tarnow and Fletcher measure when they assign a furcation subclass A, B or C?
choices: Vertical bone loss, 3 mm per step
Horizontal loss, 3 mm per step
Whether a probe passes through
How far an enamel projection reaches
why: Their subclass is vertical, in 3 mm steps: A 0-3 mm, B 4-6 mm, C 7 mm or more.
Horizontal loss in 3 mm steps is Hamp's system.
Whether the probe passes through is part of Glickman and Hamp grading.
How far a CEP reaches is the CEP grade (1-3).

q5-L32.stem: You are about to check the mesiopalatal furcation entrance of #14 with a Nabers probe. Which approach reaches it?
choices: Come in from the palatal side
Come in from the buccal side
Come in through the mesial contact
None; radiographs must be used
why: The mesiopalatal entrance is offset palatally because the mesiobuccal root is broad, so it is probed from the palatal.
From the buccal, the broad mesiobuccal root is in the way of the mesiopalatal entrance.
The contact blocks a straight approach; the entrance is reached from the palatal.
It can be probed from the palatal, and the clinical exam comes before radiographs anyway.

q5-L33.stem: A maxillary molar has bone loss in its buccal furcation, yet the periapical looks fairly normal there. What is the usual reason?
choices: The palatal root overlaps that area on the film
The zygomatic process hides every maxillary molar root
Buccal bone loss can never show on a periapical
The buccal furcation is too narrow to lose bone
why: The radiopaque palatal root sits over the buccal furcation on the film and masks the radiolucency.
The zygoma can cover apices, but it doesn't hide all the roots; the palatal root is what masks the buccal furcation.
Buccal loss can show; the trouble here is the palatal root superimposed on the furcation.
The buccal is actually the maxillary molar furcation involved most often.

q5-L34.stem: How should a furcation arrow on a radiograph be interpreted?
choices: One makes involvement likely; its absence rules nothing out
It shows up on almost every Grade II and III furcation
It signals involvement of a mandibular molar's buccal furcation
It is sufficient by itself to diagnose a furcation involvement
why: Right: an arrow makes involvement highly likely, but only about 30-55% of Grade II-III involvements show one.
Only about 30-55% of Grade II and III furcations show an arrow, far from almost all.
Arrows are a sign at the mesiopalatal and distopalatal furcations of maxillary molars, not mandibular buccal ones.
An arrow should never be the sole diagnostic tool; the Nabers probe is.

q5-L35.stem: Of all Grade II or Grade III furcation involvements, roughly how many will have a visible furcation arrow?
choices: About 30-55%
About 5-10%
About 65-80%
Almost all
why: Between about 30% and 55% of Grade II or III involvements show an arrow.
That is too low; about 30-55% show one.
Sixty-five percent is the combined clinical-plus-radiographic detection rate for maxillary molars, not the arrow rate.
Plenty of involved furcations show no arrow, which is why it can't be the only diagnostic tool.

q5-L36.stem: Dr. Litz cited a study (Ross and Thompson) on detecting furcations. When the clinical exam was paired with radiographs, in about what share of maxillary molars was involvement found?
choices: About 65%
About 3%
About 23%
About 9%
why: Clinical and radiographic exams together found involvement in about 65% of maxillary molars.
Three percent is what the clinical exam found alone in maxillary molars.
Twenty-three percent is the combined figure for mandibular molars.
Nine percent is the clinical-alone figure for mandibular molars.

q5-L37.stem: According to Dr. Litz, how should the clinical exam and the radiographs fit together when you diagnose?
choices: Examine clinically and diagnose, then confirm with films
Read the films first, then probe only the suspect sites
Use films alone whenever a furcation arrow is visible
The order doesn't matter as long as you do both
why: He wants the clinical findings and a diagnosis first, with radiographs used to confirm it.
Probing only what looks involved on the film misses the many furcations that show no arrow.
An arrow is never enough on its own; the Nabers probe is the diagnostic tool.
He insisted on the order: clinical exam first, then radiographs.

q5-L38.stem: A Class I furcation is found, and there is no local factor around it that could be removed or altered. What does it typically call for?
choices: No more than the usual SRP
A GTR membrane to regenerate it
Preparing a tunnel
Resecting a root
why: Early involvement without an alterable local factor usually needs no furcation-specific therapy beyond disease control with SRP.
GTR is a Class II option and isn't needed for early Class I involvement.
Tunneling is a Class III option for long, divergent mandibular molar roots.
Root resection is only for deep Class II and Class III furcations.

q5-L39.stem: A molar has a moderate to advanced furcation with a big horizontal component. Which approach gives the best results over the long term?
choices: Shrinking the furcation or eliminating it
SRP repeated every three months
Local antibiotics with nothing else added
Splinting the tooth to its neighbors
why: Shrinking or eliminating the furcation leaves an area the patient and hygienist can keep clean for years.
Repeated SRP can't reach most furcations, whose entrances are narrower than a curette blade.
Antibiotics alone don't change the anatomy that keeps the furcation hard to clean.
Splinting treats mobility, not the cleanable environment the furcation needs.

q5-L40.stem: Which option appears on the list of treatments for Class III furcations but is not one for Class I?
choices: Preparing a tunnel
Scaling and root planing
Taking away local factors
Furcation plasty
why: A tunnel preparation is a Class III option, along with root resection and extraction, and never a Class I one.
SRP is the basic Class I treatment.
Removing local factors is part of Class I treatment.
Furcation plasty is listed for Class I (and Class II), so it isn't Class III only.

q5-L41.stem: Among degree II furcations, which ones respond best to regenerative therapy?
choices: Mandibular molars and maxillary molar buccals
