The mesial and distal ones on maxillary molars
The furcations of maxillary premolars
Any tooth that already has a root canal filling
why: Degree II furcations on mandibular molars and on the buccal of maxillary molars do best with regeneration.
Interproximal maxillary degree II furcations are much less suited because access is limited.
Maxillary premolar furcations are narrow, deep and hard to reach, so they are poor candidates.
A root canal filling isn't a contraindication, but it doesn't make the tooth a better candidate either.

q5-L42.stem: A through-and-through (degree III) furcation is being considered for regeneration. Compared with conventional surgery, what result can be expected?
choices: About the same outcome
A clearly better outcome
It can't be done at all
Better only on maxillary molars
why: For degree III furcations, regenerative therapy gives no better outcome than conventional surgery.
Regeneration is not better for degree III; its best results come in degree II furcations.
It isn't contraindicated; it simply offers degree III no advantage.
The slides show no difference for degree III on maxillary or mandibular molars alike.

q5-L43.stem: A patient has just had a furcation grafted and covered with a membrane. How long should brushing and flossing at that site be held off?
choices: Up to 4 weeks
Up to 1 week
Up to 3 months
Not at all
why: Mechanical plaque removal at the site waits up to 4 weeks, with chlorhexidine used instead.
One week is too short; the wait is up to 4 weeks.
Three months is far too long; the restriction is up to 4 weeks.
Brushing at once would disturb the membrane and the flap; the site is left alone for up to 4 weeks.

q5-L44.stem: When a clinician tunnels a molar's furcation, what is the furcation turned into?
choices: A Glickman Grade IV
A Glickman Grade I
A tooth with one root
Positive bony architecture
why: Bone is removed so the furcation is through-and-through and open to view (Grade IV), letting an interproximal brush pass.
Grade I is incipient involvement; a tunnel opens the furcation all the way.
A single-rooted tooth is what a hemisection produces.
A tunnel opens the furcation; it doesn't reshape bone into positive architecture.

q5-L45.stem: A molar was tunneled years ago so the patient could brush through it. What problem is most likely to show up?
choices: Decay on the roots
Pulp necrosis from the surgery
Fracture of a root
Ankylosis
why: Root caries is the main complication: the tunnel exposes root surfaces, and they decay quickly.
The pulp isn't entered when a tunnel is prepared, so necrosis isn't the expected problem.
Root fracture is a risk for resected, endodontically treated roots, not the classic tunneling problem.
Ankylosis isn't what tunneled molars are known for.

q5-L46.stem: When a root is amputated and the crown kept, which root is the one taken most often?
choices: Maxillary first molar, distobuccal root
Maxillary first molar, mesiobuccal root
Maxillary second molar, palatal root
Mandibular first molar, distal root
why: The distobuccal root of the maxillary first molar is the root removed most often.
The mesiobuccal root is broad and supportive, so it is usually kept.
The palatal root is the largest and is removed less often, and this names the second molar.
Taking a mandibular molar root with its crown is usually a hemisection, and the distal isn't the classic answer.

q5-L47.stem: A hemisection and a root resection both take out a root. How does a hemisection differ?
choices: The root's share of the crown comes out with it
The full crown stays and only the root comes out
It is done on maxillary molars only, never mandibular
It can be done without endodontic treatment
why: A hemisection removes the root together with its portion of the crown, leaving a single-rooted tooth.
Keeping the whole crown and removing only the root is root resection (amputation).
Hemisection is usually done on mandibular molars.
Both procedures need endodontic treatment first.

q5-L48.stem: During root separation and resection, where should the margins of the provisional restoration finish relative to the bone crest?
choices: 3 mm or more coronal to it
Exactly level with it
Roughly 1 mm apical to it
Inside the furcation fornix
why: Provisional margins end at least 3 mm coronal to the bone crest, after surgery has removed the bone defects.
A margin at the crest would invade the attachment apparatus.
Apical to the crest means inside the bone, which is never acceptable.
Anything left at the fornix becomes a plaque trap; margins stay well coronal to the crest.

q5-L49.stem: A patient is scheduled for a root resection on a molar. Which step is done before all the others?
choices: The root canal treatment
Separating and removing the root
The periodontal surgery
The definitive restoration
why: Endodontics comes first, with the access filled directly with amalgam or composite.
Separating and resecting the root follows the endodontics and the provisional.
Periodontal surgery comes after the root has been separated and resected.
The final restoration is the last step.

q5-L50.stem: Roughly how many maxillary premolars are two-rooted, and at about what depth below the CEJ does their furcation open?
choices: Around 40%, at around 8 mm
Around 40%, at around 2.5 mm
Around 10%, at around 8 mm
Around 75%, at around 4 mm
why: About 40% have two roots, and the mean entrance sits about 8 mm from the CEJ.
About 2.5 mm is the mandibular molar's furcation depth, not the premolar's.
Ten percent is too low; about 40% of maxillary premolars are two-rooted.
Seventy-five percent is too high, and 4 mm is nearer a maxillary molar's buccal entrance.

q5-P01.stem: Given these findings, how should #30 be managed next?
choices: Raise a flap, take off the enamel projection and debride
Leave the projection and recheck the furcation at recalls
Take out #30 and replace it with an implant
Create a tunnel through the furcation
why: This Grade 3 CEP already has attachment loss (a Glickman Grade II furcation), so it is removed, usually through a flap, with debridement.
Watching suits only a CEP with no bone or attachment loss, and this one has loss.
Extraction is far too aggressive for a local cause that can be corrected in a stable patient.
Tunneling is for deep Class II-III furcations on long, divergent roots, and it invites caries.

q5-P02.stem: Keeping the bridge matters to this patient. Which treatment taught in the lecture would let him do that?
choices: Remove the fractured mesial root at the furcation
Tunnel the furcation so a brush can get through
Graft the furcation and cover it with a membrane
Keep the root and debride the furcation at recalls
why: Dr. Litz's own example: the fractured mesial root is resected at the furcation, the sound distal root keeps the bridge, and the tooth already has the root canal resection needs.
A tunnel does nothing about a fractured root, which has to come out.
Regeneration can't repair a vertically fractured root.
Debriding doesn't stop the breakdown around a vertically fractured root; that root has to come out.

q5-P04.stem: Of the factors for deciding whether a furcated tooth is worth treating, which counts most against keeping #31 here?
choices: Its low strategic value, since it doesn't function
Regeneration would work for any Grade III furcation
Its long root trunk makes it ideal to resect
No Grade III furcation can ever be maintained
why: With #2 missing, #31 doesn't function, so its strategic value is low against a Grade III furcation and mobility.
Regeneration gives degree III furcations no advantage over conventional surgery.
A long root trunk makes a tooth a poor resection candidate, not an ideal one.
Grade III furcations can be treated (tunnel, root resection); the lecture's reason against this tooth is that it doesn't function.

q5-M01.stem: Some contributors to furcation involvement are fixed anatomy, and others the clinician can take away or correct. Select every one you can correct.
choices: An enamel projection from the CEJ
A restoration margin that overhangs
A small enamel pearl
A root trunk that is short
The molar's lingual angulation
why: Correctable: a CEP can be removed with a bur (odontoplasty).
Correctable: an overhang can be corrected or the restoration replaced.
Correctable: a small enamel pearl can be taken off with a bur.
Not correctable: root trunk length is fixed anatomy, though it shapes risk and treatment.
Not correctable: the molar's lingual angulation is anatomy you can't change.

q5-M02.stem: As taught, which patient factors count against attempting regeneration of a furcation? Select all that apply.
choices: Diabetes that is not controlled
Being a smoker
Poor hygiene and poor compliance
A root canal filling in that tooth
A thick periodontal biotype
why: Counts against: uncontrolled diabetes makes a poor regeneration candidate.
Counts against: smokers are poor candidates for regeneration.
Counts against: without good hygiene and compliance the result can't be kept clean.
Doesn't count against: a root canal filling is not a contraindication.
Doesn't count against: a thicker biotype actually favors success.

q5-M03.stem: Select every statement that correctly describes root resection (root amputation).
choices: The patient is committed to endodontics and a restoration
It is reserved for deep Class II and Class III furcations
The root most often removed is the maxillary first molar's distobuccal
The root comes out together with its portion of the crown
It is the treatment of choice when the root trunk is long
why: Correct: resection needs endodontics first and a restoration after.
Correct: it is limited to deep Class II and Class III furcations.
Correct: the distobuccal root of the maxillary first molar is removed most often.
Incorrect: taking the root with its part of the crown is a hemisection; resection keeps the crown.
Incorrect: a long trunk means short roots, which makes a tooth a poor resection candidate.

q5-S01.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Furcation involvement is found more often on maxillary molars than on mandibular molars.
2. The furcation most often involved on a maxillary molar is the distopalatal.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 2 is false: the buccal is the maxillary molar furcation involved most, not the distopalatal.
Statement 1 is true: maxillary molars are involved more often than mandibular molars.
Right: statement 1 holds, and statement 2 is false because the order is buccal, then mesiopalatal, then distopalatal.
It's the other way around: statement 1 is true, and statement 2 is false since the distopalatal is involved least.

q5-S04.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. A furcation arrow on a film should never be relied on alone to detect furcation involvement.
2. The usual place to see a furcation arrow is the buccal furcation of a mandibular molar.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 2 is false: arrows appear at the mesiopalatal and distopalatal furcations of maxillary molars.
Statement 1 is true: many involved furcations have no arrow, so it can't be the only tool.
Right: statement 1 holds, and statement 2 is false because mandibular molar furcation loss is usually seen directly, with no arrow.
Reversed: statement 1 is true, and statement 2 is false because arrows are a maxillary molar sign.

q5-S05.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Maxillary molars, with three widely splayed roots, are the teeth tunneling suits best.
2. Because a brush can pass through a tunneled molar, root caries there is uncommon.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Neither holds: tunneling is limited to mandibular molars, and caries in tunneled molars is common.
Right: tunneling is limited to mandibular molars with long enough, divergent roots, and root caries in tunneled molars is common.
Statement 1 is false as well: tunneling is limited to mandibular molars with long, divergent roots.
Statement 2 is false as well: tunneled molars often get caries, since root surfaces decay quickly.

q5-E01.stem: Each of these makes furcation involvement more likely EXCEPT:
choices: Roots spaced widely apart
An enamel projection from the CEJ
An overhanging restoration
A bifurcation ridge of cementum
why: The exception: widely spaced roots are favorable because instruments can reach between them; close or fused roots are the risk.
A risk: connective tissue can't attach to enamel, so a CEP funnels plaque into the furcation.
A risk: overhangs hold plaque near the furcation.
A risk: an intermediate bifurcation ridge leaves a plaque trap above it.

q5-E02.stem: Each of these is on the list of treatments for a Class II furcation EXCEPT:
choices: Watching it without treating
Reshaping it with furcation plasty
Regenerating it under a GTR membrane
Resecting the involved root
why: The exception: watching without therapy suits early Class I involvement with no local factor to change.
Furcation plasty is a listed Class II option.
Regeneration with GTR is a listed Class II option.
Root resection is a listed option for deep Class II furcations.

q5-E03.stem: Each statement about cervical enamel projections is correct EXCEPT:
choices: Maxillary molars have them more often than mandibular molars
Second molars have them more often than first molars
The buccal has them more often than the lingual
A Grade 3 projection reaches into the furcation
why: The false one: mandibular molars have CEPs more often (about 30%) than maxillary molars (about 15%).
Correct: CEPs are more likely on second molars.
Correct: CEPs are more likely on the buccal.
Correct: Grade 3 extends into the furcation.

q5-E04.stem: Furcation regeneration surgery, as taught, includes each of these EXCEPT:
choices: Keeping enamel projections to help hold the graft
Sulcular incisions and a full-thickness flap
Cleaning the exposed root surfaces
A resorbable sling suture holding the membrane
why: The exception: enamel projections and pearls are taken off, because connective tissue won't attach to enamel.
Included: access comes from sulcular incisions and a full-thickness flap.
Included: the exposed roots are cleaned before grafting; without it nothing regenerates.
Included: the barrier membrane is secured with a resorbable sling suture.

q5-E05.stem: When separating and resecting a root, each of these is something to avoid EXCEPT:
choices: Taking away bone defects around the roots that stay
Exposing the interradicular bone while separating
Leaving pieces of the furcation fornix behind
Leaving the remaining roots with sharp angles
why: The exception: periodontal surgery to remove bone defects around the remaining roots is a step of the sequence.
Avoided: exposing the interradicular bone during separation.
Avoided: fornix left behind becomes a plaque trap.
Avoided: sharp angles on the remaining roots can't be cleaned and concentrate stress.

q6-01.stem: A clinician is screening intrabony defects for regenerative surgery. Which pairing of depth and radiographic angle marks the most promising defect?
choices: More than 3 mm deep, angled at 25° or less
Under 3 mm deep, angled at 25° or less
More than 3 mm deep, angled at 45° or more
Under 3 mm deep, angled at 45° or more
why: Deep and narrow is the pairing reported to respond best to conventional GTR-based regeneration: over 3 mm, at 25° or less.
A narrow angle helps, but a shallow defect gains less, and depth carried the strongest evidence of any feature.
The depth fits, but a wide angle leaves the defect unable to hold the clot and graft as a narrow one would.
This is the worst pairing: shallow and wide each predict less CAL and bone gain.

q6-02.stem: Ranked by how predictably they regenerate, which bony defect sits at the top?
choices: A 3-wall defect
A circumferential defect
A 2-wall crater
A 1-wall defect
why: With the most walls to hold the clot and supply cells, the 3-wall defect regenerates most predictably; the exam-review guide names it the best candidate.
On the decision tree a circumferential defect comes just after the 3-wall one (3-wall > circumferential ≥ 2-wall > 1-wall).
A 2-wall crater has one wall fewer than a 3-wall defect, so its outcome is less predictable.
A predominantly 1-wall defect counts as non-supportive anatomy, the least predictable configuration.

q6-03.stem: EMD's main active proteins are amelogenins. In normal tooth development, what process do these proteins take part in?
choices: Forming enamel and forming the periodontal attachment
Forming dentin and pulp by guiding root odontoblasts
Forming alveolar bone by signaling nearby osteoblasts
Resorbing primary roots so permanent teeth can erupt
why: As the main enamel matrix proteins, amelogenins take part in enamel formation and periodontal attachment formation during development, which EMD uses to regrow attachment.
Amelogenins are enamel matrix proteins; directing odontoblasts and dentin isn't their role.
They aren't bone signals. On the deck, rhPDGF-BB is the agent that is chemotactic and mitogenic for bone cells.
During development amelogenins help build tissue; clearing primary roots isn't what they do.

q6-04.stem: A surgeon adds rhPDGF-BB to a regenerative graft. Which description fits the job it does there?
choices: It attracts bone and PDL cells, makes them multiply and drives new vessels
It acts as a barrier that holds the gingival epithelium away from the root
It supplies amelogenins that copy how attachment forms during development
It serves as an osteoconductive scaffold that keeps the blood clot stable
why: rhPDGF-BB is chemotactic (draws bone and PDL cells in), mitogenic (makes them divide) and angiogenic (drives revascularization).
A physical barrier against epithelium is the GTR membrane; rhPDGF-BB is a growth factor.
Amelogenins come from EMD, the extract of enamel matrix proteins, not from rhPDGF-BB.
That describes the β-TCP scaffold the exam-review guide pairs with rhPDGF-BB: the scaffold is the matrix, the growth factor is the signal.

q6-05.stem: When β-TCP goes into a regenerative graft, what is it there to do?
choices: Act as an osteoconductive matrix that holds up soft tissue and steadies the clot
Release an antibiotic slowly into the defect to keep pocket bacteria down after surgery
Make a flap unnecessary, since the scaffold can be injected through the pocket
Condition the root surface so that new cementum can form on it after debridement
why: β-TCP is an osteoconductive scaffold: it stops soft tissue from collapsing into the defect and keeps the clot still while bone grows in.
No antibiotic is carried by β-TCP. Slow local drug release is the job of products like Arestin or Atridox, not a graft scaffold.
A flap is still needed for access and debridement; β-TCP is packed into an opened defect, not injected through the pocket.
Root conditioning is done with separate agents such as EDTA; the scaffold provides space and clot stability.

q6-06.stem: Which finding would make you expect a less predictable result from regenerative surgery?
choices: Gingiva that is thin and scalloped
Gingiva that is thick and flat
An intrabony defect over 3 mm deep
A defect angle of 25° or less on the film
why: A thin, scalloped biotype predicted more midfacial recession after regenerative surgery (Cosyn 2012), and a thin phenotype rates medium to high risk in the 2023 risk assessment.
A thick phenotype sits at the low-risk end of the 2023 risk assessment; it's the thin, scalloped one that recedes.
A depth over 3 mm helps: deeper defects gained more CAL and bone, and depth had the strongest evidence.
A narrow angle of 25° or less helps, because the defect can hold the clot and graft.

q6-07.stem: Used on its own or with a graft, EMD gives results comparable to which approach?
choices: GTR with a barrier membrane
Open flap debridement by itself
Resective osseous surgery
Scaling and root planing
why: EMD, alone or with a graft, produces outcomes similar to guided tissue regeneration, the barrier-membrane approach.
Open flap debridement is the baseline (about 1.5 mm of CAL gain) that regenerative techniques are measured against, not their match.
Osseous resection reshapes bone to eliminate the pocket and rebuilds nothing.
Root planing heals by repair, with a long junctional epithelium, rather than by regeneration.

q6-L01.stem: Under the 1996 World Workshop definition, which set of tissues has to form over an exposed root for the healing to count as regeneration?
choices: New bone, cementum and PDL
Bone plus a long junctional epithelium
Cementum plus new gingival epithelium
Bone plus new keratinized gingiva
why: All three together make a new functional attachment apparatus over a pathologically exposed root.
Epithelium lying along the root is repair, not regeneration.
Epithelium on the root is exactly what regeneration aims to prevent, and bone and PDL are missing.
Keratinized gingiva is soft tissue above the attachment, and cementum and PDL are missing.

q6-L02.stem: Two roots have healed after periodontal treatment, one by regeneration and one by repair. What is the defining difference between them?
choices: Only regeneration brings back the original architecture and function
Only regeneration happens when a barrier membrane has been placed
Repair requires a graft, while regeneration occurs without one
Repair lays down new cementum, while regeneration does not
why: Regeneration rebuilds bone, cementum and PDL as they were; repair heals without restoring them.
Grafts and biologics can regenerate tissue without a membrane; GTR is one route, not the definition.
Neither is defined by the material: after a flap or root planing with no graft, a root usually heals by repair, and graft bone fill alone isn't regeneration.
This is backward: new cementum belongs to regeneration, while repair usually leaves epithelium on the root.

q6-L03.stem: Months after open flap debridement, a section of the root shows a long junctional epithelium lying against it. Which type of healing is this?
choices: Repair
Regeneration
Osseointegration
Guided bone regeneration
why: Healing without new cementum and inserting PDL fibers is repair.
Regeneration would need new cementum, PDL and bone, not epithelium against the root.
Osseointegration describes bone bonding to an implant surface, not healing on a root.
Guided bone regeneration builds ridge bone for implants and says nothing about the root's attachment.

q6-L04.stem: The deck names four factors in periodontal tissue repair and regeneration. Three are cells, scaffolds and growth factors. What is the fourth?
choices: An adequate blood supply
Systemic antibiotic therapy
Adjustment of the occlusion
Extrusion with orthodontics
why: The blood supply keeps the clot and the new tissue alive; it is the fourth factor on the slide.
Antibiotics are adjuncts against infection, not one of the four factors.
Adjusting the occlusion may help a mobile tooth, but it isn't one of the four.
Orthodontic extrusion changes the bone level; it isn't one of the four factors.

q6-L06.stem: The 2021 systematic review compared intrabony defects 12 months after regenerative surgery. Which kind of defect showed the greatest CAL and radiographic bone gain?
choices: Deep and narrow, with more walls
Shallow and wide, with more walls
Deep and wide, with fewer walls
Shallow and narrow, with fewer walls
why: Greater depth, a narrower angle and more walls each improved CAL and radiographic bone gain.
Shallow, wide defects gain less, even when they have more walls.
A wide angle with few walls leaves nothing to contain the clot.
Shallow defects with few walls gain less even with a narrow angle; depth had the strongest evidence.

q6-L07.stem: The slides call one kind of defect anatomy "non-supportive" and list it as a risk factor for failure. Which defect is that?
choices: A defect that is mostly 1-wall
A defect that is mostly 3-wall
A defect that is circumferential
A shallow 2-wall interdental crater
why: Non-supportive anatomy is defined as a predominantly 1-wall defect, a risk factor for failure.
A 3-wall defect is the most supportive and the best candidate.
A circumferential defect ranks just behind the 3-wall on the decision tree, well ahead of the 1-wall.
A crater is a 2-wall defect between teeth, more supportive than a 1-wall defect.

q6-L08.stem: Cosyn's 2012 study treated defects with minimally invasive surgery and a bovine xenograft. Which two findings were risk factors for more recession at the midfacial?
choices: A 1-wall defect and thin, scalloped gingiva
A 3-wall defect and thick, flat gingiva
A deep defect with a narrow defect angle
Heavy smoking with a long root trunk
why: Both were risk factors for more midfacial recession in that study (Cosyn 2012).
These are the favorable findings, not the risk factors.
Depth and a narrow angle both favor regeneration.
Neither was the finding on the slide; root trunks belonged to the Session 5 furcation topic.

q6-L09.stem: A 3-wall and a 1-wall intrabony defect receive the same regenerative treatment. What gives the 3-wall defect its more predictable result?
choices: The walls hold the clot and bring in cells and vessels
The walls block epithelium from migrating down the root
It can be treated without any graft, membrane or biologic
Its depth and width can be measured exactly on a radiograph
why: A contained defect holds the clot and graft still and draws cells and blood from more surfaces.
Bone walls don't stop epithelium; that is the job of the membrane in GTR.
3-wall defects still get grafts, membranes or biologics.
A radiograph is 2-D; walls are confirmed at surgery, not measured exactly on a film.

q6-L10.stem: You need to know for sure how many bony walls an intrabony defect still has. When and how do you find out?
choices: At surgery, by seeing the defect once it is debrided
On a periapical, by measuring the defect angle
At the chair, by probing six sites around the tooth
On a vertical bitewing, by counting the walls
why: With the flap raised and the defect debrided, the walls can be seen directly.
The angle on a film helps with case selection, but a 2-D film can't reliably count walls.
Probing locates the defect but can't show which walls remain.
A bitewing is 2-D as well: the walls overlap and hide one another.

q6-L11.stem: Laurell's 1998 meta-analysis pooled 305 defects treated by open flap debridement alone. Roughly how much clinical attachment did they gain?
choices: Around 1.5 mm
Around 4 mm
Around 0.2 mm
Around 7 mm
why: The pooled CAL gain was 1.5 mm, with 1.1 mm of bone gain, across 305 defects.
4 mm was the probing depth left after treatment, not the gain.
0.2 mm is far too small; every study on the slide gained more than 1 mm.
7 mm was the starting probing depth.

q6-L12.stem: With open flap debridement alone, probing depths dropped by 3 mm (7.0 to 4.0 mm) while CAL gain was only 1.5 mm. Where did the other 1.5 mm of pocket reduction come from?
choices: The gingival margin receded
Bone fill lifted the pocket floor
New cementum formed coronally
The probe was angled differently
why: Probing depth reduction equals CAL gain plus recession: 3.0 = 1.5 + 1.5.
Any rise of the pocket base is already part of the 1.5 mm of CAL gain, and bone gain was only 1.1 mm.
New cementum would appear as CAL gain, which was only 1.5 mm.
These figures are averages over 305 defects, not a measuring error.

q6-L13.stem: In the slide's regeneration studies, open flap debridement alone serves what purpose?
choices: It sets the result regeneration has to exceed
It is a control in which no flap is raised
It is a regenerative procedure with a membrane
It is the test arm that receives a bone graft
why: Regenerative techniques are judged by how much they add to open flap debridement alone.
A flap is raised; that is what open flap debridement means.
Debridement alone uses no membrane; adding one makes it GTR.
Debridement alone uses no graft; it is what the graft groups are compared with.

q6-L15.stem: A surgeon packs DFDBA into an intrabony defect. What is the source of that bone?
choices: A human donor, from a tissue bank
The patient, from their own jaw or hip
A cow, with its protein removed
A lab, as synthetic calcium phosphate
why: DFDBA is an allograft, and an allograft comes from another human.
Bone from the patient's own body would be an autograft.
Bovine bone is a xenograft.
A synthetic material such as β-TCP is an alloplast.

q6-L16.stem: A barrier membrane is placed over a defect, under the flap, during GTR. What is it there to accomplish?
choices: Keep gingival epithelium and CT away from the root
Release growth factors into the bony defect
Spare the clinician from debriding the root
Seal the flap margins so sutures aren't needed
why: Shutting out the fast-growing soft tissue lets cells from the PDL and bone repopulate the root.
Growth factor release is what rhPDGF-BB and EMD do; the membrane is a barrier.
The root is still debrided before the membrane is placed.
The flap is still sutured over the membrane.

q6-L17.stem: Combination therapy puts a bone graft beneath the GTR membrane. What does the graft contribute?
choices: It supports the membrane and keeps the space open
It takes over from the membrane as the barrier
It gives off amelogenins that coat the root
It allows the membrane to come out earlier
why: The graft holds the membrane up so it can't collapse into the defect.
The membrane remains the barrier; the graft sits beneath it.
Amelogenins come from EMD, not from a bone graft.
The graft doesn't change how long the membrane stays in place.

q6-L18.stem: Radiographs of the deck's GTR and bone-graft cases were taken again 20 and 25 years later. What did they show?
choices: The regenerated bone had lasted
The new bone had been resorbed
Soft tissue had filled the defect
The defect was deeper than before
why: The bone gained after GTR and grafting was still present 20 and 25 years on.
That is the opposite of the long-term films: the regenerated bone held up.
The late films showed bone in the defect, not a radiolucency filled with soft tissue.
The defects didn't deepen; the bone gained stayed stable for decades.

q6-L19.stem: EMD alone tends to do poorly in a non-contained intrabony defect. What is the reason?
choices: No walls support the flap or the clot
EMD binds bone walls but not the root
Wide defects inactivate the amelogenins
No flap can be raised over the defect
why: Without walls the space collapses, so these defects usually get a graft as well.
EMD is applied to the root surface; binding to walls isn't how it works.
Defect width doesn't inactivate amelogenins; the problem is lack of space.
A flap can be raised over any defect; the issue is what holds it up.

q6-L20.stem: A researcher wants proof that a treated defect truly regenerated. Which method can give it?
choices: A histologic section
Probing depth and CAL
A periapical radiograph
A subtraction radiograph
why: Only a tissue section shows new cementum with inserting PDL fibers and new bone.
A probe can't distinguish new attachment from a long junctional epithelium.
Radiographs show bone fill, not attachment.
Subtraction shows bone change between two films, but still not attachment.

q6-L21.stem: A site gained 2 mm of CAL after regenerative surgery. Why doesn't that number on its own prove regeneration?
choices: A long JE stops the probe just as new attachment does
CAL is read from the gingival margin, which can move
CAL can rise only if a membrane was placed
Treated sites are never probed after surgery
why: A long junctional epithelium stops the probe just as new attachment would.
CAL is measured from the CEJ, a fixed point; it's probing depth that is read from the margin.
Open flap debridement alone gains about 1.5 mm of CAL with no membrane.
Sites are probed after surgery; that is how CAL gain is measured.

q6-L22.stem: A clinician follows a grafted defect with digital subtraction radiography. What does the subtraction image show?
choices: Only the change between two matched films
How many walls the defect still has
New cementum and PDL fibers on the root
A three-dimensional view of the defect
why: Two standardized films taken at different times are lined up and subtracted, so only what changed between them shows.
Walls are confirmed at surgery, not on a subtraction image.
Cementum and PDL fibers can only be shown by histology.
It is still 2-D: two periapicals, not a CBCT.

q6-L23.stem: MIST is on the deck's list of regenerative procedures. What kind of procedure is it?
choices: A minimally invasive surgery
A synthetic polymer barrier membrane
A mineralized donor bone graft
A root-conditioning medication
why: MIST, the minimally invasive surgical technique, works through a small flap that keeps the papilla.
Barrier membranes belong to GTR; MIST is a way of doing the surgery.
Donor bone grafts are allografts such as DFDBA.
Root biomodification on the deck means EMD or PDGF, not MIST.

q6-L24.stem: The deck's list includes "biomodification." Which pair of agents falls under that heading?
choices: PDGF and enamel matrix proteins
β-TCP and DFDBA
Chlorhexidine and doxycycline
Bovine bone and a collagen membrane
why: The slide lists enamel matrix protein and PDGF under biomodification.
These are grafts: an alloplast and an allograft.
These are antimicrobials (Session 8), not regenerative biologics.
These are a xenograft and a GTR barrier.

q6-L25.stem: Regenerative and resective periodontal surgery both treat bony defects. What sets regenerative therapy apart?
choices: It builds back lost support rather than taking bone away
It recontours the bone into a positive architecture
It treats furcations but never intrabony defects
It is done without a flap, unlike resective surgery
why: Regeneration adds bone, cementum and PDL; resection reshapes bone to eliminate the pocket.
Reshaping bone into positive architecture is resective (osseous) surgery.
Intrabony 2- and 3-wall defects are regeneration's main target.
Both are usually done through a flap.

q6-L26.stem: The deck's strategy map splits regeneration into two sides. One brings cells into the defect (tissue engineering). What is the side that adds no cells, drawing in the patient's own instead?
choices: Endogenous regeneration
Guided bone regeneration
Osseous resection
Host modulation therapy
why: Endogenous regeneration mobilizes the host's own cells to the site without adding any.
Guided bone regeneration builds ridge bone for implants; it isn't a side of the strategy map.
Osseous resection takes bone away; it isn't regeneration.
Host modulation (Session 8) dampens the inflammatory response; it isn't a regeneration strategy.

q6-S01.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Healing by repair brings the periodontium back to its original architecture and function.
2. Seeing bone fill on a radiograph is proof that the defect regenerated.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Neither is true: repair heals without restoring the original architecture and function, and a film shows bone fill rather than new attachment.
Both are false: bringing back the original architecture and function is what regeneration does, and only histology can prove it.
Statement 1 is false: repair, such as a long junctional epithelium after root planing, doesn't restore the original architecture and function.
Statement 2 is false: a radiograph shows bone fill, not new cementum with inserting PDL fibers; only histology proves regeneration.

q6-S02.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. After regenerative surgery, deep intrabony defects gain more CAL than shallow ones do.
2. Regeneration does better when the defect angle is wide.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 2 is false: narrower angles do better, and 25° or less is most amenable.
Statement 1 is true: deeper defects gained more CAL and bone at 12 months.
Statement 1 matches Nibali's review (deeper defects gain more); statement 2 is false, because a narrow angle, not a wide one, favors regeneration.
It's the other way around: statement 1 is true, and statement 2 is false because a wide angle works against regeneration.

q6-S03.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The 2023 regeneration risk assessment puts a Class III furcation in the medium-risk group.
2. A 2-wall defect is less supportive than a 1-wall defect.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Neither is true: a Class III furcation is high risk (Class I or II is medium), and the 1-wall defect is the least supportive.
A Class III furcation is high risk, not medium, and a 1-wall defect is non-supportive anatomy, so a 2-wall defect is the more supportive one.
Statement 1 is false as well: the risk assessment rates no furcation low, Class I or II medium and Class III high.
Statement 2 is false as well: a predominantly 1-wall defect is non-supportive anatomy, a risk factor for failure, so it is the less supportive one.

q6-S04.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. No attachment is gained when open flap debridement is done without regenerative materials.
2. The GTR membrane's job is to hold epithelium away from the root surface.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is false: open flap debridement alone gains about 1.5 mm of CAL.
Statement 2 is true: excluding epithelium from the root is the membrane's purpose.
Statement 1 is false: debridement alone gains about 1.3-1.5 mm of CAL. Statement 2 is true: the GTR membrane keeps epithelium off the root.
Debridement alone still gains about 1.5 mm of CAL, so statement 1 is false, and the membrane does exclude epithelium, so statement 2 is true.

q6-E01.stem: The deck lists several regenerative procedures. Each of these appears on that list EXCEPT:
choices: Recontouring of the bone (osseous surgery)
Grafting with bone
GTR with a barrier membrane
Biomodification with enamel matrix proteins
why: This is the one that doesn't belong: recontouring bone is resective therapy (Session 5), which reshapes bone to remove the pocket instead of rebuilding support.
Bone grafting is on the regenerative list; the deck's graft case used DFDBA.
GTR is on the list: a barrier membrane keeps epithelium off the root so PDL and bone cells can repopulate it.
Enamel matrix proteins are on the list, under biomodification alongside PDGF.

q6-E03.stem: Each of these is a way the slides evaluate whether periodontal regeneration happened EXCEPT:
choices: Testing pulp vitality
Histologic sections
Clinical measurements
Radiographs
why: This is the exception: a pulp test tells you nothing about the attachment apparatus.
Histology is on the slide, and it is the only proof.
Clinical measurements such as PD and CAL are on the slide.
Radiographs, subtraction included, are on the slide.

q6-M01.stem: A defect is examined histologically after surgery. Which tissues would have to be newly formed for it to count as true regeneration? Select all that apply.
choices: Bone
Cementum
Periodontal ligament
A long junctional epithelium
Keratinized gingiva
why: Belongs: new bone is one of the three required tissues.
Belongs: new cementum is one of the three required tissues.
Belongs: new PDL is one of the three required tissues.
Doesn't belong: a long junctional epithelium on the root means repair.
Doesn't belong: keratinized gingiva is soft tissue, not part of the attachment apparatus.

q6-M02.stem: You are deciding whether an intrabony defect suits regenerative surgery. Which findings count in its favor? Select all that apply.
choices: A depth over 3 mm
A radiographic angle no wider than 25°
Several bony walls remaining
Thin, scalloped gingiva
Mostly 1-wall anatomy
why: Belongs: deeper defects gain more.
Belongs: narrow defects respond best.
Belongs: more walls contain the defect.
Doesn't belong: it is a risk factor for midfacial recession.
Doesn't belong: this is non-supportive anatomy, a risk factor for failure.

q6-M03.stem: Which of these appear on the deck's list of factors in periodontal tissue repair and regeneration? Select all that apply.
choices: The cells
A scaffold
Growth factors
The blood supply
Systemic antibiotics
why: Belongs: cells are what build the new tissue.
Belongs: a scaffold gives the cells something to grow into.
Belongs: growth factors recruit the cells and make them multiply.
Belongs: the blood supply keeps the clot and new tissue alive.
Doesn't belong: antibiotics aren't one of the four factors.

q6-L27.stem: The AAP Regeneration Workshop decision tree begins with the patient. What must be dealt with first, before the site itself is evaluated?
choices: Uncontrolled systemic disease, tobacco and poor hygiene
The defect's depth, its width and how many walls remain
The height of the smile line and the gingival biotype
Which graft, membrane or biologic will be used
why: The tree says to address first uncontrolled systemic conditions, tobacco and other behaviors, and inadequate hygiene.
Defect configuration comes later, once the site is being assessed.
Esthetic risk is weighed alongside the defect, not first.
Choosing the material is the last step, driven by the defect.

q6-L28.stem: Following the decision tree, a site has an intrabony defect less than 3 mm deep and probing depths greater than 5 mm. What is the suggested path?
choices: Think about osseous surgery
Regenerate it with a GTR membrane
Use combination therapy with a graft
Extract it and replace the tooth
why: A defect under 3 mm isn't a regeneration case, and with probing depths over 5 mm the tree points to osseous surgery.
Regeneration begins at an intrabony defect of 3 mm or more.
Combination therapy is the tree's choice for a 1-wall defect of 3 mm or more.
Extraction is for an unfavorable or hopeless prognosis, not for a shallow defect.

q6-L29.stem: For intrabony defects 3 mm or deeper, how does the decision tree rank wall configurations from most to least predictable?
choices: 3-wall; circumferential or 2-wall; then 1-wall
Circumferential; 3-wall or 2-wall; then 1-wall
2-wall; 3-wall or circumferential; then 1-wall
1-wall; circumferential or 2-wall; then 3-wall
why: The tree ranks 3-wall > circumferential ≥ 2-wall > 1-wall, with narrow defects ahead of wide ones.
A circumferential defect comes after the 3-wall defect, not before it.
A 2-wall defect ranks below the 3-wall: with one wall fewer it is less predictable.
This is reversed: the 1-wall defect is least predictable and the 3-wall most.

q6-L30.stem: Surgery reveals a 3-wall intrabony defect more than 3 mm deep and less than 2 mm wide. Which treatment does the decision tree give for it?
choices: Any one of a graft, a GTR membrane or a biologic
A reinforced membrane together with a bone graft
Combination therapy or a cellular bone allograft
Osseous surgery to flatten out the defect
why: A narrow, contained defect does well with any one of the three.
Reinforced membranes and combinations are for wide (3 mm or more) or 2-wall defects.
Combination therapy or a cellular bone allograft is the choice for 1-wall defects.
Osseous surgery is for defects under 3 mm deep, not a deep 3-wall defect.

q6-L31.stem: At surgery the defect turns out to have only one bony wall. What treatment does the decision tree call for?
choices: Combination therapy, or a cellular bone allograft
EMD or another biologic placed alone in the defect
A standard GTR membrane placed without a graft
Non-surgical care followed by re-evaluation
why: With nothing to contain it, a 1-wall defect gets combination therapy or a cellular bone allograft.
A biologic alone suits narrow 3-wall defects; a 1-wall defect has no space to hold it.
A membrane on its own would collapse into a defect with no walls to support it.
Non-surgical care fits defects under 3 mm with probing depths of 5 mm or less and no bleeding.

q6-L32.stem: A patient with an intrabony defect has a high smile line, a thin biotype and a lost papilla at the site. What does the decision tree recommend?
choices: Skip the GTR membrane and consider soft-tissue grafting
Place a reinforced GTR membrane to shield the papilla
Choose osseous surgery instead of regenerating
Wait to operate until the papilla regrows
why: This is high esthetic risk: proceed only if the patient accepts the risk, avoid a GTR membrane and consider soft-tissue augmentation.
A membrane, reinforced or not, is exactly what the tree says to avoid when esthetic risk is high.
Osseous surgery takes bone away and worsens esthetics; the tree still allows regeneration if the patient accepts the risk.
A lost papilla doesn't grow back by itself, so waiting changes nothing.

q6-L33.stem: A patient smokes 15 cigarettes a day. Where does that put them in the 2023 regeneration risk assessment?
choices: In the high-risk group
In the medium-risk group
In the low-risk group
Smoking isn't rated there
why: More than 10 cigarettes a day is rated high risk.
Medium is for 10 cigarettes a day or fewer, and 15 is over that line.
Only a nonsmoker is rated low risk.
Smoking is one of the table's patient factors, rated low, medium or high.

q6-L34.stem: A patient's full-mouth plaque score is 20%. How does the 2023 risk assessment rate it?
choices: As medium risk
As low risk
As high risk
It isn't one of the factors
why: The medium band is 16 to 24%, and 20% falls inside it.
Low risk is 15% or less, and 20% is above that.
High risk starts at 25%, and 20% is below that.
Plaque control, measured by full-mouth plaque score, is one of the table's patient factors.

q6-L35.stem: The 2023 risk assessment rates a "contained" intrabony defect as low risk. What qualifies a defect as contained?
choices: It involves just 1 or 2 sides of the root
It involves 3 or more sides of the root
It measures less than 3 mm in depth
It lies inside a furcation area
why: Contained means only 1 or 2 sides of the root are involved, which is low risk.
Involving 3 or more sides makes a defect non-contained, which is high risk.
Containment refers to how many root surfaces the defect wraps, not its depth.
Furcation involvement is rated as its own factor.

q6-L36.stem: Under the 2023 regeneration risk assessment, which tooth's endodontic status falls in the high-risk group?
choices: One whose pulp is nonvital
One with adequate root canal treatment
One with existing root canal therapy to check
A vital one whose defect ends short of the apex
why: A nonvital tooth is high risk, as are inadequate RCT and a defect reaching the apex of a vital tooth.
Adequate endodontic treatment is rated low risk.
Existing root canal therapy is medium risk and needs careful evaluation.
A vital tooth whose defect doesn't reach the apex is low risk.

q6-L37.stem: The 2023 risk assessment rates the root surface at the defect. Which root anatomy lands in the high-risk group?
choices: Two roots fused together
A root with a concavity
A root that is flat
A root trunk that is long
why: Two fused roots are high risk: hard to debride and to regenerate.
A concave root is rated medium risk.
A flat root surface is rated low risk.
Root trunk length isn't a row in the table; it was a Session 5 furcation topic.

q6-L38.stem: Of the morphology features compared in the 2021 meta-analysis, which one was backed by the strongest evidence as a predictor of bone gain?
choices: How deep the defect is
How wide its angle is
How many walls it has
How thick the gingiva is
why: Depth had the strongest evidence: defects shallower than 4 mm gained about 0.75 mm less bone.
A narrower angle helped (under 37°: about 0.94 mm more bone), but its evidence was weaker than depth's.
More walls helped (1-wall vs 3-wall: about 1.2 mm less bone), but the evidence was weaker than for depth.
Gingival thickness is soft tissue, not defect morphology; the review compared depth, angle and walls.

q6-P04.stem: Using the patient box and the AAP decision tree, which treatment suits the defect on the mesial of #30?
choices: A graft combined with a GTR membrane or a biologic
EMD or another biologic, placed by itself in the defect
Osseous surgery to remove the defect
Extraction followed by an implant
why: A 2-wall defect gets a reinforced GTR membrane, a graft plus membrane, or a graft plus biologic.
A biologic alone is for narrow 3-wall or circumferential defects; a 2-wall defect needs more support, such as a reinforced GTR membrane or a graft with a membrane or a biologic.
Osseous surgery is for defects under 3 mm; this one is 5 mm deep and regenerable.
A low-risk patient with a regenerable defect isn't a case for extraction.

q7-01.stem: An implant is being judged against the criteria for success. Which finding fits a successful implant?
choices: Under 0.2 mm of vertical bone lost per year after the first year in function
Under 1 mm of vertical bone lost each year once the first year in function is over
A little mobility (less than 0.5 mm) after the implant is loaded
A thin radiolucency around the implant, provided the patient has no pain
why: Right: after its first year in function, a successful implant loses less than 0.2 mm of bone a year, and it is also immobile, free of radiolucency and painless.
Wrong: a full millimeter a year is five times what success allows; the limit after year one is under 0.2 mm a year.
Wrong: success requires an immobile implant. Mobility of the implant body once it is loaded signals lost osseointegration.
Wrong: a successful implant has no radiolucency around it, whether or not it hurts.

q7-02.stem: Smoking makes certain periodontal pathogens harder to clear. Which group did the lecture name?
choices: P. gingivalis, B. forsythus and A. actinomycetemcomitans
Lactobacilli, Streptococcus mutans and Actinomyces species
Oral yeasts such as Candida albicans
Actinomyces species and Lactobacillus acidophilus
why: Right: in current smokers, A.a., P. gingivalis and B. forsythus are the pathogens that are harder to eradicate.
Wrong: S. mutans and lactobacilli go with caries, and Actinomyces is a gram-positive early colonizer; none of them is on the smokers' list.
Wrong: Candida and its relatives are fungi, not the periodontal pathogens named for smokers.
Wrong: lactobacilli are caries bacteria and Actinomyces is an early gram-positive colonizer; neither was named as harder to clear in smokers.

q7-03.stem: A smoker is about to have implant surgery. Which change in their immune response did the lecture link to smoking?
choices: Neutrophils move to and engulf bacteria poorly
More T helper cells and B lymphocytes circulate
Less IL-6 and TNF-alpha is made by the tissue
Collagenase activity in the healing tissue falls
why: Right: smoking impairs neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis, so the first line of defense in a healing wound is weaker.
Wrong: smoking lowers T helper and B cell numbers rather than raising them.
Wrong: smoking pushes IL-6 and TNF-alpha up, which adds inflammation.
Wrong: smoking increases collagenase activity, adding to the breakdown of tissue.

q7-04.stem: Through what physiologic effect does nicotine hurt healing after implant surgery?
choices: Revascularization is impaired in both soft and hard tissue
Soft tissue heals poorly, while bone heals normally
Bone heals poorly, while soft tissue heals normally
New vessels form faster at first, but the mature tissue is weak
why: Right: nicotine impairs revascularization, the first step of healing, in soft and hard tissue alike, so wounds heal poorly and more implants fail.
Wrong: hard tissue is affected too; the revascularization problem reaches bone as well as soft tissue.
Wrong: soft tissue is affected too; nicotine impairs revascularization in both tissues.
Wrong: nicotine constricts vessels and impairs revascularization from the start; it doesn't speed it up.

q7-05.stem: A patient with diabetes asks for an implant. Which situation makes implant therapy contraindicated?
choices: Their glycemic control is poor
They were diagnosed more than 10 years ago
They have type 1, not type 2, diabetes
They are also a smoker
why: Right: poorly controlled diabetes contraindicates implants; with optimal control, even the number of years since diagnosis didn't change implant survival.
Wrong: how long someone has had diabetes didn't affect survival under optimal control; control, measured by HbA1c, is the deciding factor.
Wrong: the lecture didn't make the type the issue; glycemic control matters in both type 1 and type 2.
Wrong: smoking is a separate risk factor with its own dose-response, but whether diabetes rules out an implant depends on glycemic control.

q7-06.stem: A patient smokes and also tests positive for the IL-1 genotype. How do the two combine for peri-implantitis risk?
choices: They act synergistically, giving the highest risk
They add together, without interacting
The genotype outweighs smoking, which adds little
Smoking outweighs the genotype, which adds little
why: Right: the combination is synergistic and carries the highest peri-implantitis risk, more than either factor on its own.
Wrong: the two interact, so together they are worse than a simple sum.
Wrong: smoking contributes a great deal on top of the genotype; the pair carries the highest risk.
Wrong: the IL-1 genotype contributes a great deal on top of smoking; the two are synergistic.

q7-08.stem: A patient carries an IL-1 gene polymorphism. How is their inflammatory response to bacteria likely to differ?
choices: They overreact with hyper-responsive inflammation
They underreact, with a blunted inflammation
They react normally but build up more plaque
They mount only an anti-inflammatory response
why: Right: IL-1 polymorphisms are linked to a hyper-responsive inflammatory reaction to the same bacterial challenge, and smoking makes it synergistic.
Wrong: the reaction is exaggerated, not dampened; that overreaction is what destroys tissue.
Wrong: the polymorphism changes how the host reacts, not how much plaque forms.
Wrong: IL-1 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine, and the polymorphisms amplify inflammation instead of suppressing it.

q8-01.stem: A clinician is deciding where antibiotics fit in a periodontal treatment plan. What role does the course give them?
choices: A supplement to SRP or surgery, not a stand-alone treatment
The opening treatment, given before any debridement
A routine prescription for every new periodontitis diagnosis
A substitute for SRP when the patient would rather skip it
why: Right: systemic or local, antibiotics only ever add to surgical or non-surgical therapy and come after SRP; they are never a monotherapy.
Wrong: an intact biofilm shields the bacteria from the drug, so debridement has to come first; antibiotics alone aren't indicated.
Wrong: they are kept for selected cases (acute infection with systemic signs, aggressive and refractory periodontitis), not given routinely.
Wrong: the biofilm and calculus still have to come off mechanically, so an antibiotic never takes the place of SRP.

q8-02.stem: A patient presents with acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (ANUG). Which drug does the lecture name for this condition?
choices: Metronidazole
Azithromycin
Ciprofloxacin
Doxycycline
why: Right: it kills obligate anaerobes like the spirochetes behind ANUG, and it is often combined with amoxicillin.
Wrong: azithromycin is the macrolide taken away from meals, not the lecture's ANUG drug.
Wrong: anaerobes are largely resistant to ciprofloxacin, which is why it gets paired with metronidazole when it is used at all.
Wrong: doxycycline, a tetracycline, is for A.a. or, at sub-antimicrobial doses, for collagenase; it isn't the ANUG choice.

q8-03.stem: You tell a patient to take their antibiotic 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating, since a meal would cut how much they absorb. Which drug did you prescribe?
choices: Azithromycin
Clarithromycin
Augmentin
Metronidazole
why: Right: food markedly lowers azithromycin absorption, so the Z-Pak goes down 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal.
Wrong: clarithromycin (Biaxin) is the macrolide that absorbs well whether or not there is food.
Wrong: Augmentin is taken with food, to soften the GI upset it can bring.
Wrong: food slows metronidazole's absorption without lowering it; its warnings are alcohol and orange-red urine.

q8-04.stem: A patient is warned to avoid excessive sun and told the drug absorbs fastest 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. Which antibiotic fits?
choices: Ciprofloxacin
Clarithromycin
Metronidazole
Clindamycin
why: Right: ciprofloxacin is absorbed most rapidly 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals and carries a phototoxic-reaction risk.
Wrong: clarithromycin absorbs well with or without food, and its caution is pregnancy, not phototoxicity.
Wrong: food delays metronidazole without reducing it, and its cautions are alcohol and urine color.
Wrong: clindamycin's known risk is C. difficile colitis, not a reaction to sunlight.

q8-05.stem: Several days into an antibiotic course, a patient develops pseudomembranous colitis from C. difficile overgrowth. Which drug is the classic culprit?
choices: Clindamycin
Amoxicillin
Metronidazole
Doxycycline
why: Right: clindamycin is the drug classically linked to C. difficile overgrowth and pseudomembranous colitis.
Wrong: amoxicillin's usual problems are allergy and GI upset, not this colitis.
Wrong: the lecture doesn't tie metronidazole to colitis; its warnings are alcohol (a disulfiram-like reaction), orange-red urine and a stronger warfarin effect.
Wrong: doxycycline disturbs gut flora less than tetracycline; its cautions are the tetracycline ones (dairy, sun, developing teeth).

q8-06.stem: The lecture says tetracycline may be indicated when one particular pathogen is the prominent one. Which pathogen is it?
choices: A. actinomycetemcomitans
Porphyromonas gingivalis
Spirochetes like Treponema
Early gram-positive cocci
why: Right: the lecture ties tetracycline's indication to sites where A.a. is the prominent pathogen.
Wrong: P. gingivalis is a red-complex pathogen, but tetracycline's indication is linked to A.a.
Wrong: spirochetes are obligate anaerobes, metronidazole's target (as in ANUG).
Wrong: gram-positive cocci are early plaque colonizers, not the organism that calls for tetracycline.

q8-07.stem: A patient asks why they can't wash down their tetracycline with milk or take it with an antacid. What is the reason?
choices: Di- and trivalent cations block its absorption
Calcium makes the kidneys clear it faster
A higher stomach pH degrades the drug
It turns bactericidal instead of bacteriostatic
why: Right: calcium, magnesium, aluminum and iron bind tetracycline in the gut, so far less of it is absorbed.
Wrong: the trouble is in the gut, not the kidneys; the cations bind the drug before absorption.
Wrong: stomach pH isn't destroying the drug; the cations bind it so it can't be absorbed.
Wrong: tetracycline stays bacteriostatic; the cations just keep it from being absorbed.

q8-08.stem: What job does the clavulanic acid in Augmentin do for the amoxicillin it is combined with?
choices: It counters beta-lactamase resistance
It kills the bacteria by itself
It relieves GI upset from the drug
It lengthens the drug's absorption window
why: Right: clavulanic acid inactivates β-lactamase, the bacterial enzyme that would otherwise destroy amoxicillin.
Wrong: amoxicillin does the killing; clavulanate only protects it.
Wrong: it doesn't treat GI upset; Augmentin tends to cause more GI upset than amoxicillin alone.
Wrong: absorption isn't changed; clavulanate blocks β-lactamase so the amoxicillin survives.

q8-09.stem: A pregnant patient needs an antibiotic. Which of these is flagged to avoid because it caused fetal abnormalities in animal studies?
choices: Clarithromycin
Azithromycin
Clindamycin
Amoxicillin
why: Right: clarithromycin (Biaxin) caused fetal abnormalities in animals and is pregnancy category C, so it is avoided in pregnancy.
Wrong: the lecture's azithromycin cautions are food timing (1 hour before or 2 hours after meals) and the macrolide interactions, not pregnancy.
Wrong: clindamycin's caution is C. difficile colitis, not pregnancy.
Wrong: amoxicillin's cautions are allergy and β-lactamase inactivation, not fetal abnormalities.

q8-10.stem: Which group of bacteria falls within metronidazole's spectrum?
choices: Only obligate anaerobes, such as spirochetes
Only aerobic gram-positive cocci
Aerobes and anaerobes alike, as with amoxicillin
Facultative anaerobes, A.a. above all
why: Right: metronidazole disrupts the DNA of obligate anaerobes like spirochetes and nothing else.
Wrong: it has no effect on aerobes, gram-positive cocci included.
Wrong: unlike amoxicillin it does nothing to aerobes; its spectrum is obligate anaerobes only.
Wrong: A.a. is a facultative anaerobe that metronidazole covers poorly, which is why amoxicillin is added.

q8-12.stem: Arestin was just placed in a pocket. For how long should the patient leave that site unflossed?
choices: 10 days
7 days
12 hours
24 hours
why: Right: no flossing the Arestin site for 10 days (brushing waits only 12 hours).
Wrong: 7 days is Atridox's rule for brushing, flossing and chewing at the site.
Wrong: 12 hours is the Arestin wait for brushing, not flossing.
Wrong: 24 hours isn't an Arestin rule; brushing waits 12 hours and flossing 10 days.

q8-13.stem: Through which mediator do NSAIDs mainly support periodontal healing?
choices: PGE2, which upregulates osteoclastic resorption
Collagenase, which they inhibit in the gingiva
IL-1 receptors on fibroblasts and osteoclasts
Bacterial DNA gyrase in the subgingival flora
why: Right: NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis, PGE2 included, and PGE2 upregulates osteoclastic bone resorption.
Wrong: collagenase inhibition is how sub-antimicrobial doxycycline (Periostat) works.
Wrong: NSAIDs act on prostaglandin synthesis, not IL-1 receptors.
Wrong: DNA gyrase is the fluoroquinolones' target (ciprofloxacin); NSAIDs aren't antibacterial.

q8-14.stem: Periostat delivers doxycycline at a dose too low to be antimicrobial. What, then, is its benefit in periodontal disease?
choices: It inhibits collagenase rather than acting as an antibiotic
It kills anaerobes directly, just at a smaller dose than usual
It numbs the gingiva so SRP and maintenance are easier to tolerate
It stands in for SRP in patients who can't manage mechanical therapy
why: Right: the dose can't kill bacteria; it works on the host by inhibiting collagenase, the enzyme that breaks down attachment.
Wrong: the sub-antimicrobial dose is deliberate; it kills nothing and acts on host collagenase.
Wrong: Periostat is a host-modulation drug with no anesthetic action.
Wrong: host modulation only adds to SRP and maintenance; it never replaces mechanical therapy.

q8-15.stem: A patient on bisphosphonates needs an extraction. Which complication is the main dental concern?
choices: Osteonecrosis of the jaw
Staining of the teeth
Overgrowth of the gingiva
Dry mouth (xerostomia)
why: Right: bisphosphonates suppress osteoclasts, and the risk after extractions or surgery is osteonecrosis of the jaw.
Wrong: tooth staining belongs to the tetracyclines.
Wrong: gingival overgrowth comes from phenytoin, cyclosporine and calcium channel blockers.
Wrong: many drugs cause xerostomia, but the key bisphosphonate risk is osteonecrosis of the jaw.

q9-01.stem: A patient asks which teeth and surfaces are the usual places for gums to pull back. What do you tell him?
choices: The buccal surfaces of maxillary molars and mandibular incisors
The lingual surfaces of mandibular molars and maxillary incisors
The palatal surfaces of maxillary premolars and molars
The distal surfaces of third molars in both arches
why: Correct: recession is most common on the buccal of maxillary molars (the first molars especially) and of mandibular central incisors, with canines also often affected.
Recession is not most common on lingual surfaces; the buccal of maxillary molars and mandibular incisors is where it usually shows up.
The palate is thick orthokeratinized tissue and the usual graft donor site; recession is most common buccally.
Third molar distals are not one of the common sites; the buccal of maxillary molars and mandibular incisors is.

q9-02.stem: Both grafts come from the palate. What separates a free gingival graft (FGG) from a connective tissue graft (CTG) in what they contain?
choices: The FGG carries epithelium and the CTG does not
The CTG carries epithelium and the FGG does not
Both carry epithelium, and the CTG is the thicker one
Neither carries epithelium, and the FGG is the wider one
why: Correct: an FGG is palatal epithelium together with the lamina propria beneath it; a CTG is the connective tissue alone, with no epithelium.
This is backward: the FGG keeps the epithelium and the CTG has none.
Only the FGG has epithelium; a CTG is connective tissue alone, not simply a thicker FGG.
The FGG does have epithelium, which is why it can be left exposed; only the CTG lacks it.

q9-03.stem: You want to avoid harvesting the palate and use donated human tissue instead. Which allograft is used most often in periodontal plastic surgery?
choices: An acellular dermal matrix
A free gingival graft
A connective tissue graft
A porcine collagen matrix
why: Correct: processed human dermis with the cells removed (AlloDerm is one example) is the most common soft tissue allograft, and it spares the patient a palatal donor site.
An FGG comes from the patient's own palate, which makes it an autograft rather than an allograft.
A CTG is taken from the patient's own palate, so it is an autograft rather than an allograft.
Porcine (and bovine) products exist, but tissue from another species is a xenograft, not an allograft.

q9-04.stem: When planning a palatal harvest, what does a high, deep palatal vault give the surgeon?
choices: More room for error during the harvest
A donor site that heals faster
A thicker epithelial layer to harvest
A donor site that needs no sutures
why: Correct: in a high, deep vault the greater palatine neurovascular bundle lies farther from the harvest site, so there is the most margin for error.
The advantage is anatomic safety, the distance from the greater palatine bundle, not quicker healing.
Palatal epithelium is thin (0.3-0.6 mm) whatever the vault's shape; depth matters because of the distance to the bundle.
The donor site is managed as usual; the vault's depth is about safety, not about skipping sutures.

q9-05.stem: Probing finds deep readings from swollen gingiva, but there is no attachment loss. What is the right management for this pseudopocket?
choices: Better home care with professional scaling
A gingivectomy to cut away the extra tissue
An apically positioned flap to reduce the pocket
Extracting the involved teeth
why: Correct: a pseudopocket is gingival swelling without attachment loss, so improved oral hygiene and professional scaling manage it.
Surgery is not the first step; with no attachment loss, plaque control and scaling resolve the swelling.
An apically positioned flap is surgical pocket reduction for true pockets with bone loss, not for a pseudopocket.
Extraction is never indicated here; with no attachment loss, the teeth are not threatened.

q9-06.stem: A patient on a calcium channel blocker has fibrotic gingival overgrowth. Which plan covers the management?
choices: Hygiene and scaling, a gingivectomy, and asking the physician about the drug
Hygiene and scaling only, because plaque is the primary factor
Antibiotics only, because infection rather than the drug drives the growth
Watching it, because drug-induced overgrowth always goes away as the patient adapts
why: Correct: hygiene and scaling come first, but the fibrotic tissue must be resected with a gingivectomy, and the physician may be asked about switching the drug.
Plaque is the primary factor, but the drug makes the tissue fibrotic with extra collagen, so hygiene and scaling alone won't resolve it.
Plaque-induced gingivitis is the primary factor and the drug modifies it; antibiotics don't remove fibrotic overgrowth.
It does not resolve while the drug continues; the fibrotic tissue must be resected, and a drug change may be needed.

q9-07.stem: Which treatment do Type 1B and Type 2B altered passive eruption both call for?
choices: A flap with osseous surgery
A gingivectomy by itself
An apically positioned flap by itself
Orthodontics with orthognathic surgery
why: Correct: with the crest at or within about 1 mm of the CEJ, there is no room for the supracrestal attachment, so bone is removed under a full-thickness flap (in 2B the flap is also positioned apically).
A gingivectomy alone suits only Type 1A, where the bone is in its normal range; in 1B the tissue would grow back.
An apically positioned flap without bone surgery suits Type 2A, where the bone is in place; the B types also need bone recontouring.
Orthognathic surgery treats vertical maxillary excess, a long maxilla; altered passive eruption is treated with crown lengthening.

q9-08.stem: Coslet's Type 1 and Type 2 altered passive eruption differ in what way?
choices: Type 1: a wide gingival band, MGJ apical to the crest; Type 2: a normal band, MGJ at the CEJ
Type 1: the crest at or near the CEJ; Type 2: the crest 1.5 to 2 mm from it
Type 1: naturally short crowns; Type 2: gingiva covering normal-length crowns
Type 2: a wide gingival band, MGJ apical to the crest; Type 1: a normal band, MGJ at the CEJ
why: Correct: the type is set by the band of gingiva. Type 1 is wide with the MGJ apical to the alveolar crest; Type 2 is normal with the MGJ usually at the CEJ.
The crest's position defines the subcategory, A (1.5-2 mm from the CEJ) or B (at or within about 1 mm), not the type.
Both types are gingiva still covering part of normal-length crowns; naturally short anatomical crowns are a different cause of short clinical crowns.
This reverses them: the wide band with the MGJ apical to the crest is Type 1.

q9-09.stem: On the facial exam of a patient with a gummy smile, the lower third of the face is longer than the other two. Which diagnosis does that point to?
choices: Vertical maxillary excess
Altered passive eruption
RT3 recession
Necrotizing gingivitis
why: Correct: an increased lower facial third suggests vertical maxillary excess, a skeletal cause of a gummy smile.
Altered passive eruption is a tooth and gingiva problem (short clinical crowns); it doesn't change facial proportions.
RT3 is a recession class and has nothing to do with facial proportions.
Necrotizing gingivitis is an acute infection and doesn't change the lower facial third.

q9-12.stem: Using the cited tooth-width proportion, a central incisor measures 1.6 units. About what width does that predict for the lateral incisor?
choices: About 1 unit
About 1.6 units
About 0.6 units
About 2 units
why: Correct: in the golden proportion, a central of about 1.6 units pairs with a lateral of about 1 unit.
1.6 units is the central's own width, not the lateral's.
About 0.6 units is the figure for the visible canine, not the lateral.
2 units would be wider than the central; the lateral is narrower, about 1 unit.

q1-S03.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The preferred measure for staging is interdental CAL, and radiographic bone loss is the second-choice measure.
2. A patient's stage comes from the worst single site in the whole mouth.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Both hold: interdental CAL is the gold standard with radiographic bone loss as the second choice, and the worst site sets the stage.
Both are true: CAL comes first, radiographic bone loss second, and the single worst site decides the stage.
Statement 2 is true as well: each patient gets one stage, taken from the worst site.
Statement 1 is true as well: interdental CAL is the gold standard and radiographic bone loss is second.

q2-S01.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Of the six sutures compared on the course chart, none irritates tissue more than silk.
2. Compared with a single-strand suture, a braided one holds on to more bacteria.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Right: both hold; silk's tissue reaction is the worst on the chart, and a braid wicks and traps bacteria more than a monofilament.
Neither is false: silk irritates tissue the most, and braiding does trap more bacteria.
Statement 2 is true as well: a braid wicks and traps bacteria, which is the reason silk scores so poorly.
Statement 1 is true as well: silk is rated very bad for tissue reaction, the worst of the six.

q2-S02.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Like poly-glycolic acid (PGA), poly(glycolide-co-caprolactone) (PGCL) is a synthetic resorbable with a braided construction.
2. PGA is gentler on tissue than PGCL.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Neither holds: PGCL is a single strand (only silk and PGA are braided), and PGCL, not PGA, is the gentler one.
Right: both are false; PGCL is a monofilament, and its tissue reaction is rated great while braided PGA's is bad.
Statement 1 is false: PGCL is a monofilament; on the chart only silk and PGA are braided.
Statement 2 is false: braided PGA irritates tissue more; monofilament PGCL is the gentle one.

q2-S04.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. For a pure soft-tissue graft, PTFE is the suture usually picked.
2. Poly-propylene is a non-resorbable suture made of braided strands.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Neither holds: PTFE is used for every surgery except pure soft-tissue grafts, and poly-propylene is a single strand.
Right: both are false; PTFE isn't the soft-tissue graft suture, and of the six only silk and PGA are braided.
Statement 1 is false: PTFE is used for every type of surgery except pure soft-tissue grafting.
Statement 2 is false: poly-propylene is a nylon-like monofilament; only silk and PGA are braided.

q3-S02.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Roughly one person in ten stays free of periodontitis no matter how good or poor their oral hygiene is.
2. Roughly 10-15% of people fail to respond to standard periodontal therapy.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 2 is false: non-responders to standard therapy are 20-25%; 10-15% is the share at risk for severe disease.
Statement 1 is true: about 10% of people resist periodontitis whatever their hygiene.
Right: about 10% are resistant, so 1 is true; non-responders are 20-25%, not 10-15%, so 2 is false.
This is backwards: statement 1 is true (10% resistant) and statement 2 is false (non-responders are 20-25%).

q3-S03.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Once McGuire & Nunn labels a tooth questionable, it usually keeps that label at later visits.
2. A tooth McGuire & Nunn calls poor can still be retained, though it takes significant effort.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is false: a questionable tooth doesn't stay questionable; it worsens to hopeless or improves to poor.
Statement 2 is true: a poor tooth (attachment loss, Class II furcation, mobility) can be kept with significant effort.
This is backwards: statement 1 is false (a questionable tooth moves on to hopeless or back to poor) and statement 2 is true.
Right: a questionable tooth doesn't stay put, so 1 is false; a poor tooth can be kept with significant effort, so 2 is true.

q4-S01.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The main reason for doing scaling and root planing is to eliminate the pocket.
2. One aim of SRP is to move the pocket flora away from gram-negative and toward gram-positive organisms.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is false: pockets get shallower after SRP, but eliminating them isn't the rationale.
Statement 2 is true: shifting the flora from gram-negative toward gram-positive is one of SRP's goals.
This has it backward: statement 1 is false (pocket elimination isn't the rationale) and statement 2 is true.
Correct: pocket elimination isn't why SRP is done, so 1 is false, and the flora shift toward gram-positive is a goal, so 2 is true.

q4-S02.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Following SRP, reattachment of the junctional epithelium takes about 4-6 weeks.
2. Following SRP, connective tissue is reattached to the root by about 7-10 days.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Neither statement is true: the junctional epithelium reattaches in about 7-10 days, and connective tissue takes about 4-6 weeks.
Correct: both are false, because the two times are swapped. The junctional epithelium takes about 7-10 days; connective tissue takes about 4-6 weeks.
Statement 1 isn't true: the junctional epithelium reattaches in about 7-10 days, not 4-6 weeks.
Statement 2 isn't true: connective tissue reattaches in about 4-6 weeks, not 7-10 days.

q4-S03.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Scaling works on surfaces above and below the gingival margin.
2. Root planing works on surfaces above and below the gingival margin.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 2 is false: root planing is subgingival only and works on root surfaces alone.
Statement 1 is true: scaling removes deposits from tooth and root surfaces both supra- and subgingivally.
Correct: scaling works both above and below the margin, so 1 is true; root planing is subgingival only, so 2 is false.
This has it backward: statement 1 is true (scaling is both) and statement 2 is false (root planing is subgingival only).

q4-S04.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Scaling and root planing is done without direct vision, relying on the sense of touch.
2. One limitation of SRP is that motile bacteria invade the soft-tissue lining of the pocket.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Correct: both are true. SRP is blind and tactile, and it can't reach motile bacteria that have invaded the pocket lining.
Neither is false; both appear on the taught list of SRP limitations.
Statement 2 is true as well: SRP reaches only the root surface, not bacteria that have moved into the soft-tissue lining.
Statement 1 is true as well: SRP is done blind, guided by tactile sensation, which is one of its limitations.

q1-A01.stem: Of these complexity factors, which one is on the Stage 4 list and not the Stage 3 list?
choices: Drifting, flaring or a collapsed bite
Class II furcation involvement
An angular bony defect of 3 mm or more
Pockets that probe 6 mm or deeper
why: Bite collapse, drifting or flaring mean complex rehabilitation is needed, a Stage 4 factor.
A Class II furcation is one of the Stage 3 complexity factors.
