Vertical (angular) bone loss of 3 mm or more is a Stage 3 complexity factor.
Pockets of 6 mm or more are on the Stage 3 complexity list.

q1-A02.stem: Each of these findings is on the Stage 4 complexity list EXCEPT:
choices: Class II or III furcation involvement
Under 20 teeth left (10 opposing pairs)
Trouble chewing (masticatory dysfunction)
Mobility of degree 2 or greater
why: A Class II or III furcation is a Stage 3 complexity factor, so it is the one that doesn't fit.
Fewer than 20 remaining teeth (10 opposing pairs) is a Stage 4 factor.
Masticatory dysfunction is a Stage 4 factor, a sign complex rehabilitation is needed.
Mobility of degree 2 or more, from secondary occlusal trauma, is a Stage 4 factor.

q1-A03.stem: A patient has a defect in the edentulous ridge. What role does it play in staging?
choices: Moderate is Stage 3; severe is Stage 4
Any ridge defect at all means Stage 4
It changes the grade, not the stage
It is counted only toward Stage 2
why: A moderate ridge defect is on the Stage 3 complexity list, and a severe one is on the Stage 4 list.
Only a severe ridge defect is a Stage 4 factor; a moderate one counts toward Stage 3.
Ridge defects are complexity factors for staging and never change the grade.
Ridge defects are on the Stage 3 and 4 lists, not on Stage 2.

q1-A04.stem: Which set of complexity findings matches a Stage 2 case?
choices: Deepest PD 5 mm or less, bone loss mainly horizontal
Deepest PD 4 mm or less, bone loss mainly vertical
Deepest PD 6 mm or more, bone loss mainly horizontal
Deepest PD 5 mm or less, plus a Class II furcation
why: Stage 2 is a deepest pocket of 5 mm or less with bone loss that is mostly horizontal.
A deepest pocket of 4 mm or less is Stage 1, and mostly vertical loss fits neither Stage 1 nor 2.
A pocket of 6 mm or more is a Stage 3 complexity factor.
A Class II furcation moves the case to Stage 3 even with shallower pockets.

q1-A05.stem: At what point does the extent of periodontitis change from localized to generalized?
choices: Once 30% or more of the teeth are involved
Once 50% or more of the teeth are involved
Once more than one quadrant is affected
Once both of the arches are affected
why: Generalized means 30% or more of teeth involved; under 30% is localized.
The cutoff is 30% of the teeth, not half of them.
Extent is counted as a share of the teeth, not by quadrant.
Extent is counted as a share of the teeth, not by arch.

q1-A06.stem: Records span 5 years. How much CAL or bone loss over that time counts as direct evidence of Grade C?
choices: At least 2 mm
Any loss, however small
Anything past 1 mm
None; only the ratio can set Grade C
why: Over 5 years of records, 2 mm or more of CAL or bone loss is direct evidence of Grade C.
Over 5 years, no loss is Grade A and under 2 mm is Grade B, so just having some loss isn't C.
Under 2 mm over 5 years is still Grade B; Grade C starts at 2 mm.
Records are the gold standard when they exist; the ratio is the fallback when there are none.

q1-A07.stem: The patient's plaque levels are low, yet the periodontal destruction is far greater than that biofilm could account for. What grade does this case phenotype suggest?
choices: Grade C
Grade A
Grade B
None; phenotype isn't used
why: Destruction out of proportion to the biofilm is the Grade C phenotype.
Grade A is the opposite picture: lots of biofilm but little destruction.
Grade B is destruction that matches the amount of biofilm.
Case phenotype is indirect evidence for the grade, so it is used.

q1-S07.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. A Stage 1 case has no pocket deeper than 4 mm, and its bone loss is mostly horizontal.
2. On top of that, Stage 3 complexity includes pockets of 6 mm or more, vertical bone loss of 3 mm or more, a Class II or III furcation and a moderate ridge defect.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Both match the 2018 staging table: Stage 1 is a PD of 4 mm or less with horizontal loss, and Stage 3 adds those factors.
Both are true as the 2018 AAP/EFP staging table states them.
Statement 2 is true too: Stage 3 adds PD of 6 mm or more, vertical loss of 3 mm or more, a Class II-III furcation and a moderate ridge defect.
Statement 1 is true too: Stage 1 is a deepest pocket of 4 mm or less with mostly horizontal bone loss.

q1-S09.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. A case needs a higher interdental CAL to reach Stage 4 than to reach Stage 3.
2. A mouth with plenty of biofilm but little destruction is the Grade C case phenotype.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Neither is true: Stages 3 and 4 use the same CAL cutoff, and heavy biofilm with little destruction is Grade A.
Both are false: Stages 3 and 4 share the CAL cutoff of 5 mm or more, and Grade C is destruction beyond what the biofilm explains.
Statement 1 is false: Stages 3 and 4 share CAL cutoffs, and tooth loss and complexity tell them apart.
Statement 2 is false: plenty of biofilm with little destruction is the Grade A phenotype, not Grade C.

q1-E01.stem: Each of these findings pushes a case to Stage 3 or higher whatever the CAL numbers say, EXCEPT:
choices: 6 mm pockets throughout, without bone loss
An angular bony defect 3 mm deep or more
Class II furcation involvement
Loss of one tooth to periodontitis
why: Deep pockets by themselves never set a stage; with no attachment or bone loss they could be gingivitis, so this is the exception.
An angular (vertical) defect of 3 mm or more does force at least Stage 3, whatever the CAL.
A Class II furcation does force at least Stage 3, whatever the CAL.
Any tooth lost to periodontitis does force at least Stage 3, whatever the CAL.

q1-E02.stem: Each of these statements about grading is true EXCEPT:
choices: A nonsmoker is moved down to Grade A
Grade B is where grading starts
HbA1c at or above 7% means Grade C
A ratio above 1.0 points to Grade C
why: This is the false one: modifiers can only raise a grade, so not smoking never moves a case down to A.
True: Grade B is the default until the evidence shifts it.
True: an HbA1c of 7% or more pushes the grade to C.
True: a bone-loss/age ratio over 1.0 points to Grade C.

q1-E04.stem: Each of these is part of Phase I therapy EXCEPT:
choices: Seating the permanent crown
Controlling the caries
Teaching oral hygiene
Counseling to quit smoking
why: A permanent crown waits until periodontal therapy is finished (a temporary fills the gap), so it isn't Phase I.
Caries control is Phase I, done before or alongside SRP.
Teaching oral hygiene is one of the core steps of Phase I.
Counseling a patient to quit smoking is Phase I control of a risk factor.

q1-E05.stem: Consider a patient whose periodontitis was treated and who has stayed stable on maintenance. Which of these statements about them is NOT correct?
choices: A new stage is assigned at every maintenance visit
Their diagnosis is health on a reduced periodontium
They remain on perio maintenance, not a prophylaxis
Their healed tissue has a long junctional epithelium
why: This is the wrong one: a stable treated patient is diagnosed as healthy on a reduced periodontium and is not re-staged unless disease returns.
Correct: a stable treated patient is healthy on a reduced periodontium.
Correct: they stay on periodontal maintenance even when the pockets are shallow.
Correct: treated tissue heals with a long junctional epithelium, which breaks down more easily.

q1-E06.stem: Each of these statements about clinical attachment level is true EXCEPT:
choices: A 7 mm pocket always means 7 mm or more of CAL
CAL equals the probing depth plus the recession
With visible recession, CAL exceeds the PD
With a covered CEJ, CAL is less than the PD
why: This is the false one: when the CEJ is under the gum, a 7 mm pocket can mean far less CAL, such as 3 mm.
True: CAL is probing depth plus recession, with recession negative when the CEJ is covered.
True: visible recession is positive and gets added, so CAL ends up larger than the PD.
True: with the CEJ below the margin, CAL ends up smaller than the PD.

q2-E03.stem: Each of these sutures resorbs in the body EXCEPT one. Which one has to be removed or left in place?
choices: ePTFE
Chromic gut
Plain gut
PGCL, poly(glycolide-co-caprolactone)
why: Right: ePTFE is non-absorbable; it must be removed or left long-term, so it is the exception.
Chromic gut does resorb: it is gut treated with chromium salts so it lasts a bit longer.
Plain gut does resorb: it is untreated natural gut, the fastest of the gut sutures to go.
PGCL does resorb: it is a synthetic monofilament gone in about 22-55 days.

q2-F02.stem: Instead of placing it at a line angle, a surgeon runs a vertical release straight through the papilla between #8 and #9. What complication is this most likely to cause?
choices: A black triangle between the centrals
Necrosis at the flap's free edge
Too little access to the bony defect
The flap margin rolling inward at closure
why: Right: cutting through the middle of the papilla can kill it, and losing it leaves a black triangle; verticals belong at the line angle.
Free-edge necrosis comes from a base narrower than the free edge, not from where the vertical crosses.
A vertical through the papilla still releases the flap; the harm is to the tissue, not to access.
Margin inversion is a closure issue (a horizontal mattress prevents it), not caused by where the vertical sits.

q2-F03.stem: A surgeon is outlining the two verticals of a trapezoidal flap for a large ridge augmentation. Which path should they take?
choices: Spreading apart as they run apically, base wider than edge
Converging as they run apically, base narrower than edge
Cutting through the middle of the papilla at each end
Lying right over the mesial and distal sides of the defect
why: Right: verticals that spread apart make a base wider than the free edge, and the base carries the reflected flap's only blood supply.
A base narrower than the edge starves the coronal part of the flap, which can necrose; this is the mistake to avoid.
Verticals go at the line angles; cutting through the papilla can kill it and leave a black triangle.
Incisions are kept at a distance from the defect, never over it; that is one of the five principles.

q2-F04.stem: Only one of these statements about absorbable versus non-absorbable sutures is false. Which one?
choices: Nylon is a synthetic that resorbs, in the same group as Vicryl and Monocryl
Absorbable sutures are broken down by hydrolysis or enzymatic cleavage
Vicryl keeps its tensile strength for about 2-3 weeks, then fully resorbs later
Absorbables spare a removal visit, so they suit quick pediatric cases and simple extractions
why: This is the false one: nylon is non-absorbable, along with silk, ePTFE and polypropylene (Prolene); Vicryl and Monocryl are the synthetic absorbables.
True: gut, chromic gut and the Vicryl/Monocryl family degrade by hydrolysis or enzymatic cleavage, so nobody has to take them out.
True: synthetic absorbables like Vicryl hold tensile strength for 2-3 weeks and fully resorb over a longer time.
True: where a removal visit is a burden, as in a quick pediatric case or a simple extraction, absorbables are the natural choice.

q2-F05.stem: Over a major bone graft, many surgeons close with a non-absorbable such as ePTFE. What justification does the course give for that choice?
choices: Plaque resistance and strength that doesn't fail too early
It dissolves as the graft heals, so no removal visit
About 2-3 weeks of tensile strength, then full resorption
It is the cheapest suture, keeping a big closure affordable
why: Right: ePTFE resists plaque attraction, holds high tensile strength and won't break down prematurely over the graft.
ePTFE doesn't dissolve: it must be removed by the clinician or left long-term.
That describes Vicryl, a synthetic absorbable; ePTFE never resorbs.
PTFE is the highest-cost option on the chart, not the cheapest, and cost isn't the reason it's chosen.

q2-F06.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Just as with silk and nylon, Vicryl and Monocryl must be taken out by the clinician.
2. ePTFE and other non-absorbables keep high tensile strength and do not break down too early.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is false, so both can't be true: Vicryl and Monocryl are synthetic absorbables that break down by hydrolysis or enzymatic cleavage; silk and nylon are the ones that must come out.
Statement 2 is not false: non-absorbables like ePTFE keep high tensile strength and don't break down early, which, along with resisting plaque, is why they are favored over major bone grafts.

This reverses both: statement 1 is false (Vicryl and Monocryl are synthetic absorbables that break down by hydrolysis or enzymatic cleavage; silk and nylon must come out), and statement 2 is true (ePTFE keeps high tensile strength and doesn't break down early, part of why it is favored over major bone grafts).

Right: statement 1 is false, since Vicryl and Monocryl are synthetic absorbables that break down by hydrolysis or enzymatic cleavage while silk and nylon must come out; statement 2 is true, since ePTFE keeps high tensile strength and doesn't break down early, part of why it is favored over major bone grafts.

q3-E02.stem: Each statement below about periodontal maintenance is accurate EXCEPT one. Which is the EXCEPTION?
choices: Roughly 80-90% of patients keep up with it
Patients whose teeth are being moved orthodontically are seen every 4-6 weeks
Pathogens begin to return 4-8 weeks after treatment
How regularly patients come, not only how often, predicts tooth loss
why: The exception: maintenance compliance is only about 30-40%, not 80-90%.
Accurate: inflammation during active tooth movement can uncouple bone formation from resorption, so these patients come about every 4-6 weeks.
Accurate: subgingival pathogens begin returning about 4-8 weeks after treatment and are near pre-treatment levels by 9-11 weeks.
Accurate: regular maintenance predicts tooth-loss risk, especially in Stage 3/4 and Grade C patients.

q3-E03.stem: Three of these combine a patient's findings into an overall risk level. Which one is NOT a whole-patient risk-assessment tool?
choices: McGuire & Nunn
UniFe
The PRA (Lang & Tonetti)
PreViser/PAT
why: The exception: McGuire & Nunn is a tooth prognosis system (can the tooth be maintained), not a whole-patient risk tool.
UniFe is a whole-patient risk tool: five scored inputs added into a risk tier.
The PRA (Lang & Tonetti) is a whole-patient risk tool, drawn as a spider-web plot.
PreViser/PAT (Page et al.) is a whole-patient risk tool that agreed fairly well with UniFe.

q3-E04.stem: Every statement here about the periodontal inflamed surface area (PISA) is correct EXCEPT:
choices: Stage 1-2 periodontitis gives a PISA about the size of a paper cut
PISA is the area of inflamed epithelium lining the pockets
In a periodontally healthy mouth it averages about 34 mm²
It frames periodontitis as an inflammatory load on the whole body
why: The exception: a paper cut (about 34 mm²) is the healthy mouth; Stage 1-2 periodontitis averages about 2,309 mm², a wound the size of cellulitis.
Correct: PISA measures the area of inflamed pocket epithelium.
Correct: health averages about 34 mm², roughly a paper cut.
Correct: the jump from about 34 mm² in health to about 2,309 mm² in Stage 1-2 periodontitis is the lecture's case that periodontitis is a systemic inflammatory burden, not a local nuisance.

q3-F01.stem: Long-term follow-up tested how well McGuire & Nunn predictions hold up. Which of these findings are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Overall, the predictions hold about 80% of the time
Without the 'good' teeth, they hold only about 50% of the time
Teeth tend, on average, to outperform their prognosis
Even with maintenance, hopeless teeth usually go sooner than predicted
Smokers' teeth beat their prognosis by more than anyone's
why: Correct: overall accuracy is about 80% (81% at 8 years).
Correct: take out the good teeth and accuracy falls to about 50%, a coin flip.
Correct: on average teeth do better than predicted; we judge them more harshly than how they actually do.
Incorrect: in well-maintained patients even hopeless teeth are often kept much longer than expected.
Incorrect: smokers are the exception; their teeth don't outdo the prediction the way most teeth do.

q4-E03.stem: Each statement below describes a prophylaxis correctly EXCEPT one. Which is the exception?
choices: It is the care for patients already treated for periodontitis
It is a preventive procedure rather than a therapeutic one
It can include removing calculus 1-2 mm below the gingival margin
It is meant for patients with gingival health or gingivitis
why: This is the false one: patients already treated for periodontitis get periodontal maintenance, not a prophylaxis.
True: a prophylaxis is preventive, not therapeutic.
True: a prophylaxis can still remove calculus 1-2 mm subgingivally.
True: a prophylaxis is for gingival health or gingivitis.

q4-E04.stem: Based on the evidence presented in class, which statement about SRP outcomes is NOT true?
choices: Splitting instrumentation across several visits gets more calculus off
Pocket reduction is about the same with hand and ultrasonic instruments
Chlorhexidine irrigation provides no added benefit to SRP
In pockets ≥5 mm, root debridement falls short about 65% of the time
why: This is the untrue one: spreading instrumentation over several visits has no real advantage, because calculus left behind stays for the same reasons.
True as taught: there's no statistical difference in pocket reduction between hand and ultrasonic instruments.
True as taught: chlorhexidine irrigation adds nothing to SRP.
True as taught: root debridement is inadequate about 65% of the time in pockets ≥5 mm.

q4-E06.stem: Each statement about the source of periodontal destruction is true EXCEPT:
choices: The bacteria carry osteoclasts into the tissue
About 75% of the damage comes from the host response
The disease is initiated by plaque bacteria
The bacteria contribute endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide)
why: This is the false one: bacteria bring endotoxin, not osteoclasts; the osteoclasts belong to the host.
True: the host response accounts for about 75% of the damage.
True: plaque bacteria initiate the disease.
True: bacteria bring endotoxin (LPS), part of their roughly 25% share of the damage.

q7-L01.stem: A restored implant is still in place, but its abutment screw has come loose and the mucosa around it has receded. Which term fits it?
choices: It is surviving but not successful
It is successful because it is in function
It has failed because it has complications
It is ailing because of a prosthetic problem
why: Right: survival only requires an implant that is present and loaded; any biologic or prosthetic complication means it isn't a success.
Wrong: being in function only shows survival. Success requires no complications at all, clinically or on the radiograph.
Wrong: in Meffert's terms a failed implant has progressive bone loss, mobility and lost function; a loose screw and recession are not that.
Wrong: an ailing implant has static radiographic bone loss without inflammation or mobility; the term isn't about prosthetic problems.

q7-L02.stem: Albrektsson's 1986 criteria set a limit on vertical bone loss at the end of the implant's first year in function. What is that limit?
choices: No more than 1.5 mm
No more than 0.2 mm
No more than 3 mm
Zero bone loss
why: Right: the slide's criterion allows 1.5 mm or less of vertical bone loss at 1 year in function.
Wrong: 0.2 mm is the yearly limit for the years after the first one, not the first-year allowance.
Wrong: 3 mm is double the first-year allowance and isn't in the criteria.
Wrong: some crestal remodeling is expected during the first year, which is why up to 1.5 mm is allowed.

q7-L03.stem: A radiograph shows a radiolucency around the apical third of an implant. What did Dr. Kaur call this?
choices: Retrograde peri-implantitis
Peri-implant mucositis
Crestal remodeling
A soft and hard tissue deficiency
why: Right: that is her term for a radiolucency at the apical third of the implant.
Wrong: mucositis is inflammation of the mucosa around the implant, with no bone loss beyond remodeling.
Wrong: remodeling takes place at the crest, the top of the bone, during the first year in function.
Wrong: that deficiency is loss of mucosa and bone at the margin, not a radiolucency at the apex.

q7-L04.stem: The 2017 classification gives no 3 mm probing cutoff for a healthy implant and compares each reading with earlier exams instead. What is the reason?
choices: A healthy implant may probe deeper than 3 mm
The 3 mm cutoff is kept for the esthetic zone
A plastic probe always overreads by 2 mm
Implants are no longer meant to be probed
why: Right: the depth depends on how deep the implant was placed, the abutment's height and the tissue's thickness, so each implant is compared with its own baseline.
Wrong: there is no cutoff anywhere in the mouth; depth depends on each implant's placement, abutment and tissue.
Wrong: probing implants accurately is hard, but no fixed error was taught; the point is each implant's own anatomy.
Wrong: implants are still probed, gently and with plastic probes, and the readings are compared with baseline.

q7-L05.stem: Once an implant is loaded, the crestal bone adapts. What amount of this physiologic remodeling did Dr. Kaur describe?
choices: Roughly 2 mm, leveling off in the first year
Roughly 0.2 mm a year, continuing for life
None at all, since all bone loss is disease
Roughly 5 mm, spread over the first five years
why: Right: about 2 mm as the crest adapts to load, plateauing within about the first year; that is physiologic.
Wrong: 0.2 mm a year is the success limit after the first year, not the initial remodeling.
Wrong: the classification allows the initial crestal remodeling; only loss beyond it is pathologic.
Wrong: no such number was taught; remodeling levels off within the first year.

q7-L06.stem: An implant site is clearly inflamed, and you must decide whether it is peri-implant mucositis or peri-implantitis. Which finding settles it?
choices: Bone lost beyond the initial remodeling
Bleeding or pus on gentle probing
A probing depth above the baseline
Redness and swelling of the peri-implant mucosa
why: Right: only peri-implantitis has bone loss beyond initial remodeling; the other three findings appear in both conditions.
Wrong: bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing occurs in both mucositis and peri-implantitis.
Wrong: probing depth increases in both, from swelling in mucositis and also from bone loss in peri-implantitis.
Wrong: signs of inflammation belong to both diagnoses.

q7-L07.stem: According to the 2017 workshop, how does peri-implant mucositis bleed when it is probed gently?
choices: Profusely, as a line or a drop
As a pinpoint that shows up slowly
Only when a firm force is used
It doesn't; only suppuration counts
why: Right: the mucositis criterion is profuse (line or drop) bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing.
Wrong: a little blood that appears slowly may not mean disease; mucositis calls for profuse bleeding.
Wrong: implants are probed gently, around 0.25 N; bleeding after a firm push may come from the force, not disease.
Wrong: the criterion is bleeding and/or suppuration, so either one counts.

q7-M01.stem: At the last visit an implant probed 4 mm; today the same site probes 6 mm. According to Dr. Kaur, which of these could explain the change? Select all that apply.
choices: An inaccurate reading
Swollen, inflamed mucosa adding height
Real loss of bone
Osseointegration becoming stronger
A crown that was just cemented
why: Correct pick: measurement error is the first of her three reasons, and implants are hard to probe accurately.
Correct pick: in mucositis the pocket gets deeper because inflamed tissue adds volume.
Correct pick: true bone loss is her third reason, and it is the one that means peri-implantitis.
Wrong pick: osseointegration is bone bonding to the implant; it doesn't make a pocket deeper.
Wrong pick: she listed only three reasons (measurement, swelling, bone loss), and a new crown isn't among them.

q7-L08.stem: During maintenance, pus comes from the sulcus around an implant. How should you read this finding?
choices: The disease is active and must be treated now
It is expected during the first year
Record it and look again next year
The implant has lost osseointegration
why: Right: suppuration means active bacterial disease, around a tooth or an implant, and it needs a response now.
Wrong: crestal remodeling is normal in the first year, but pus never is.
Wrong: she was clear that suppuration can't be put on watch.
Wrong: lost osseointegration shows up as mobility of the implant body, not as pus.

q7-L09.stem: A patient has just been diagnosed with peri-implant mucositis. What is true of their condition?
choices: It can be reversed, as gingivitis can
It has bone loss beyond remodeling
It typically leaves the implant mobile
Watching it is the best management
why: Right: mucositis is the implant's version of gingivitis, and it is reversible.
Wrong: bone loss beyond remodeling defines peri-implantitis; mucositis has none.
Wrong: mobility means lost osseointegration, which even peri-implantitis rarely causes.
Wrong: she said not to watch it; treat it before it moves on to peri-implantitis.

q7-L10.stem: The 2017 definition says peri-implantitis is plaque-associated and starts with inflammation of the peri-implant mucosa. What does the definition say follows?
choices: Supporting bone is lost, progressively
The periodontal ligament is lost
The abutment screw gradually works loose
The mucosa recedes with no bone lost
why: Right: the definition reads inflammation in the mucosa followed by progressive loss of supporting bone.
Wrong: an implant has no PDL, so there is none to lose.
Wrong: a loose screw is a prosthetic complication, not part of the disease's definition.
Wrong: recession with no bone loss isn't peri-implantitis; the definition requires bone loss.

q7-L11.stem: Only bone fill is needed around an implant, yet treating peri-implantitis rarely regrows bone well. What is the main obstacle?
choices: The rough surface can't be cleaned reliably
Cementum must first form on the implant
Its periodontal ligament won't regenerate
Its bony defects are always the deep, narrow, vertical kind
why: Right: implants are roughened so osteoblasts attach, plaque attaches too, and no method decontaminates the surface better than another.
Wrong: an implant needs no cementum or PDL, only bone fill; that part should be easier.
Wrong: implants have no PDL, so missing one isn't the problem.
Wrong: the opposite is true; bone loss around implants usually doesn't form the deep, narrow defects that regenerate best.

q7-L12.stem: Saline, chlorhexidine, citric acid, EDTA and lasers have all been used to clean an infected implant surface. Which did the evidence Dr. Kaur cited favor?
choices: No method was better than the others
Lasers, which clearly beat the others
Citric acid
Chlorhexidine (Peridex)
why: Right: all of them gave the same or similar results; none is superior.
Wrong: lasers performed about the same as the rest, not better.
Wrong: citric acid performed about the same as the rest, not better.
Wrong: chlorhexidine performed about the same as the rest, not better.

q7-L13.stem: Radiographs show an implant losing more bone at each visit, and it bleeds on probing, but it doesn't move. Under Meffert's terms, it is:
choices: Failing
Ailing
Failed
Successful
why: Right: progressive bone loss with inflammation and no mobility is a failing implant.
Wrong: an ailing implant's bone loss is static, with no inflammation.
Wrong: a failed implant is mobile and has lost function.
Wrong: progressing bone loss with inflammation is nowhere near success.

q7-L14.stem: Years ago an implant lost some bone, and the level has held steady ever since. It isn't inflamed or mobile. How is it classified and managed?
choices: Ailing; keep monitoring it
Failing; open and graft it
Failed; take it out
Peri-implantitis; give antibiotics
why: Right: static bone loss with no inflammation or mobility is ailing; monitor it and record clinical and radiographic data at every visit.
Wrong: a failing implant has progressive bone loss and inflammation, and this one is stable and quiet.
Wrong: a failed implant is mobile, and this one isn't.
Wrong: without inflammation or progression there is no active peri-implantitis to treat.

q7-L15.stem: You confirm that the implant body itself moves. How is it treated?
choices: Take the implant out
Splint it to a neighboring tooth
Graft around it, then wait
Place a local antibiotic and watch
why: Right: mobility means osseointegration is lost, which can't be reversed, so removal is the only treatment.
Wrong: splinting is an option for a tooth; a mobile implant has lost its bond to the bone for good.
Wrong: a graft can't bring back lost osseointegration.
Wrong: an antibiotic treats infection; it can't reintegrate an implant.

q7-L16.stem: An implant seems loose and you are planning to remove it. What has to be confirmed first?
choices: That the body moves, not the crown or abutment
That the patient's HbA1c is now below 8
That the bone loss reaches the apex on the film
That peri-implantitis caused the looseness
why: Right: a loose abutment or crown can feel like a mobile implant, and either can be fixed.
Wrong: HbA1c matters when placing implants, not when confirming mobility.
Wrong: mobility is the deciding sign; the bone loss doesn't have to reach the apex.
Wrong: lost osseointegration usually isn't from peri-implantitis, and the cause doesn't change the treatment.

q7-L17.stem: After years of peri-implantitis, only the apical third of an implant remains in bone. Which statement is most likely true?
choices: The implant may well not be mobile
The implant has to be mobile by now
It is still considered a success
That bone can be predictably regrown
why: Right: peri-implantitis very rarely makes an implant mobile, even this far along, though with no future it is still judged failed.
Wrong: implants with only a third left in bone are often still immobile.
Wrong: bone loss beyond remodeling rules out success.
Wrong: peri-implantitis responds poorly to treatment, and regrowing this much bone isn't predictable.

q7-L18.stem: If asked what starts peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis, what is the answer?
choices: The plaque biofilm
Occlusal overload
Smoking
The titanium itself
why: Right: the disease is multifactorial, but bacteria in plaque biofilm start it.
Wrong: parafunction is among the slide's other risk factors, but a risk factor isn't the cause; the inflammation and bone loss start with plaque.
Wrong: smoking, current or former, is a major risk factor on both lists, not the primary cause.
Wrong: the implant material wasn't taught as a cause; its rough surface matters only because plaque collects on it.

q7-L19.stem: A new implant is about to be exposed to the mouth. What decides which bacteria will settle around it?
choices: The flora in the mouth before placement
How the implant surface was treated
What material the abutment is made of
What the patient eats in the weeks after surgery
why: Right: the oral flora present before implantation determines the flora around the implant.
Wrong: a rough surface holds plaque, but it doesn't choose which species colonize.
Wrong: the abutment is just another surface for plaque; the species come from the mouth's existing flora.
Wrong: diet wasn't taught as a factor; the existing flora seeds the implant, which is why periodontitis is treated first.

q7-L20.stem: An implant has just been exposed in the mouth. Within what time does a pellicle begin to coat it?
choices: Roughly 30 minutes
Roughly 24 hours
Roughly one week
Not until it's restored
why: Right: the pellicle starts forming as early as 30 minutes after exposure.
Wrong: a day is much too late; the pellicle begins within about 30 minutes, just as on a tooth.
Wrong: a week is much too late; it forms within minutes, and the early colonizers then attach.
Wrong: it begins as soon as the implant is exposed, whether or not it has been restored.

q7-L21.stem: Plaque is just beginning to form on a newly exposed implant. Which bacteria arrive first?
choices: Gram-positive cocci and rods, Actinomyces among them
Gram-negative anaerobes like P. gingivalis
Spirochetes
Candida species
why: Right: as on teeth, gram-positive cocci and rods, including Actinomyces, are the early colonizers.
Wrong: these gram-negative anaerobes come later as the biofilm matures, and they cause peri-implantitis.
Wrong: these motile anaerobes are late arrivals, not first.
Wrong: yeasts weren't taught as early colonizers.

q7-L22.stem: Before planning implants, you ask the patient why their teeth were lost. What does the answer tell you?
choices: Periodontitis marks a susceptible host
Loss to caries means the implant could decay
It sets how long the implant should be
It decides between one and two stages
why: Right: susceptibility to periodontal disease raises the risk of peri-implant disease, even when no teeth remain.
Wrong: an implant can't get caries; the history that matters is periodontitis, which marks a susceptible host.
Wrong: implant length follows the available bone, not the reason the tooth was lost.
Wrong: staging depends on the bone and tissue at surgery.

q7-L23.stem: A patient was treated for periodontitis, and it has stayed stable across several maintenance visits. What is the answer on implants?
choices: Yes, with maintenance suited to their risk
No, a periodontitis history rules them out
Only once all remaining teeth are removed
Only with antibiotics for the rest of life
why: Right: treated, arrested periodontitis in a compliant patient isn't a contraindication.
Wrong: the contraindication is untreated or partly treated periodontitis, not a history of it.
Wrong: there is no such rule; what matters is that the disease is treated and stable.
Wrong: antibiotics aren't part of the plan; maintenance and plaque control are.

q7-L24.stem: Periodontally involved teeth have just been extracted. For how long might putative periodontal pathogens remain in the mouth?
choices: Up to about a year
Up to about a week
Up to about a month
They go with the teeth
why: Right: the slide says they may still be present a year after the extractions.
Wrong: a week is far too short; they may persist a year.
Wrong: a month is still too short; they can last a year, one reason periodontal treatment comes first.
Wrong: they don't leave with the teeth, because the host and the flora remain.

q7-M02.stem: The slide lists risk factors for peri-implantitis. Which of these are on it? Select all that apply.
choices: An implant placed in the wrong position
Diabetes that isn't controlled
Too little bone width
A thick soft tissue phenotype
A long healing period before loading
why: Correct pick: implant malposition is on the peri-implantitis list, not the mucositis one.
Correct pick: uncontrolled diabetes is on the peri-implantitis list; control, measured by HbA1c, matters, not the years with diabetes.
Correct pick: limited bone width is on the peri-implantitis list, along with malposition and uncontrolled diabetes.
Wrong pick: the phenotype on the slides is a thin one, and it is on the mucositis list; thin tissue recedes faster than thick.
Wrong pick: the time before loading is on neither list.

q7-L25.stem: One risk factor appears on the slide's list for peri-implant mucositis but is missing from its peri-implantitis list. Which?
choices: A thin soft tissue phenotype
Current or former smoking
A history of periodontitis
Obesity or metabolic syndrome
why: Right: it is on the mucositis list only; the peri-implantitis list has malposition, uncontrolled diabetes, limited bone width and depression instead.
Wrong: smoking, current or former, is on both lists.
Wrong: a history of periodontitis is on both lists, as is active periodontitis.
Wrong: obesity and/or metabolic syndrome is on both lists.

q7-L26.stem: Ferreira and colleagues (2006) looked at plaque control and peri-implant disease. How much did poor plaque control raise the odds?
choices: Roughly fourteenfold
Roughly one and a half times
Roughly threefold
Not to a significant degree
why: Right: the odds ratio on the slide is 14.3.
Wrong: 1.5 is far too low; the odds ratio was 14.3, which fits plaque as the primary cause.
Wrong: three understates it; the odds rose about fourteenfold (14.3).
Wrong: the effect was strong, an odds ratio of 14.3.

q7-L27.stem: In Bain and Moy's 1993 study of 2,194 implants, what were the failure rates for smokers and nonsmokers?
choices: Smokers 11.3%, nonsmokers 4.76%
Smokers 23.5%, nonsmokers 16.5%
Smokers 4.76%, nonsmokers 11.3%
Smokers 30%, nonsmokers 1.5%
why: Right: smokers' implants failed more than twice as often.
Wrong: those are Simonis 2010's peri-implantitis rates, not Bain and Moy's failure rates.
Wrong: this reverses the numbers; smokers had the higher rate.
Wrong: those are the bleeding-on-probing figures (4 of 4 visits vs none of 4).

q7-L28.stem: Alsaadi (2007) studied smokers with implants. What was the finding?
choices: The heavier the smoking, the worse the outcome
Once integrated, the implant was unaffected
Former smokers fared worse than current ones
Only cigar smoking raised the risk
why: Right: a dose-response relationship, with the worst rates in heavy smokers.
Wrong: smoking affects healing and long-term disease, not only integration.
Wrong: the finding was about dose, not former versus current smoking; the risk lists count both.
Wrong: the study was about how much someone smokes, not what they smoke.

q7-L29.stem: How does smoking tilt the oral environment toward the bacteria behind peri-implantitis?
choices: Less oxygen, which gram-negative anaerobes like
A higher pH in the mouth
More saliva that washes away gram-positive cocci
Direct killing of gram-positive cocci
why: Right: smoking depletes oxygen, and the anaerobes behind peri-implantitis and implant failure thrive in that.
Wrong: the mechanism taught was oxygen, not pH.
Wrong: smoking doesn't wash bacteria away; it shifts the flora by lowering oxygen.
Wrong: it favors the anaerobes by depleting oxygen, not by killing the gram-positive early colonizers.

q7-L30.stem: A patient asks whether vaping is a safer choice with implants. What was Dr. Kaur's view?
choices: Healing may be spared; immunity is still suppressed
Vaping poses no risk to implants
It harms the healing blood supply more than cigarettes
Decades of studies show it adds no extra risk
why: Right: without combustion the vasoconstrictive effect may be missing, but the immune response is still suppressed.
Wrong: she said vaping is bad too.
Wrong: the reverse; the combustion effect on healing may be absent.
Wrong: there is little long-term evidence so far.

q7-L31.stem: When you assess a patient with diabetes for an implant, which factor counts most?
choices: Glucose control, as measured by HbA1c
The number of years since diagnosis
Whether the diabetes is type 1 or type 2
The fasting glucose on the surgery day
why: Right: under optimal control the years with diabetes didn't affect implant survival, and poorly controlled diabetes contraindicates implants.
Wrong: duration didn't affect survival under optimal control.
Wrong: the type wasn't the factor taught; control was.
Wrong: a single day's reading says little; HbA1c reflects the last 3-4 months.

q7-L32.stem: HbA1c gives a picture of glucose control over roughly the past 3-4 months. What sets that time span?
choices: The lifespan of red blood cells
How long insulin stays in the blood
How long the liver holds glucose
How often physicians order the test
why: Right: glycated hemoglobin lasts as long as the red cell carrying it, about 3-4 months.
Wrong: insulin is cleared within minutes, not months.
Wrong: HbA1c is glucose bound to hemoglobin, not stored glucose, so it lasts as long as the red cell.
Wrong: the testing interval follows the red cell's lifespan, not the other way around.

q7-L33.stem: An implant is being placed as the first step of a two-stage approach. What is done at this surgery?
choices: It gets a cover screw and the tissue is closed over it
It gets a healing abutment that comes through the tissue
The final crown is cemented on it
A provisional crown loads it right away
why: Right: the implant heals buried, and a second surgery uncovers it.
Wrong: that is single-stage placement, or the second stage of a two-stage implant.
Wrong: the final crown comes months later, after uncovery, a healing abutment and the impression.
Wrong: a two-stage implant heals buried under the tissue, so it isn't loaded at placement.

q7-E01.stem: Periodontally compromised patients face several soft tissue problems when they get implants. Each of these is one of them EXCEPT:
choices: Extra keratinized tissue
Lost papillae
Black triangles
Lost keratinized tissue
why: The exception: periodontal disease takes keratinized tissue away; it doesn't leave extra.
On the list: papillary loss is one of the slide's soft tissue losses.
On the list: black triangles, the open spaces where papillae are lost, are there too.
On the list, and worse with a thin periodontium phenotype.

q7-L35.stem: A periodontally compromised patient has reduced bone volume at a planned implant site. Which biomechanical risk does that raise?
choices: Implant fracture from a poor crown-implant ratio
Mucositis caused by the tissue being thick
Paresthesia brought on by probing
Screws that loosen because the abutments are too short
why: Right: short bone puts a long crown on the implant, which was the slide's biomechanical concern.
Wrong: thin tissue is the phenotype risk, and it is a soft tissue factor.
Wrong: probing doesn't cause paresthesia.
Wrong: screw loosening is a prosthetic complication; the slide's concern with reduced bone was implant fracture from the crown-implant ratio.

q7-L36.stem: Growing back which dimension of bone at an implant site is the bigger challenge?
choices: Bone height, gained vertically
Bone width, gained horizontally
Height and width are about equal
Neither one can be rebuilt
why: Gaining height is far harder; in the #31 case, #30 was extracted so the ridge could be rebuilt vertically.
Width is the dimension that grows back more easily.
She said plainly that height is the harder of the two.
Both can be augmented; height is just much harder, and a sinus lift is the easier kind of height.

q7-L38.stem: At which point in an implant patient's care is the patient's risk assessed?
choices: At each stage, starting before placement
A single time, before placement
Only at placement and then again at loading
Only after disease shows up
why: It is done before placement, during osseointegration, through maintenance and after any removal.
Risk shifts over time (diabetes control, smoking), so it is reassessed at each stage.
It goes on through maintenance and after any removal too.
It begins before the implant is placed, not when disease appears.

q7-L39.stem: When you check an implant for bleeding on probing, how hard do you press?
choices: Lightly, about 0.25 N
Firmly, about 2.5 N
Hard enough to touch the bone
Not at all; implants aren't probed
why: The slide calls for a light force of about 0.25 N.
That is ten times too much; a heavy force makes a site bleed falsely.
That much force makes the site bleed by itself.
Implants are probed, gently, with plastic probes.

q7-L40.stem: Which statement about bleeding on probing around implants holds up?
choices: Its absence is a good sign of stability
Any bleeding shows the disease is progressing
Probing technique can't produce it
It counts only around natural teeth
why: When a site doesn't bleed, stable peri-implant conditions are well predicted.
Bleeding shows inflammation, but it may not predict progression.
Probing with the wrong force or at the wrong angle can make a site bleed by itself.
It is part of every peri-implant evaluation.

q7-L41.stem: Over a year of maintenance, one implant site bled each time it was probed (4 of 4 visits). By the study on the slide, roughly how likely is attachment loss there?
choices: Roughly 30%
Roughly 14%
Roughly 6%
Roughly 1.5%
why: Bleeding at all 4 visits carried a 30% chance.
14% goes with bleeding at 3 of 4 visits.
6% goes with bleeding at 2 of 4 visits.
1.5% is for a site that never bled at any of the 4 visits.

q7-L42.stem: Once the baseline film is taken at the final restoration, what radiograph schedule follows for an implant that stays healthy?
choices: Every 6 months the first year, then yearly
Every 3 months, for life
Only when the patient reports pain or swelling
Once every 5 years
why: That is the slide's schedule while the implant stays healthy.
Every 3 months is far more than the schedule, which is every 6 months for the first year, then yearly.
Yearly films are taken even when there are no symptoms.
Every 5 years is far too seldom: after the first year, films are yearly.

q7-L43.stem: Later bone levels around an implant are measured against the film taken at which point?
choices: The final cementation or restoration
The day the implant is placed
Just before uncovery
One year after loading, the first annual film
why: The slide marks this film as the baseline.
A film is taken at placement, but the baseline is the one at the final restoration, when the implant goes into function.
There is a film before uncovery too, but the implant isn't in function yet; the baseline comes at the final restoration.
That film is the one compared with the baseline, not the baseline itself.

q7-L44.stem: How does the slide describe the job of radiographs at implant maintenance visits?
choices: They confirm, rather than explore
They explore, to find hidden disease
They take the place of probing
They are needed at every visit
why: A film is taken to confirm a clinical change (deeper PD, BOP, suppuration) and is read with the clinical findings.
The slide says just the opposite (Lang and Hill 1977).
Films are read together with the clinical parameters, not instead of them.
Healthy implants get a yearly film; extra ones only when clinical signs change.

q7-P01.stem: Using the 2017 categories, how did Dr. Kaur classify what has happened around #31?
choices: Soft and hard tissue deficiency at the implant
A healthy peri-implant state
Mucositis around the implant
Retrograde peri-implantitis near the implant apex
why: That was her answer in class: around #31 both the mucosa and the bone beneath it are gone.
Health allows no bone loss past the initial remodeling, and here both bone and mucosa are lost.
Mucositis has no bone loss past remodeling; here the bone and mucosa are gone.
Retrograde peri-implantitis is a radiolucency at the apex; this loss is at the margin.

q7-P02.stem: What was the underlying mistake that set this case up to fail?
choices: Placing the implant while periodontitis was untreated
Choosing a two-stage implant rather than a single-stage one
Seating the crown too long after uncovery
Grafting #30 with allograft instead of autograft
why: Untreated periodontitis is a contraindication: a diseased, susceptible host with no maintenance doomed both the graft and the implant.
Staging depends on the bone and tissue at surgery; the untreated disease, not the staging, was the problem.
The crown's timing wasn't the issue; the implant went into untreated periodontitis and got no maintenance.
The graft failed because of the diseased site (it couldn't regenerate between avascular cementum and metal), not because of the graft material.

q7-P03.stem: What did Dr. Kaur say should be done for this implant?
choices: Open, debride, graft and place a membrane
Take the implant out right away
Monitor it and reprobe at next year's visit
Systemic antibiotics with nothing else
why: The bone peaks and the lingual plate are still there, so regenerative treatment is still worth trying.
It is still in function with its peaks and lingual plate intact; she would try to save it.
Bleeding and suppuration mean active disease, which is never put on watch.
Antibiotics by themselves don't clean the implant surface; she would open, clean, graft and cover it.

q7-P04.stem: Before any implant planning for this patient, what is the first step?
choices: SRP and extraction of hopeless teeth; implants later
Immediate implants into the hopeless teeth's sockets
Place the implants, then treat the periodontitis
Antibiotics by themselves, then implants
why: Disease control comes first: SRP and extraction of the hopeless teeth with no immediate implants, then healing, re-evaluation and any Phase II surgery, and only then implant planning.
Immediate implants aren't placed during the disease-control phase.
Treating periodontitis is "not an afterthought": it comes first, implants after.
Antibiotics never stand in for mechanical treatment.

q7-S01.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. An implant that is in place and carries its restoration counts as surviving.
2. Once an implant counts as surviving, it cannot have biologic complications.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: a surviving implant can still have mucositis, peri-implantitis and bone loss.
Statement 1 is true, not false: survival, as she defined it, is just a restored (loaded) implant being present.

Statement 1 is true: survival, as she defined it, is just a restored (loaded) implant being present. Statement 2 is false: a surviving implant can still have mucositis, peri-implantitis and bone loss.

Statement 1 is true, not false: survival, as she defined it, is just a restored (loaded) implant being present. Statement 2 is false, not true: a surviving implant can still have mucositis, peri-implantitis and bone loss.

q7-S02.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. A healthy implant can show bone loss past the initial crestal remodeling.
2. A healthy implant probes no deeper than it did at earlier exams.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: bone loss past remodeling is what makes it peri-implantitis.
Statement 2 is true, not false: health is judged by comparing the implant with its own earlier exams.
Statement 1 is false, not true: bone loss past remodeling is what makes it peri-implantitis. Statement 2 is true, not false: health is judged by comparing the implant with its own earlier exams.
Statement 1 is false: bone loss past remodeling is what makes it peri-implantitis. Statement 2 is true: health is judged by comparing the implant with its own earlier exams.

q7-S03.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. In Meffert's terms, an ailing implant has bone loss that has stopped, without inflammation.
2. In Meffert's terms, a failed implant has ongoing bone loss, is mobile and no longer functions.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is true: Meffert's ailing implant has static bone loss on the film, with no inflammation or mobility. Statement 2 is true: his failed implant has progressive bone loss, clinical mobility and loss of function.

Statement 1 is true, not false: Meffert's ailing implant has static bone loss on the film, with no inflammation or mobility. Statement 2 is true, not false: his failed implant has progressive bone loss, clinical mobility and loss of function.
Statement 2 is true, not false: Meffert's failed implant has progressive bone loss, clinical mobility and loss of function.
Statement 1 is true, not false: Meffert's ailing implant has static bone loss on the film, with no inflammation or mobility.

q7-S04.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. In a diabetic patient, how many years have passed since the diagnosis is what sets implant risk.
2. The more a patient smokes, the higher the implant risk climbs.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: under good glycemic control, duration didn't change survival; HbA1c is what counts.
Statement 2 is true, not false: Alsaadi 2007 found heavier smokers did worse.
Statement 1 is false, not true: under good glycemic control, duration didn't change survival; HbA1c is what counts. Statement 2 is true, not false: Alsaadi 2007 found heavier smokers did worse.
Statement 1 is false: under good glycemic control, duration didn't change survival; HbA1c is what counts. Statement 2 is true: Alsaadi 2007 found heavier smokers did worse.

q7-S05.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. A healthy implant is radiographed every 3 months for as long as it is in the mouth.
2. Later bone loss is judged against the film taken on the day the implant was placed.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: films are every 6 months in the first year, then yearly. Statement 2 is false, not true: the baseline is the film at the final cementation or restoration.
Statement 1 is false: films are every 6 months in the first year, then yearly. Statement 2 is false: the baseline is the film at the final cementation or restoration.
Statement 1 is false, not true: films are every 6 months in the first year, then yearly.
Statement 2 is false, not true: the baseline is the film at the final cementation or restoration.

q7-T01.stem: True or false: Within about 30 minutes of an implant being exposed in the mouth, a pellicle can begin to form on it.
choices: True
False
why: True: the slide gives 30 minutes, the same timing as on a tooth.
It is true: a pellicle forms within about 30 minutes, and the early colonizers then attach to it.

q7-T03.stem: True or false: Once a patient's periodontitis has been treated and is stable, implants are contraindicated.
choices: True
False
why: Untreated periodontitis is what contraindicates implants, not disease that is treated and stable.
False: a treated, arrested, compliant patient can have implants, with maintenance matched to their risk.

q7-T04.stem: True or false: Once an implant has lost its osseointegration, that loss is permanent.
choices: True
False
why: True: lost osseointegration can't come back, so removal is the only treatment.
It is true: it can't be reversed, and the implant has to come out.

q7-T05.stem: True or false: The 2017 definition of peri-implant health requires probing depths of no more than 3 mm.
choices: True
False
why: A healthy implant can probe deeper than 3 mm; the test is no increase over earlier exams.
False: there is no fixed cutoff, since placement depth, abutment height and tissue thickness set each implant's normal depth.

q7-T06.stem: True or false: Like gingivitis, peri-implant mucositis can be reversed.
choices: True
False
why: True: it is the implant's version of gingivitis, and it can be reversed.
It is true: it reverses like gingivitis, which is why it has to be treated early.

q7-T07.stem: True or false: The bacteria around stable implants look like the subgingival bacteria of a person with teeth and healthy periodontium.
choices: True
False
why: True: the slide says the flora of stable implants resembles that of a periodontally healthy dentate patient.
It is true; and because the flora present before placement sets the implant's flora, untreated periodontitis seeds an implant with pathogens instead.

q7-T08.stem: True or false: Implants often become mobile as a result of peri-implantitis.
choices: True
False
why: Peri-implantitis seldom makes an implant mobile.
False: an implant with peri-implantitis may not move even with only a third of it left in bone.

q7-N01.stem:
Which of these statements on the 2017 peri-implant diagnoses are true?
1. Peri-implant mucositis bleeds and/or suppurates when probed gently.
2. Peri-implantitis includes bone loss past the initial crestal remodeling.
3. A healthy implant may probe deeper than it did at the previous exam.
4. Peri-implant mucositis includes bone loss past the initial crestal remodeling.
choices: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3
1 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
why: 1 and 2 are true. 3 is false: a healthy implant shows no increase in probing depth over earlier exams. 4 is false: mucositis has no bone loss past remodeling.
It takes in 3, which is false: a healthy implant shows no increase in probing depth over earlier exams.
It takes in 3, which is false: a healthy implant shows no increase in probing depth over earlier exams. It misses 2, which is true: bone loss past remodeling defines peri-implantitis.
It takes in 4, which is false: mucositis has no bone loss past remodeling. It misses 1, which is true: mucositis bleeds and/or suppurates on gentle probing.

q7-N02.stem:
Albrektsson's success criteria on the slide include which of these?
1. The implant does not move.
2. No radiolucency is seen around the implant.
3. The patient has no pain, infection, paresthesia or neuropathy.
4. Up to 3 mm of vertical bone loss is acceptable after 1 year in function.
choices: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3
2, 3 and 4
why: It misses 3, which is true: having no pain, infection, paresthesia or neuropathy is a criterion.
1, 2 and 3 are true. 4 is false: the 1-year limit is 1.5 mm, not 3 mm.
It takes in 4, which is false: the 1-year limit is 1.5 mm, not 3 mm.
It takes in 4, which is false: the 1-year limit is 1.5 mm, not 3 mm. It misses 1, which is true: an immobile implant is the first criterion.

q7-N03.stem:
Which of these statements on smoking and implants are true?
1. Nicotine hampers the revascularization of soft and hard tissue.
2. Smokers carry more T helper cells and B lymphocytes than nonsmokers.
3. Smoking lowers the oxygen in the mouth, an environment anaerobes favor.
4. Bain and Moy reported implant failure near 11% in smokers and near 5% in nonsmokers.
choices: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4
3 and 4 only
why: It takes in 2, which is false: smokers have fewer T helper cells and B lymphocytes. It misses 4, which is true: Bain and Moy found 11.3% vs 4.76%.
It misses 4, which is true: Bain and Moy found 11.3% vs 4.76%.
1, 3 and 4 are true. 2 is false: smokers have fewer T helper cells and B lymphocytes.
It misses 1, which is true: nicotine hampers revascularization, the first step of healing.

q7-N04.stem:
Which of these statements on bleeding on probing around implants are true?
1. Probing with the wrong force or at the wrong angle can make a site bleed.
2. Heavy bleeding that floods the sulcus while you probe points toward disease.
3. A site that bled at 1 of 4 visits had a 30% chance of attachment loss.
4. When a site doesn't bleed, that predicts stability well.
choices: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3
1, 2 and 4
why: It misses 4, which is true: no bleeding predicts stable peri-implant conditions.
It takes in 3, which is false: 1 of 4 visits carried 3%, and 30% was for 4 of 4. It misses 4, which is true: no bleeding predicts stable peri-implant conditions.
It takes in 3, which is false: 1 of 4 visits carried 3%, and 30% was for 4 of 4.
1, 2 and 4 are true. 3 is false: 1 of 4 visits carried 3%, and 30% was for 4 of 4.

q8-L01.stem: Without which factor would periodontal disease not develop at all?
choices: Plaque bacteria
Smoking tobacco
Diabetes mellitus
Parafunctional occlusal trauma
why: Right: bacteria in plaque are the primary etiologic factor: the answer to circle on the test.
Wrong: smoking makes the disease worse but can't cause it without bacteria.
Wrong: diabetes makes the disease worse but can't cause it without bacteria.
Wrong: with no bacteria there's no attachment or bone loss, whatever the occlusion; parafunction isn't the primary cause.

q8-M01.stem: Which of these cases fall within the course's indications for a systemic antibiotic? Select all that apply.
choices: Acute infection plus fever, malaise or swollen lymph nodes
A patient with aggressive periodontitis
A patient with refractory periodontitis
Any patient just diagnosed with periodontitis
A localized abscess without systemic signs
why: Correct: an acute infection with systemic manifestations is spreading and qualifies.
Correct: aggressive periodontitis is treated aggressively, antibiotics included.
Correct: refractory disease keeps losing attachment despite everything else.
Incorrect: antibiotics are for selected cases, never routine for every new diagnosis.
Incorrect: with no systemic manifestations, drain and debride; a systemic antibiotic isn't needed.

q8-L02.stem: A chart labels a patient's periodontitis as refractory. What does that label mean?
choices: Attachment loss despite thorough care
Fast, severe bone loss in a young patient
Periodontitis that has never been treated
Gingivitis remaining after a prophylaxis
why: Right: refractory periodontitis is attachment loss that continues even though patient and clinicians did everything right.
Wrong: rapid, severe loss in a young patient describes aggressive periodontitis, the other antibiotic indication.
Wrong: disease that was never treated can't be refractory; the term means it progresses after thorough treatment.
Wrong: refractory periodontitis involves attachment loss, which gingivitis doesn't have.

q8-L03.stem: When antibiotics are part of Phase I therapy, at what point in the sequence do they come in?
choices: Following scaling and root planing
Ahead of oral hygiene instructions
As a replacement for scaling and root planing
Before the first periodontal exam
why: Right: SRP disrupts the biofilm first, so the drug can then reach the bacteria.
Wrong: OHI is the first Phase I appointment.
Wrong: antibiotics are never a monotherapy.
Wrong: an antibiotic comes after a diagnosis and debridement, not before the exam.

q8-E01.stem: A biofilm shields its bacteria from antibiotics in each of these ways EXCEPT:
choices: Reducing the drug's level in the serum
Acting as a barrier the drug must penetrate
Holding a high concentration of β-lactamase
Slowing the bacteria's rate of growth
why: This is the exception: the biofilm doesn't change the blood level (a systemic drug spreads evenly through the body); it protects the bacteria locally through a barrier, β-lactamase and slower growth.
A real mechanism: the physical barrier makes it hard for the antibiotic to get in.
A real mechanism: the β-lactamase destroys the beta-lactam ring of our strongest antibiotics.
A real mechanism: bactericidal drugs need dividing cells, so slower growth protects the bacteria.

q8-L05.stem: Systemic delivery can reach only a certain antibiotic level. Some biofilm organisms can survive a concentration how many times greater?
choices: 2-5 times
10-20 times
Roughly 50 times
why: Right: the slide gives 500-1000 times what systemic delivery achieves, which is why the biofilm must be removed first.
Wrong: far too low; the figure is 500-1000 times.
Wrong: still well short of the slide's 500-1000 times.
Wrong: still about ten times too low; the slide says 500-1000 times.

q8-L06.stem: A patient with periodontitis takes a systemic antibiotic, yet the subgingival biofilm survives it. Why?
choices: The biofilm has to be disrupted mechanically first
The drug never gets into the crevicular fluid
Most periodontal pathogens are viruses
Saliva inactivates the drug before it reaches the pocket
why: Right: the GCF concentration is too low to kill biofilm organisms unless the biofilm is mechanically debrided.
Wrong: the drug does reach the GCF; the level there just can't overcome an intact biofilm.
Wrong: the pathogens are bacteria, mostly gram-negative anaerobic rods.
Wrong: a systemic drug reaches the pocket from the blood via the GCF, not through saliva; the level is simply too low for an intact biofilm.

q8-L07.stem: A bactericidal antibiotic can kill a bacterium only if that bacterium is:
choices: Dividing at the time
Dormant
A gram-positive species
Located outside the bloodstream
why: Right: bactericidal drugs have a narrow window: they act only on replicating bacteria.
Wrong: dormant bacteria escape bactericidal drugs.
Wrong: gram type isn't the requirement; cell division is.
Wrong: location doesn't matter; the bacteria must be actively dividing.

q8-L08.stem: What goes wrong if you prescribe a bacteriostatic antibiotic alongside a bactericidal one?
choices: One halts the growth the other relies on to kill
The liver breaks both down so they cancel each other
Both fight over the same ribosomal target
Combining them doubles the chance of an allergy
why: Right: bactericidal drugs need dividing bacteria, and a bacteriostatic drug stops division, closing that window.
Wrong: the conflict happens at the bacteria, not in the liver.
Wrong: they needn't share a target (amoxicillin acts on the cell wall, tetracycline on the 30S subunit); the issue is that one stops growth.
Wrong: allergy depends on each drug's class, not on mixing the two categories.

q8-L09.stem: By what mechanism does amoxicillin kill bacteria?
choices: Blocking synthesis of the cell wall
Binding the 30S ribosomal subunit
Blocking DNA gyrase
Reacting directly with bacterial DNA
why: Right: amoxicillin, a semisynthetic penicillin, is bactericidal by inhibiting cell wall synthesis.
Wrong: the 30S subunit is the bacteriostatic tetracyclines' target.
Wrong: DNA gyrase is inhibited by ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone.
Wrong: reacting with bacterial DNA is how metronidazole works.

q8-L11.stem: A prescription reads "1 tab po bid." How often does the patient take it?
choices: Two times a day
One time a day
Three times a day
Four times a day
why: Right: bid is twice a day (qd once, tid three times, qid four times).
Wrong: once a day is written qd.
Wrong: three times a day is tid, as in amoxicillin 1 tab po tid.
Wrong: four times a day is qid.

q8-L12.stem: On the health history a patient wrote "codeine allergy." When asked, they explain it gives them an upset stomach. How should you classify this?
choices: As a side effect, not a true allergy
As a genuine allergic reaction to codeine
As an episode of anaphylaxis to the drug
As an interaction between two drugs
why: Right: stomach upset is a side effect; a true allergy shows as hives or trouble breathing.
Wrong: the patient reported no hives or breathing difficulty.
Wrong: anaphylaxis presents with hives or difficulty breathing.
Wrong: no second drug is involved, so it can't be an interaction.

q8-M02.stem: A patient lists a drug allergy. Which described reactions would mean it is a true allergy? Select all that apply.
choices: Breaking out in hives
Trouble breathing
Stomach upset
Feeling drowsy
why: Correct: hives signal a true, anaphylactic reaction; nothing from that drug's class.
Correct: trouble breathing (the throat closing) is anaphylaxis and can be fatal.
Incorrect: stomach upset is a side effect, the one patients most often call an allergy.
Incorrect: drowsiness is a side effect; only hives or breathing trouble mean true allergy.

q8-L13.stem: Roughly what percentage of adults report an allergic response to penicillin?
choices: Around 50%
why: Right: about 10-15% of adults, so confirm verbally before handing over any prescription.
Wrong: far below the slide's 10-15%.
Wrong: well above the slide's 10-15%.
Wrong: far above the slide's 10-15%.

q8-L14.stem: How can an antibiotic make a patient's Coumadin (warfarin) stronger?
choices: It reduces gut flora that produce vitamin K
It slows warfarin's renal excretion
It adds extra vitamin K to the body
It acts as an anticoagulant all on its own
why: Right: fewer gut bacteria means less vitamin K, warfarin's antagonist, so bleeding time goes up.
Wrong: lowering renal excretion is metronidazole's effect on lithium, not the warfarin mechanism.
Wrong: vitamin K opposes warfarin; more of it would weaken the drug.
Wrong: antibiotics have no anticoagulant action; the effect runs through vitamin K from gut flora.

q8-L15.stem: Your patient takes Coumadin and you want to prescribe amoxicillin for 7 days. What is the correct step?
choices: Write the prescription and let the physician know
Reduce the Coumadin dose on your own
Tell them to hold their Coumadin during the antibiotic
Don't prescribe any antibiotic at all
why: Right: notify the physician, who decides whether the Coumadin needs adjusting.
Wrong: you never alter a medication another clinician prescribed.
Wrong: you never take a patient off another clinician's medication.
Wrong: you can, and sometimes must, prescribe; just inform the physician.

q8-L16.stem: Compared with plain amoxicillin, what is a downside of switching to Augmentin?
choices: Greater GI upset and more expense
Loss of its gram-negative coverage
It must be taken without food
It turns into a bacteriostatic drug
why: Right: Augmentin can cause more GI upset (give it with food) and costs significantly more than other penicillins.
Wrong: coverage improves, since clavulanic acid stops β-lactamase producers from inactivating amoxicillin.
Wrong: the reverse; it is given with food to ease GI upset.
Wrong: like amoxicillin, it remains bactericidal.

q8-L18.stem: What changes in coverage as cephalosporins move from the early generations to the later ones?
choices: Toward gram-negatives and β-lactamase resistance
Coverage narrows to gram-positives only
They become bacteriostatic
Bone penetration and gram-negative reach both drop
why: Right: later generations shift from mostly gram-positive toward gram-negative coverage with more β-lactamase resistance, which perio favors.
Wrong: mostly gram-positive coverage describes the early generations.
Wrong: every cephalosporin generation is bactericidal.
Wrong: backwards; gram-negative coverage grows. Bone penetration isn't what differs by generation (the class shows some evidence of increased bone penetration).

q8-L19.stem: A patient breaks out in hives from penicillin and isn't sure whether cephalosporins cause a reaction too. Should you prescribe one?
choices: No, since about 10% cross-react
Yes, because the classes are unrelated
Yes, as long as it's a later generation
Yes, if you give half the normal dose
why: Right: about 10% of penicillin-allergic patients react to cephalosporins as taught, so move to another class when they're unsure.
Wrong: cephalosporins are β-lactams structurally similar to the penicillins; about 10% cross-react.
Wrong: later generations gain gram-negative coverage and β-lactamase resistance but are still β-lactams that can cross-react.
Wrong: a lower dose won't prevent anaphylaxis; the drug class is the problem.

q8-L20.stem: According to the course, how often is a patient with a cephalosporin allergy also allergic to penicillin?
choices: Every time (100%)
About 10% of the time
About half of the time
Only with amoxicillin
why: Right: as taught, it's a 100% chance, so assume penicillin allergy too and choose another class, usually clindamycin.
Wrong: 10% is the reverse direction: penicillin-allergic patients reacting to cephalosporins.
Wrong: the slide says 100%, not half.
Wrong: the slide refers to penicillins as a class, not amoxicillin alone.

q8-L21.stem: Your patient is truly allergic to both penicillins and cephalosporins. Which antibiotic do you usually reach for first?
choices: Clindamycin
Erythromycin
Ciprofloxacin
Tetracycline
why: Right: clindamycin is "typically the first antibiotic that we turn to" here.
Wrong: erythromycin isn't recommended for perio because of high resistance.
Wrong: ciprofloxacin sits much further down the list, usually given with metronidazole.
Wrong: widespread resistance pushes tetracycline to a later choice.

q8-L22.stem: Clindamycin stops bacterial protein synthesis by acting where?
choices: On the 50S ribosomal subunit
On the 30S ribosomal subunit
On cell wall synthesis
On DNA gyrase
why: Right: clindamycin binds the 50S subunit reversibly, like the macrolides, and blocks protein synthesis.
Wrong: the 30S subunit is where the tetracyclines act.
Wrong: cell wall synthesis is the penicillins' and cephalosporins' target.
Wrong: DNA gyrase is ciprofloxacin's target.

q8-L24.stem: What is the reason tetracyclines are avoided in pregnant patients and in children younger than 8?
choices: They are laid down in calcifying teeth and bone
They bring on C. difficile colitis
They make the urine orange-red
They react with alcohol the way disulfiram does
why: Right: tetracycline deposits in bone and teeth during calcification, causing intrinsic stain and enamel hypoplasia.
Wrong: C. difficile colitis is clindamycin's known risk.
Wrong: orange-red urine is a metronidazole warning.
Wrong: the disulfiram-like alcohol reaction belongs to metronidazole.

q8-L26.stem: Erythromycin isn't a recommended drug for periodontal disease. What is the reason given?
choices: Bacteria are often resistant to it
Its action is bactericidal
Its spectrum is limited to obligate anaerobes
It discolors developing teeth
why: Right: its high incidence of bacterial resistance rules it out for periodontal disease.
Wrong: erythromycin is bacteriostatic like the other macrolides, and being bactericidal wouldn't be a drawback anyway.
Wrong: an obligate-anaerobe-only spectrum describes metronidazole.
Wrong: staining developing teeth is a tetracycline problem.

q8-L28.stem: A patient on a cardiac medication is prescribed a macrolide. Which heart drug's level could rise to toxic amounts?
choices: Digoxin
Metoprolol
Lisinopril
Amlodipine
why: Right: macrolides can raise digoxin levels, and digoxin's narrow therapeutic range makes toxicity a risk (Van Gogh's halos).
Wrong: metoprolol, a beta-blocker, isn't among the drugs macrolides potentiate.
Wrong: lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor, isn't on the list; the narrow-range heart drug is digoxin.
Wrong: amlodipine is the calcium channel blocker known for gingival overgrowth, not a macrolide interaction.

q8-L29.stem: What is metronidazole's mechanism against bacteria?
choices: It reacts with their DNA, halting replication
It attaches to the 50S subunit of the ribosome
It blocks cell wall synthesis
It blocks DNA gyrase
why: Right: metronidazole reacts with bacterial DNA and inhibits replication; it is almost always bactericidal and only against obligate anaerobes.
Wrong: the 50S subunit is where clindamycin and the macrolides bind.
Wrong: blocking cell wall synthesis is the β-lactams' mechanism (penicillins, cephalosporins).
Wrong: DNA gyrase is ciprofloxacin's target, a different DNA-level mechanism.

q8-L30.stem: You're handing a patient a metronidazole prescription. Which two warnings must you give?
choices: Orange-red urine is possible; avoid alcohol
Stay away from dairy products and the sun
Take it with milk and skip a dose when queasy
Cut out caffeine; take it at bedtime
why: Right: urine may turn orange-red, and alcohol triggers a disulfiram-like reaction with a severe headache.
Wrong: dairy and sun are tetracycline cautions (cations block absorption; photosensitivity).
Wrong: milk matters for tetracycline, and skipping doses is never the advice.
Wrong: caffeine comes up with ciprofloxacin, which impedes its metabolism, not with metronidazole.

q8-L31.stem: Which of these antibiotic pairs could be given at the same time under the lecture's combination rule? Select all that apply.
choices: Amoxicillin with metronidazole
Ciprofloxacin with metronidazole
Amoxicillin with doxycycline
Metronidazole with tetracycline
Amoxicillin with azithromycin
why: Correct: both are bactericidal, and together they broaden the spectrum with highly effective results.
Correct: both are bactericidal, and metronidazole picks up the anaerobes ciprofloxacin misses.
Incorrect: doxycycline is bacteriostatic and would halt the growth amoxicillin needs to kill.
Incorrect: tetracycline is bacteriostatic, and metronidazole kills only dividing bacteria.
Incorrect: azithromycin, a macrolide, is bacteriostatic while amoxicillin is bactericidal.

q8-L32.stem: Ciprofloxacin is far down the list for periodontal infections. What limitation explains this?
choices: Anaerobes are mostly resistant to it
It misses gram-negative bacteria
It only stops bacterial growth
It isn't something a patient can take by mouth
why: Right: anaerobes, the drivers of periodontal attachment loss, are largely resistant to it.
Wrong: gram-negative coverage is its strength.
Wrong: it inhibits DNA gyrase and is bactericidal, not bacteriostatic.
Wrong: it is an oral drug (po), so that isn't a weakness.

q8-L34.stem: A patient worries about GI trouble and yeast infections from an antibiotic course. What does the course recommend to prevent them?
choices: Lactobacillus, plus an antifungal if yeast-prone
Taking the antibiotic with a glass of milk
Doubling each dose and cutting the course in half
Adding a second antibiotic to the course
why: Right: prophylactic Lactobacillus acidophilus (yogurt or buttermilk with active cultures), plus nystatin or Diflucan for patients prone to yeast infections.
Wrong: milk blocks tetracycline absorption and does nothing for the gut flora.
Wrong: a bigger dose disrupts gut flora more, and it isn't a taught strategy.
Wrong: a second antibiotic adds to the flora disruption behind these complications.

q8-L35.stem: At what point in treatment is a locally delivered antimicrobial put into the pocket?
choices: When SRP is finished and the biofilm disrupted
Ahead of SRP, to soften the calculus and biofilm
In place of SRP
Only during a surgical flap procedure
why: Right: as with systemic drugs, debridement comes first; the agent goes in at the end of SRP.
Wrong: local agents don't soften calculus, and debridement comes first.
Wrong: they don't replace conventional therapy.
Wrong: they are placed non-surgically, at the end of SRP, not only during surgery.

q8-L36.stem: Which patient does Dr. Litz consider the best candidate for local drug delivery?
choices: A stable maintenance patient with one site breaking down
A patient with generalized residual pockets after Phase I
A patient with aggressive periodontitis
Any patient with sites over 4 mm at Phase I re-evaluation
why: Right: a single site breaking down (say 3 mm for years, now 5 mm and bleeding) in a stable maintenance patient; a last try before surgery.
Wrong: generalized residual pockets call for surgery, not a dozen cartridges.
Wrong: local delivery isn't indicated for aggressive periodontitis.
Wrong: local delivery is for specific sites, not every site over a threshold.

q8-L37.stem: Whether given locally or systemically, which of these is beyond what an antibiotic can accomplish?
choices: Fixing the bone defects the disease created
Getting into the periodontal pocket
Acting on the gram-negative periodontal pathogens
Being used in combination with SRP
why: Right: antibiotics can't alter the anatomical bone deformities the disease left; that's surgery's job.
Wrong: local delivery places the drug directly in the pocket.
Wrong: many antibiotics cover gram-negatives.
Wrong: they are always used together with SRP, as an adjunct.

q8-L38.stem: For roughly how long does Arestin maintain a therapeutic level of minocycline at the site?
choices: 14 days
2 hours
9 days
3 months
why: Right: the slide gives a therapeutic concentration for 14 days.
Wrong: about 2 hours is when PerioChip's release peaks.
Wrong: about 9 days is how long PerioChip's release tapers.
Wrong: much longer than the slide's figure.
