q8-L39.stem: A PerioChip has just been placed in a pocket. How long until its chlorhexidine level is at its highest?
choices: Roughly 2 hours
Roughly 14 days
Roughly 24 hours
No peak: it releases evenly for 3 months
why: Right: the release peaks at about 2 hours, then tapers off over about 9 days.
No: 14 days is the therapeutic window for Arestin, not PerioChip's peak.
No: the peak comes sooner than a day, at about 2 hours.
No: there is a clear peak at about 2 hours, and the release tapers over about 9 days.

q8-L41.stem: Periodontitis can't happen without bacteria. Which factor actually carries out most of the tissue damage?
choices: The patient's own immune-inflammatory reaction
Enzymes and toxins from the bacteria on their own
Forces from the bite
Enzymes in the saliva
why: Right: the host's MMPs and the osteoclasts that cytokines turn on do most of the damage.
No: bacteria do make some enzymes, but most of the loss is mediated by the host response.
No: occlusal forces don't start or drive this attachment loss; the host response to bacteria does.
No: saliva lays down the pellicle and feeds early colonizers; it doesn't mediate the destruction.

q8-L42.stem: Which products does IL-1 (also called osteoclast activating factor) drive up?
choices: Collagenase and PGE2
New bone, through osteoblasts
Mast-cell histamine
Clumping of platelets
why: Right: IL-1 stimulates collagenase and PGE2, which release MMPs, so connective tissue and bone are lost.
No: IL-1 drives breakdown; a blast builds and a clast destroys, and IL-1 turns on the clasts.
No: histamine from mast cells is part of complement's cascade (the edema), not IL-1's output.
No: platelet aggregation comes up with NSAIDs, which lower it; it isn't something IL-1 makes.

q8-L43.stem: NSAIDs have been tried as host modulators. What has kept them from becoming a long-term therapy?
choices: Ulcers and bleeding with prolonged use
They increase PGE2 and hasten bone loss
Their effect lasts only about a week
Periodontal bacteria become resistant
why: Right: prolonged use risks GI trouble (a bad gastric ulcer), bleeding from reduced platelet aggregation, and kidney or liver impairment.
No: NSAIDs lower PGE2, which is why they slowed bone loss; the side effects are the problem.
No: a week or two does nothing; the benefit needed daily dosing for up to 3 years.
No: NSAIDs aren't antibiotics, so bacterial resistance isn't the concern.

q8-L44.stem: Where do bisphosphonates stand today as a treatment for periodontal disease?
choices: None approved, chiefly due to BRONJ
Used first-line to modulate the host
Approved in the form of a local gel
Approved IV for periodontal patients
why: Right: the risk of osteonecrosis has stunted their development as host modulators.
No: BRONJ stunted their development; none is approved for periodontal disease, first-line or not.
No: no form, local or systemic, is approved for periodontal disease.
No: the high-dose IV forms carry most of the BRONJ complications, and none is approved for periodontal disease.

q8-E02.stem: Periostat should be withheld from each of these patients EXCEPT:
choices: An adult who has diabetes
A woman who is pregnant or nursing
A child younger than 12
A patient with a tetracycline allergy
why: This is the exception: host modulation can be considered for patients with hard-to-modify risk factors such as diabetes.
Listed contraindication: pregnant or lactating women, as with the tetracyclines.
Listed contraindication: children under 12 for Periostat (the line for tetracycline antibiotics is under 8).
Listed contraindication: Periostat is doxycycline, so a tetracycline allergy rules it out.

q8-L47.stem: Caton's 2000 trial compared SRP plus Periostat with SRP plus a placebo. What did it find?
choices: A real but modest extra benefit
The two groups were the same
Pocket reduction was doubled
Benefits shown to last five years
why: Right: PD and CAL improved significantly at 3, 6 and 9 months, but the net changes were small.
No: the differences were statistically significant.
No: the extra reductions were only fractions of a millimeter.
No: efficacy beyond 9 months hasn't been established.

q8-L48.stem: According to the slide, which patient should be considered for host modulation therapy?
choices: One whose risks are hard to change
Any patient who has just had SRP
One who is unable to brush
One who skips maintenance visits often
why: Right: for example smoking or diabetes, and only with full compliance.
No: controlling the bacteria is still the main focus; HMT is used selectively.
No: the pill never takes the place of home care.
No: the patient still has to keep up with maintenance.

q8-P01.stem: What makes a systemic antibiotic appropriate for this man?
choices: Signs that the infection is spreading
All periodontal abscesses require one
Drainage and debridement are ruled out
His diagnosis is aggressive periodontitis
why: Right: fever, malaise and enlarged nodes are systemic manifestations, a localized infection beginning to spread, the first indication on the slide.
No: only acute infections with systemic manifestations qualify; an abscess without them doesn't.
No: the antibiotic is an adjunct; drainage and debridement still happen.
No: nothing here points to it (aggressive disease is rapid loss in a young patient); the indication is the spread.

q8-P02.stem: Working through the lecture's order of choices, which antibiotic should she get?
choices: Azithromycin (a Z-Pak)
Cephalexin (a cephalosporin)
Clindamycin
Augmentin
why: Right: penicillin is ruled out, her cephalosporin history is unknown, and the colitis rules out clindamycin.
No: not with a penicillin allergy and an uncertain cephalosporin history.
No: avoid it in a patient with a history of colitis.
No: it contains amoxicillin, which is a penicillin.

q8-P03.stem: How should the change at #14 be managed?
choices: Debride the site, then place Arestin
Systemic amoxicillin with metronidazole
Osseous surgery across the quadrant
Place Arestin and skip debridement
why: Right: a single site breaking down in a stable maintenance patient calls for debridement, then local delivery.
No: one site doesn't call for systemic antibiotics.
No: for a single site, local delivery is the last attempt to avoid surgery.
No: the biofilm has to be disrupted by debridement first.

q8-P04.stem: You've told her about the urine color and the alcohol. What is the other step to take?
choices: Tell her physician about the warfarin
Hold the warfarin until the course ends
Have her double the warfarin dose
None: the two drugs don't interact
why: Right: metronidazole increases warfarin's anticoagulant effect, so the physician needs to know.
No: you never change another clinician's prescription.
No: the interaction increases warfarin's effect, and the dose isn't yours to change anyway.
No: they do interact; metronidazole increases the anticoagulant effect.

q8-S01.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Chronic periodontitis can be treated with an antibiotic on its own, as monotherapy.
2. A systemic antibiotic seeks out the periodontal pocket and collects there.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: No: statement 1 is false, since antibiotics are never used alone, only as an adjunct after SRP. Statement 2 is false too: a systemic antibiotic spreads evenly through the body ("not a heat-seeking missile"), and its GCF level is too low for an intact biofilm.

Right: statement 1 is false, since antibiotics are never used alone, only as an adjunct after SRP. Statement 2 is false: a systemic antibiotic spreads evenly through the body ("not a heat-seeking missile"), and its GCF level is too low for an intact biofilm.
No: statement 1 is false, since antibiotics are never a monotherapy; they're an adjunct after SRP.
No: statement 2 is false, since a systemic antibiotic spreads evenly through the body ("not a heat-seeking missile"), and its GCF level is too low for an intact biofilm.

q8-S02.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The ribosomal subunit clindamycin attaches to is the 50S.
2. The ribosomal subunit tetracycline attaches to is the 30S.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Right: clindamycin reversibly binds the 50S subunit, as the macrolides do, and tetracycline reversibly binds the 30S subunit.
No: both are true. Clindamycin reversibly binds 50S, like the macrolides, and tetracycline reversibly binds 30S.
No: statement 2 is true as well; tetracycline reversibly binds the 30S subunit.
No: statement 1 is true as well; clindamycin reversibly binds the 50S subunit, like the macrolides.

q8-S03.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Taking azithromycin with food cuts its absorption significantly.
2. Ciprofloxacin is absorbed best when it is taken with food.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: No: statement 2 is false, since ciprofloxacin is absorbed most rapidly 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals.
No: statement 1 is true, which is why azithromycin is given 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals.
Right: azithromycin should be given 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals, and ciprofloxacin is absorbed most rapidly 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals, not with them.
No: it's the reverse. Statement 1 is true (azithromycin goes 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals), and statement 2 is false (ciprofloxacin is absorbed fastest away from meals).

q8-S04.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Metronidazole works against aerobic bacteria.
2. Erythromycin is a recommended antibiotic for periodontal disease.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: No: statement 1 is false, since metronidazole works only on obligate anaerobes, and statement 2 is false, since erythromycin's high resistance means it is not recommended.
Right: metronidazole acts only on obligate anaerobes, and erythromycin is not recommended because resistance to it is high.
No: statement 1 is false; metronidazole is effective only against obligate anaerobes.
No: statement 2 is false; resistance to erythromycin is high, so it is not recommended.

q8-S05.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Periostat's mechanism is to inhibit the host's collagenase.
2. Periostat, used along with SRP, was the first systemic host modulation drug the FDA approved.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Right: it blocks collagenase rather than bacteria, and the slide calls it the first FDA-approved systemic drug for host modulation.
No: both are true. It blocks collagenase, not bacteria, and the slide calls it the first FDA-approved systemic drug for host modulation.
No: statement 2 is true as well; the slide calls it the first FDA-approved systemic drug for host modulation.
No: statement 1 is true as well; it blocks collagenase, not bacteria.

q8-T01.stem: True or false: β-lactamase is able to inactivate amoxicillin.
choices: True
False
why: True: amoxicillin has a beta-lactam ring, and β-lactamase destroys it.
It is true, which is why Augmentin adds clavulanic acid to the amoxicillin.

q8-T02.stem: True or false: A bacteriostatic drug works by killing the bacteria outright.
choices: True
False
why: False: killing bacteria is what bactericidal drugs do; bacteriostatic drugs only halt their growth.
False is right: a bacteriostatic drug stops growth, and the body then clears the bacteria.

q8-T04.stem: True or false: Taking tetracycline with a glass of milk is a good way to ease stomach upset.
choices: True
False
why: False: the calcium in milk blocks tetracycline's absorption.
False is right: keep milk and dairy away from tetracycline and take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals.

q8-T05.stem: True or false: Clarithromycin falls in pregnancy category C.
choices: True
False
why: True: the slide lists it as pregnancy category C.
It is true: clarithromycin is pregnancy C, so it's avoided in pregnancy.

q8-T06.stem: True or false: Lithium's renal excretion can be reduced by metronidazole.
choices: True
False
why: True: it is one of the cautions the slide lists for metronidazole.
It is true and on the slide: lithium levels can climb.

q8-T07.stem: True or false: A patient with aggressive periodontitis is a candidate for locally delivered antimicrobials.
choices: True
False
why: False: the slide says local delivery is not for aggressive periodontitis.
False is right: aggressive periodontitis gets aggressive treatment, with systemic antibiotics as the adjunct.

q8-T08.stem: True or false: After Atridox is placed, the patient needs a visit to have it taken out.
choices: True
False
why: False: there is no removal visit, because it dissolves on its own.
False is right: it dissolves by itself, though the patient still returns in 4-6 weeks for re-evaluation.

q8-N01.stem:
Which of these statements about biofilms are true?
1. Because they don't dissolve, they are difficult to remove.
2. They contain a high concentration of β-lactamase.
3. Mouthrinses and water irrigation can be counted on to remove them.
4. They make the bacteria living in them grow faster.
choices: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3
1 and 3 only
2 and 4 only
why: Right: 1 and 2 are true. Statement 3 is false, since rinses and water piks leave biofilms in place, and statement 4 is false, since biofilms slow bacterial growth, which shields them from bactericidal drugs.
No: statement 3 is false; mouthrinses and water piks leave biofilms in place.
No: statement 3 is false (rinses and water piks leave them in place), and statement 2, left out, is true: the biofilm is saturated with beta-lactamase.
No: statement 4 is false (biofilms slow growth, which protects them from bactericidal drugs), and statement 1, left out, is true: being insoluble is why they must be scrubbed off.

q8-N02.stem:
Which of these drugs kill bacteria (are bactericidal)?
1. Amoxicillin
2. Tetracycline
3. Metronidazole
4. Ciprofloxacin
choices: 1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
1 and 4 only
3 and 4 only
why: No: tetracycline (2) is bacteriostatic, and ciprofloxacin (4), left out, is bactericidal.
Right: amoxicillin, metronidazole and ciprofloxacin are bactericidal; tetracycline (2) is bacteriostatic.
No: metronidazole (3), left out, is almost always bactericidal.
No: amoxicillin (1), left out, kills by inhibiting cell wall synthesis.

q8-N03.stem:
Which of these statements about macrolides are true?
1. Their target is the 50S ribosomal subunit.
2. They stop bacterial growth rather than kill (bacteriostatic).
3. They can reduce the blood level of digoxin.
4. Against anaerobes, azithromycin and clarithromycin do better than erythromycin.
choices: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3
1, 2 and 4
2 and 4 only
why: No: statement 4, left out, is true; azithromycin and clarithromycin are more active against anaerobes than erythromycin.
No: statement 3 is false, since macrolides raise digoxin levels and risk toxicity, and statement 4, left out, is true.
Right: 1, 2 and 4 are true. Statement 3 is false: macrolides raise (potentiate) digoxin levels, which is how digoxin toxicity happens, rather than lowering them.
No: statement 1, left out, is true; macrolides bind the 50S subunit, as clindamycin does.

q8-N04.stem:
Which of these statements about local delivery agents are true?
1. A PerioChip has to be taken out at a later visit.
2. Arestin is 1 mg of minocycline in microspheres.
3. Atridox is 10% doxycycline in a polymer that biodegrades.
4. The chlorhexidine in a PerioChip reaches its peak release about 2 hours after it is placed.
choices: 1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4
why: No: statement 1 is false (PerioChip biodegrades, so there's no removal visit), and statement 4, left out, is true: release peaks at 2 hours and tapers over about 9 days.
No: statement 1 is false (PerioChip biodegrades, so there's no removal visit), and statement 2, left out, is true: Arestin is 1 mg minocycline microspheres.
No: statement 4, left out, is true; the release peaks at 2 hours and tapers over about 9 days.
Right: 2, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 1 is false: PerioChip is biodegradable, so no removal visit is needed.

q8-L49.stem: Dr. Litz compares periodontal disease to a car in the garage. Which part of the car stands for the host response?
choices: Its engine
Its key
Its driver
Its fuel
why: Right: the host response is what takes a patient from health to periodontal disease, but it sits idle until the key is turned.
No: the key is the bacteria, the primary etiologic factor; without them the engine never starts.
No: the analogy has a key and an engine, and no one steers the host response.
No: the analogy has a key (bacteria) and an engine (host response); fuel isn't in it.

q8-L50.stem: Beyond lysing bacteria itself, what is complement chiefly doing in periodontal defense?
choices: Drawing PMNs and other phagocytes in
Laying down the pellicle on the tooth
Producing antibodies to the red complex
Turning on osteoblasts to rebuild bone
why: Right: complement works mainly as a chemoattractant for the host's phagocytic cells.
No: the pellicle is made of salivary proteins on the tooth; complement is serum proteins in the blood.
No: making antibodies isn't complement's role; it's a group of serum proteins that calls in phagocytes.
No: nothing in this cascade builds bone; the cytokines it leads to activate osteoclasts.

q8-L51.stem: Inflamed gingiva puffs up. By what route does complement produce that swelling?
choices: Mast-cell histamine makes vessels leak
Lymph can no longer drain the gingiva
Gingival epithelial cells are lysed
New capillaries grow into the gingiva
why: Right: increased vascular permeability lets fluid and cells leak into the soft tissue, which is edema.
No: that isn't the mechanism taught; the swelling is fluid leaking out of the vessels.
No: complement can lyse bacterial membranes, not the patient's own epithelium.
No: that isn't the mechanism taught; the vessels already there become leaky.

q8-L52.stem: Bacteria have just challenged the gingiva. When should the first neutrophils show up?
choices: In roughly 24-48 hours
In just a few minutes
In about two weeks
Not until macrophages arrive
why: Right: neutrophils are the first responders, like paramedics at a wreck.
No: a few minutes is how quickly the salivary pellicle forms after a prophylaxis.
No: that's far too slow for the first responders.
No: that's backwards; neutrophils come first, and macrophages arrive later if neutrophils can't keep up.

q8-L54.stem: What risk makes Dr. Litz urge caution with host modulation?
choices: Damping it too far could make an infection lethal
Bacteria quickly grow resistant to it within weeks
It is outside what dentists may prescribe
It keeps the gingiva from healing after SRP
why: Right: turn the host response down too far and a seemingly innocent infection could turn serious, even lethal. "You better know what you're doing before you start monkeying around with this."
No: Periostat's sub-antimicrobial dose shows no resistance.
No: Periostat is FDA-approved as an adjunct to SRP.
No: that isn't his reason; HMT aims to tip the balance toward healing.

q8-L55.stem: What makes bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (BRONJ) such a hard lesion to manage?
choices: Scraping off dead bone is trauma, its very cause
It's an infection that most antibiotics can't touch
A week off the drug reverses it, but few patients comply
The exposed bone regrows too quickly to be debrided
why: Right: the lesion can return larger, a quarter instead of a dime, in a vicious cycle.
No: it isn't an infection, though it can look like one (exposed dead bone can get infected).
No: the drugs have a very long half-life and stay in the body for years, so a short break does nothing.
No: necrotic bone is dead and doesn't grow back.

q8-L56.stem: Periostat adds only fractions of a millimeter. In which patients does Dr. Litz think it does the most good?
choices: Those with refractory or aggressive disease
Those with gingivitis and no attachment loss
Every new periodontitis case, instead of SRP
Stable maintenance cases without deep pockets
why: Right: these are the cases where we need all the help we can get.
No: he didn't place it there; plaque control treats gingivitis.
No: it is never used instead of SRP; it's an adjunct, and controlling the bacteria comes first.
No: he didn't place it there; he named refractory and aggressive cases.

q8-M03.stem: On Dr. Litz's dosing chart, which regimens carry a note that they aren't recommended under age 16? Select all that apply.
choices: Metronidazole
Amoxicillin with metronidazole
Augmentin (amoxicillin/clavulanic acid)
Doxycycline
why: Belongs: it is not recommended for children under 16.
Belongs: the combination has the same note.
Doesn't belong: the chart gives a weight-based dose for children.
Doesn't belong: the chart doses it for children over 8 (below 8, tetracyclines stain developing teeth).

q8-T09.stem: True or false: Periodontal disease belongs among the autoimmune diseases.
choices: True
False
why: False: the body doesn't destroy itself without a stimulus, and the stimulus is bacteria.
False is right: it isn't autoimmune; bacteria are the key that starts the host-response engine.

q8-T10.stem: True or false: The high-dose IV bisphosphonates account for most cases of bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw.
choices: True
False
why: True: most of the complications come with the high-dose IV forms.
It is true: the oral forms carry less of the risk than the high-dose IV forms.

q8-T11.stem: True or false: Taking ibuprofen daily for just a week or two will slow periodontal bone loss.
choices: True
False
why: False: the effect takes daily dosing for years; a week or two shows nothing real.
False is right: the benefit needed daily dosing for up to 3 years.

q8-T12.stem: True or false: Because resistance to Periostat doesn't develop, it can be taken long-term.
choices: True
False
why: True: at its sub-antimicrobial dose, resistance isn't evident, so long-term use is possible.
It is true: the dose is too low to select for resistant bacteria.

q8-S06.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Macrophages reach the site before neutrophils do.
2. Another name for IL-1 is osteoclast activating factor.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: No: statement 1 is false; neutrophils are the first responders, and macrophages come later if neutrophils can't keep up.
No: statement 2 is true; IL-1 is known as osteoclast activating factor, turning on osteoclasts and stimulating collagenase and PGE2.

No: it's the reverse. Statement 1 is false (neutrophils respond first; macrophages come later if needed), and statement 2 is true (IL-1 is osteoclast activating factor, which turns on osteoclasts and stimulates collagenase and PGE2).

Right: neutrophils are the first responders, with macrophages arriving later if neutrophils can't keep up, and IL-1 is osteoclast activating factor, which turns on osteoclasts and stimulates collagenase and PGE2.

q8-S08.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. In medicine, host modulation is used for chronic progressive conditions like arthritis and osteoporosis.
2. Once taken, bisphosphonates remain in the body for years.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Right: host modulation is routine in medicine for chronic progressive disorders and fairly new in dentistry (the 1990s), and bisphosphonates have a very long half-life, so stopping for days or weeks doesn't clear them.

No: both are true. Host modulation is routine in medicine for chronic progressive disorders (fairly new in dentistry, the 1990s), and bisphosphonates' very long half-life keeps them in the body for years.
No: statement 2 is true as well; bisphosphonates have a very long half-life, and stopping for days or weeks doesn't clear them.
No: statement 1 is true as well; host modulation is routine in medicine for chronic progressive disorders and fairly new in dentistry (the 1990s).

q8-N05.stem:
Which of these statements about periodontal tissue destruction are true?
1. Bacteria by themselves are enough to produce attachment loss.
2. Collagenase and PGE2 are stimulated by IL-1.
3. Complement's main role is to attract PMNs to the site.
4. After a bacterial challenge, neutrophils are the first cells to respond.
choices: 1, 2 and 3
2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4
why: No: statement 1 is false (bacteria are required but not sufficient; the host response does the destruction), and statement 4, left out, is true: neutrophils arrive within about 24-48 hours, before macrophages.
No: statement 1 is false; bacteria are required but not sufficient, and the host response to them mediates the destruction.
No: statement 4, left out, is true; neutrophils arrive within about 24-48 hours, and macrophages come later.
Right: 2, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 1 is false: bacteria are required but not sufficient; the host response to them mediates the destruction.

q8-N06.stem:
Which of these statements about host modulation drugs are true?
1. At its low dose, Periostat kills periodontal bacteria.
2. To slow periodontal bone loss, NSAIDs have to be taken every day.
3. There is no bisphosphonate approved for periodontal disease.
4. In a smoker, Periostat can be used in place of SRP.
choices: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4
why: No: statement 1 is false; at 20 mg bid Periostat has no antimicrobial effect and instead inhibits host collagenase.
No: statement 1 is false (at 20 mg bid it has no antimicrobial effect; it inhibits host collagenase), and statement 2, left out, is true: the benefit came with daily dosing for up to 3 years.

Right: 2 and 3 are true. Statement 1 is false, since at 20 mg bid it has no antimicrobial effect and inhibits host collagenase. Statement 4 is false, since it is an adjunct to SRP, never a replacement, even with a hard-to-modify risk like smoking.
No: statement 4 is false; Periostat is an adjunct to SRP and never replaces it, even with a hard-to-modify risk like smoking.

q8-F01.stem: Following a prophylaxis, what explains why the orange- and red-complex species settle in only after the early colonizers?
choices: Plaque inflames the gingiva, giving them blood and GCF
The pellicle they cling to needs weeks to form
Their food, salivary dietary protein, builds up later
Neutrophils hold them off for the first 24-48 hours
why: Right: colonization is sequential; plaque at the gingival margin inflames the soft tissue, and the late colonizers (orange, then red) feed on the blood and GCF.
No: the pellicle forms within minutes of a prophylaxis (before the patient has paid at the front desk) and is the foundation for the first colonizers.
No: dietary proteins in saliva feed the first colonizers, mostly gram-positive cocci; the late colonizers feed on blood and GCF.
No: neutrophils arrive within 24-48 hours to fight bacteria, but they don't set the order of colonization.

q8-F02.stem: Why does an untreated periodontal pocket that is getting deeper tend to keep worsening?
choices: More bacteria provoke more host-driven breakdown
After a pocket forms, the body starts to attack itself
The bacteria's enzymes become the main destroyers
Neutrophils can't get down to the deep part anymore
why: Right: a deeper pocket houses more bacteria, a bigger load calls in a bigger cellular response and more cytokines, and that means more breakdown, a vicious cycle.
No: periodontal disease isn't autoimmune; the body doesn't destroy itself without a stimulus, and the stimulus is always bacteria.
No: bacteria can make tissue-destroying enzymes, but most of the destruction is mediated by the host (MMPs and cytokine-driven osteoclasts).
No: the problem taught is a larger host response, not a blocked one; more bacteria call in more cells, which release more cytokines.

q8-F03.stem: Amoxicillin and the cephalosporins share an interaction the lecture links to almost all antibiotics. Which one?
choices: Less effective oral contraceptives
Raised digoxin levels and toxicity
A disulfiram-like alcohol reaction
Reduced renal excretion of lithium
why: Right: like nearly every antibiotic, they can interfere with oral contraceptives; reduced contraceptive effectiveness is on the list of complications of systemic antibiotics.
No: raising digoxin levels is the macrolides' interaction (Van Gogh's halos), not one shared by nearly all antibiotics.
No: the disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol is metronidazole's warning, not amoxicillin's or the cephalosporins'.
No: slowing lithium's renal excretion is a metronidazole caution, not one shared by nearly all antibiotics.

q8-F04.stem: SRP is complete for a 19-year-old patient with aggressive periodontitis who has no drug allergies. Which antibiotics does the lecture name as useful for this disease? Select all that apply.
choices: Amoxicillin
Augmentin
Metronidazole
Clindamycin
Azithromycin
why: Belongs: a bactericidal, extended-spectrum penicillin that is useful in both localized and generalized aggressive periodontitis.
Belongs: its clavulanic acid stops β-lactamase from inactivating the amoxicillin, and it is useful in aggressive or refractory periodontitis.
Belongs: it kills obligate anaerobes and is useful in aggressive periodontitis and ANUG, often paired with amoxicillin (both bactericidal).
Doesn't belong: clindamycin is the usual first pick for a patient truly allergic to penicillins and cephalosporins; she has no allergies, and the lecture doesn't link it to aggressive disease.
Doesn't belong: azithromycin is a bacteriostatic, generally narrow-spectrum macrolide (better than erythromycin against anaerobes); the lecture doesn't link it to aggressive periodontitis.

q9-L01.stem: With a probe in the facial sulcus of #8, you can make out the probe through the tissue. What have you learned?
choices: The phenotype is thin: 1 mm or less
The phenotype is thick: over 1 mm
The phenotype is thin: 2 mm or less
#8 has facial recession
why: Correct: this is the validated probe test; seeing the probe through the tissue means a thin phenotype, 1 mm or less of soft tissue.
Backward: thick tissue hides the probe, so seeing it means thin tissue.
The cutoff is 1 mm: thin is 1 mm or less and thick is over 1 mm.
Recession is the margin sitting apical to the CEJ, measured margin to CEJ; a visible probe measures thickness.

q9-L02.stem: Before orthodontics, Dr. Abou-Arraj grafted a young patient who had no recession yet but such thin tissue over the incisors that the roots showed. What was the graft for?
choices: Making a thin phenotype thick before tooth movement
Freeing a high frenum before the teeth move
Making a shallow vestibule deeper for the brackets
Bringing the attached gingiva up to a 5 mm band
why: Correct: tooth movement and years of brushing would put thin tissue at risk of recession, so a CTG under the flap thickened it first.
There was no frenum problem; the tissue's thickness was the issue, and the graft changed it from thin to thick.
The vestibule was not the problem in this case; the thin tissue was.
No width goal was set; the aim was to change the phenotype from thin to thick.

q9-L03.stem: You are charting recession at the six sites. Between which two landmarks do you measure it?
choices: The gingival margin and the CEJ
The CEJ and the pocket base
The gingival margin and the pocket base
The gingival margin and the MGJ
why: Correct: recession is how far the margin sits apical to the CEJ, so it runs margin to CEJ, at the same six sites as probing depth.
CEJ to pocket base is the clinical attachment level, which adds recession to probing depth.
Margin to pocket base is the probing depth.
Margin to MGJ is the width of keratinized gingiva.

q9-L04.stem: Dr. Abou-Arraj explained why recession shows up more in older patients. What was his reason?
choices: Over the years they have collected more risk factors
Aging thins the gingiva on its own, regardless of risk factors
Older people brush harder than younger people
After 65, alveolar bone resorbs by itself
why: Correct: it isn't age itself; older patients have had more predisposing factors acting on them for longer.
He attributed it to accumulated risk factors, not to tissue thinning with age.
Aggressive brushing is a factor at any age; it wasn't his explanation for the trend with age.
He didn't blame age-related bone loss; he pointed to years of risk factors.

q9-L05.stem: Among the kinds of trauma that predispose to recession, which one did he name as most common?
choices: Brushing the teeth
The way a patient flosses
Habits with fingernails or pens
Caustic medicaments placed on the gingiva
why: Correct: "Toothbrushing seems to be the most common one," whether hard bristles or an aggressive brusher using any brush.
Flossing is on the trauma list but is not the most common.
Foreign-object habits are on the list, but toothbrushing is the most common.
Caustic medicaments are on the list, but rare compared with toothbrushing.

q9-L06.stem: He described one combination of findings as "the perfect storm" for recession. Which is it?
choices: Dehiscence, thin phenotype and aggressive brushing
Fenestration, thick phenotype and a soft brush
Gingivitis, thick phenotype and wide attached gingiva
Low frenum, thick phenotype and flossing
why: Correct: missing facial bone, thin tissue over it, and trauma on top, several predisposing factors at once.
Thick tissue and gentle brushing protect the margin; only the fenestration predisposes.
Gingivitis seldom causes recession, and thick tissue with a wide band of KG resists it.
A low frenum doesn't pull the margin, and thick tissue resists recession.

q9-L07.stem: A mandibular incisor is tipped buccal to the arch, with thin facial tissue and recession. If orthodontics brings it back into the arch, what can happen to the recession?
choices: Some of it can resolve without a graft
Nothing, since only grafting changes recession
The root becomes fully covered every time
It begins to get worse more quickly
why: Correct: once back in its alveolar housing the tissue thickens, and the recession can partly resolve.
He said that in some cases repositioning alone gives partial resolution.
He described at least partial resolution in some cases, not full coverage every time.
Moving teeth out of the housing is the risk; moving a tooth back in helps.

q9-L08.stem: A patient has finished Phase I and resective Phase II surgery and now shows recession on many teeth. What caused most of it?
choices: The surgery, which eliminates pockets by design
Brushing trauma in the months after the surgery
The periodontitis, before treatment started
A thin phenotype that the surgery exposed
why: Correct: "We caused most of this recession," to leave a pocket-free environment the patient can keep clean.
Brushing trauma also causes recession, but here the resection itself exposed the roots.
The disease caused some, but he said the treatment caused most of it.
The phenotype isn't the source here; resecting tissue to remove pockets is.

q9-L09.stem: Behind every pathway to recession, Dr. Abou-Arraj named one key word. What was it?
choices: Inflammation
Trauma
Thin phenotype
Plaque
why: Correct: "The key word here is inflammation": it is what actually produces recession, while the listed factors only predispose.
Trauma begins one pathway, but it leads to recession through inflammation and ulceration.
A thin phenotype predisposes to recession but doesn't cause it.
Plaque begins the other pathway, again acting through inflammation.

q9-L11.stem: On a recession site, more attachment has been lost interproximally than on the buccal. What result should you expect from a root-coverage graft?
choices: No coverage of the root; at best thicker tissue
Coverage of the root up to the interproximal level
Coverage of close to 100% of the root
Full coverage, provided a CTG is the graft
why: Correct: interproximal loss greater than buccal is RT3; the interproximal support is too far apical, so a graft "would not end up achieving that root coverage at all," and at most thickens the tissue.
Partial coverage to the interproximal level is RT2, where interproximal loss is less than or equal to buccal; here it is greater.
Close to 100% coverage is RT1, with no interproximal attachment loss.
No graft overcomes the missing interproximal support; a graft lives on the bone and tissue beside the root, whatever its type.

q9-L12.stem: In an RT2 recession, coverage stops short of the CEJ. What is the reason?
choices: Nothing interproximal holds tissue that high
In RT2 the CEJ cannot be located clinically
A coronally advanced flap cannot reach that far
RT2 roots are too sensitive to graft
why: Correct: with no interproximal framework and no blood supply there, coverage stops at about the interproximal attachment level.
In RT2 the CEJ is visible interproximally; that is how the loss is detected.
The limit is biological, the interproximal support, not how far a flap advances.
Sensitivity is a reason to treat, not a limit on coverage.

q9-L13.stem: #28 has a 2 mm RT1 recession that is neither sensitive nor visible. According to the Chambrone and Tatakis review, what happens to recession that is not treated?
choices: It usually goes on progressing
It holds steady if there are no symptoms
It reverses once brushing is gentler
It progresses in smokers only
why: Correct: untreated recession defects keep progressing, with the margin moving further apical.
The review contradicts this assumption: no symptoms doesn't mean no change.
Gentler brushing removes one factor, but the review found untreated defects progress.
The finding was not limited to smokers.

q9-L14.stem: What makes the palate the usual place to harvest a gingival graft?
choices: Its keratinized tissue induces keratinization
It has no major nerves or vessels to avoid
Its wound always closes by primary intention
Its tissue is thin and elastic like mucosa
why: Correct: palatal tissue is orthokeratinized, and its connective tissue induces keratinization at the recipient site.
The greater palatine artery and nerve run through the palate; a harvest has to stay away from them.
An FGG donor site is left open and heals by secondary intention.
Palatal tissue is thick, firm and keratinized, unlike alveolar mucosa.

q9-L15.stem: In a palatal cross section, which layer is usually the thickest one?
choices: The lamina propria
The surface epithelium
The fatty submucosal layer
The periosteum over the bone
why: Correct: the lamina propria, 1.25-3.0 mm on the slide; a CTG is this layer without the epithelium.
The epithelium is thin, 0.3-0.6 mm; an FGG includes it and a CTG doesn't.
The adipose and glandular layer lies under the lamina propria and is usually trimmed off the graft.
The periosteum covers the bone beneath the submucosa and isn't harvested as the graft.

q9-L16.stem: You plan to bury the graft entirely under a coronally advanced flap. Which graft is the right choice, and why?
choices: A CTG, since epithelium under a flap won't heal
An FGG, because its epithelium shields the root
An FGG, because it brings more keratinization
Either, because the flap's inner surface is epithelium
why: Correct: the inner side of the flap is connective tissue, and epithelium placed against it "just would not heal properly."
An FGG's epithelium is meant for a graft left exposed; under a flap it would not heal.
Both grafts carry the palate's keratinization; what decides is whether the graft is covered or exposed.
The flap's inner surface is connective tissue, which is why a covered graft must be connective tissue only.

q9-L17.stem: For root coverage on #10 and #11 with a connective tissue graft, what did he do with the flap?
choices: Moved it coronally, without tension, to cover the graft
Moved it apically and left the graft exposed
Returned it to its old level with half the graft showing
Left it open to heal by secondary intention
why: Correct: a coronally advanced flap covered the graft completely, tension free so it stays in its coronal position.
That is the FGG approach for gaining keratinized gingiva, not root coverage with a CTG.
A CTG is covered completely; an exposed CTG would heal poorly.
An FGG's palatal donor site heals that way; here the recipient flap was sutured over the graft.

q9-L18.stem: A tissue bank supplies an acellular dermal matrix. What is it made of?
choices: Human dermis with the epidermis and cells taken out
Bovine collagen formed into a membrane
The patient's own palatal tissue with the epithelium removed
A synthetic polymer scaffold seeded with fibroblasts
why: Correct: processed human skin, a matrix of collagen, elastic and reticular fibers with no cells left.
Bovine and porcine products exist, but ADM is human dermis.
That describes a connective tissue graft, which is an autograft.
ADM is processed human tissue with its cells removed, not a seeded synthetic.

q9-L19.stem: Which case is the best fit for an acellular dermal matrix rather than a graft from the palate?
choices: Covering roots on six teeth in a single surgery
Creating KG on one tooth with the graft left exposed
Thickening the tissue over one central incisor
Covering the root of an RT3 incisor
why: Correct: no donor site and "unlimited" quantity make it suited to many defects in one procedure, like his canine-to-canine case.
ADM has to be covered; making KG with an exposed graft is an FGG's job.
A small site needs only a small palatal harvest; he thickened his young patient's two centrals with a CTG.
No graft gains root coverage in RT3; ADM's advantage is many teeth at once without a donor site.

q9-L20.stem: An acellular dermal matrix has to be buried completely under the flap. Why?
choices: It has no cells or blood supply of its own
If exposed, the body rejects it as foreign
Its epidermis can't heal against the flap
Saliva breaks the matrix down within days
why: Correct: it is "more or less a dead piece of skin," like a band-aid; once covered it is remodeled and replaced by the patient's tissue.
His reason was the absence of cells and blood supply, not rejection.
ADM has no epidermis; processing removes it.
His reason was that it can't heal on its own without a blood supply.

q9-L21.stem: Which feature defines a tunnel, or pouch, flap?
choices: The papillae stay attached; the sulci are joined below
Two vertical releasing incisions are made
It is moved apically so the graft is exposed
It is elevated full thickness all the way to the crest
why: Correct: it works like an envelope flap without raising the papillae, entering through each sulcus and joining them into one plane.
Two vertical releases make a trapezoidal flap, which he used for single sites.
That is the apically positioned flap of the FGG technique.
What defines it is the attached papillae, not how thick the flap is.

q9-L22.stem: To record the width of keratinized gingiva, which two points do you measure between?
choices: The gingival margin and the MGJ
The CEJ and the MGJ
The gingival margin and the sulcus base
The MGJ and the vestibular depth
why: Correct: keratinized gingiva spans from the gingival margin to the mucogingival junction.
KG begins at the gingival margin, which may sit above or below the CEJ.
Margin to sulcus base is the probing depth.
That stretch is alveolar mucosa, not keratinized gingiva.

q9-L23.stem: Holding a probe horizontally, you roll the tissue from the alveolar mucosa toward the margin. What tells you the MGJ has been reached?
choices: The tissue no longer moves with the probe
The tissue blanches under the probe tip
The probe drops into the sulcus
The tissue begins bleeding
why: Correct: loose mucosa rolls with the probe; at the MGJ the attached tissue stops rolling.
Blanching isn't the sign he described; the stop in rolling is.
The sulcus is at the gingival margin, coronal to the MGJ.
Bleeding is not how the MGJ is located.

q9-L24.stem: A patient controls plaque well and has no traumatic factors. Does attached gingiva, on its own, have to be present to maintain periodontal health and attachment?
choices: No, not as a requirement in itself
Yes, a minimum of 2 mm
Yes, a minimum of 1 mm
Only around the mandibular incisors
why: Correct: when plaque is controlled and other trauma is absent, it isn't an essential prerequisite by itself (Kennedy 1985; Scheyer 2015).
2 mm is the figure for suboptimal plaque control, not good plaque control.
No minimum is required when plaque is controlled and there's no trauma.
The finding is not specific to any tooth.

q9-L25.stem: A patient's plaque control is not ideal. What width of keratinized gingiva does the slide give to prevent attachment loss?
choices: 2 mm or more
1 mm or more
4 mm or more
None if the tissue is thick
why: Correct: the slide's figure, and his point that teeth with less than 2 mm of KG are likely prone to recession.
1 mm is the phenotype cutoff (thin is 1 mm or less), not the KG figure.
4 mm is more than the slide calls for; at least 2 mm prevents attachment loss when plaque control is suboptimal.
The 2 mm figure holds whenever plaque control is suboptimal; thick tissue resists recession but doesn't replace it.

q9-L26.stem: A site has alveolar mucosa only, no keratinized gingiva. Why won't a CTG buried under a coronally advanced flap give it keratinized gingiva?
choices: The mucosa over the graft stays nonkeratinized
A CTG only takes if it is left exposed
The flap would cut off the blood supply to the graft
CTGs succeed only on RT3 recessions
why: Correct: putting mucosa over the graft doesn't turn that mucosa into keratinized gingiva.
Backward: a CTG must be covered by the flap; a graft left exposed is an FGG.
A covered CTG lives on the bed beside and apical to the root; its blood supply isn't the issue, what covers it is.
RT3 is where root coverage fails, not where CTGs work.

q9-L28.stem: In what way does a frenum attached high on the gingiva contribute to recession?
choices: Lip movement makes it tug on the margin
It cuts off the papilla's blood supply
It thins the bone covering the root
It stops the patient brushing there
why: Correct: with the lip and every muscle movement it pulls on the margin, which helps plaque accumulate.
That isn't the mechanism he described; the pull on the margin is.
Thin bone is an anatomic variation; the frenum's problem is its pull.
He described the pull and the plaque it traps, not brushing being blocked.

q9-L29.stem: A woman shows too much gingiva when she smiles. Her facial thirds are equal, her teeth are normally proportioned, her lip moves 7 mm, and her upper lip measures 17 mm at rest. What explains the display?
choices: Her upper lip is short
Her upper lip is hypermobile
Vertical maxillary excess
Altered passive eruption
why: Correct: the slide's sign of a short lip is a length under 20 mm, and women normally measure 20-22 mm.
Hypermobility means lip mobility over 8 mm; 7 mm is inside the normal 6-8 mm.
Its sign is an increased lower facial third, and her thirds are equal.
Its sign is short clinical crowns with abnormal proportions, and her teeth are normally proportioned.

q9-L30.stem: A man with a gummy smile has equal facial thirds, normally proportioned teeth and a 23 mm upper lip, which travels 11 mm when he smiles fully. How would you treat it?
choices: Botox, or surgery to reposition the lip
Orthodontics with orthognathic surgery
Crown lengthening, then restorations
Dermal filler injected into the upper lip
why: Correct: over 8 mm of lip mobility is a hypermobile upper lip, and these options may reduce the display.
That treats vertical maxillary excess, which would show an increased lower facial third.
That treats altered passive eruption, which would show short, abnormally proportioned crowns.
Fillers can mask some display from a short upper lip; 23 mm is normal for a man, and his problem is the 11 mm of lip travel.

q9-L31.stem: The teeth look short. The gingival band is normal in width with the MGJ at the CEJ, and sounding puts the crest 2 mm from the CEJ. Which crown-lengthening approach matches?
choices: Apically positioned flap
Gingivectomy by itself
Apically positioned flap plus osseous surgery
Restorations only, no surgery
why: Correct: a normal band with the MGJ at the CEJ is Type 2, and a crest more than 1 mm away is subcategory A, so this is Type 2A.
A gingivectomy alone is only for Type 1A, which has a wide band of gingiva.
Osseous surgery is for the B types, with the crest close to the CEJ; here it is 2 mm away.
Altered passive eruption is treated with crown lengthening first.

q9-L32.stem: With altered passive eruption, what is the relationship between the clinical crown and the anatomical crown?
choices: The clinical crown is the shorter of the two
The clinical crown is the longer of the two
They are equal, but the roots are short
The anatomical crown is shorter because of wear
why: Correct: the gingiva never migrated apically and still covers part of the enamel, so the teeth look short.
A clinical crown longer than the anatomical one describes recession, with root exposed.
Root length isn't what makes the teeth look short; gingiva over the crown is.
Wear shortens the anatomical crown; APE is gingiva covering a normal-length crown.

q9-L33.stem: On an ideal maxillary gingival line, where is the lateral incisor's margin relative to the centrals and canines?
choices: Roughly 1 mm more coronal
At the same level
Roughly 1 mm more apical
Roughly 2 mm more coronal
why: Correct: on the slide's gingival line the centrals and canines are level and the laterals sit 1 mm coronal.
Only the centrals and canines are level; the laterals sit 1 mm coronal to them.
The other way around: the lateral sits coronal, toward the incisal edge.
2 mm is too far; the slide puts the lateral about 1 mm coronal to the central-canine line.

q9-L34.stem: The cause of a gummy smile is vertical maxillary excess. What treatment does the slide list?
choices: Orthodontics with orthognathic surgery
Botox or lip repositioning surgery
Crown lengthening and then restorations
Nothing, as there are no good options
why: Correct: it is a skeletal cause, so orthodontics and orthognathic surgery, and the slide adds that periodontics may be needed to correct the display.
These treat a hypermobile upper lip.
These treat altered passive eruption.
That is the slide's verdict on a short upper lip.

q9-L35.stem: Patient 1 is 28. Her facial thirds are equal and her upper lip has normal length and mobility, but at full smile her lip line is high, her anterior gingival margins are flat and uneven, and her centrals are short and square. What is causing the gummy smile?
choices: Clinical crowns that are short
A maxilla that is too long vertically
An upper lip that moves too much
An upper lip that is too short
why: Correct: with normal thirds and a normal lip, the display comes from teeth and gingiva; square centrals and an uneven gingival line mean short clinical crowns, and the plan was crown lengthening followed by veneers.
Vertical maxillary excess shows an increased lower facial third, and her thirds are equal.
Her lip mobility is normal, so it isn't hypermobile.
Her lip length is normal, so it isn't short.

q9-L36.stem: A thick graft taken from the palate comes with its fatty layer. Why is that layer usually trimmed away?
choices: It would slow down healing
It lets the graft keep its epithelium
It helps the graft fit a tunnel
It protects the greater palatine artery
why: Correct: a thick graft brings much of the adipose layer with it, and it is removed so it doesn't slow healing.
The epithelium is the outer layer; the fat is on the deep side.
His reason was healing, not fit.
Avoiding the artery depends on where and how deep you harvest, not on trimming the graft.

q9-E01.stem: Before crown lengthening, a radiograph is used to assess each of these EXCEPT:
choices: How wide the keratinized gingiva is
How far apically a fracture or caries extends
The length and form of the roots
Where the alveolar crest sits
why: Correct: KG width is a clinical parameter, measured with a probe from the MGJ to the gingival margin; a radiograph can't show it.
Radiographic: the slides list the apical extent of any fracture or caries.
Radiographic: roots already shortened by resorption or orthodontics limit how far a tooth can be lengthened.
Radiographic: the crest's level, although sounding to bone shows exactly where it is relative to the CEJ.

q9-E02.stem: The slide lists reasons to treat gingival recession. Each of these is one EXCEPT:
choices: The tooth has become more mobile
The exposed dentin is hypersensitive
Caries has started on the root surface
Plaque is harder to remove mechanically
why: Correct: not on the list; recession exposes the root but doesn't loosen the tooth.
On the list: exposed dentin is sensitive to cold and air.
On the list: exposed roots raise the caries risk.
On the list: recession interferes with adequate plaque control.

q9-M01.stem: A patient's medication list is being reviewed. Which of these drugs does the slide name as causes of gingival enlargement? Select all that apply.
choices: Phenytoin
A calcium channel blocker
Cyclosporine
Metformin
Amoxicillin
why: Correct: an anticonvulsant and the most documented cause.
Correct: common blood pressure drugs, and the class seen most often in everyday practice.
Correct: an immunosuppressant, the third class.
Not one of them: a diabetes drug, outside the three classes (anticonvulsants, calcium channel blockers, immunosuppressants).
Not one of them: an antibiotic, outside the three classes that cause gingival enlargement.

q9-M02.stem: Compared with harvesting tissue from the patient's palate, what does an acellular dermal matrix offer? Select all that apply.
choices: The patient has no second surgical wound
Patients accept it more readily
Several defects can be grafted in a single visit
It stays put without any sutures
It carries keratinization of its own
why: Belongs: nothing is harvested from the roof of the mouth, so there is no donor site.
Belongs: patients accept it more easily because the palate is left alone.
Belongs: it isn't limited by how much tissue the palate can give.
Doesn't belong: in his canine-to-canine case, sling sutures held the ADM under the tunnel.
Doesn't belong: keratinization comes with palatal tissue, which is why an FGG can create KG; the ADM has no cells.

q9-S01.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. A free gingival graft consists of palatal connective tissue with the epithelium removed.
2. When a coronally advanced flap will cover the graft entirely, the graft of choice is an FGG.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: an FGG keeps its epithelium along with the lamina propria beneath it; connective tissue alone is a CTG. Statement 2 is false, not true: a fully covered graft has to be connective tissue only, since epithelium facing the inside of the flap won't heal.

Statement 1 is false: an FGG keeps its epithelium along with the lamina propria beneath it; connective tissue alone is a CTG. Statement 2 is false: a fully covered graft has to be connective tissue only, since epithelium facing the inside of the flap won't heal.
Statement 1 is false, not true: an FGG keeps its epithelium along with the lamina propria beneath it; connective tissue alone is a CTG.
Statement 2 is false, not true: a fully covered graft has to be connective tissue only, since epithelium facing the inside of the flap won't heal.

q9-S02.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. An RT2 recession is defined by interproximal attachment loss that exceeds the buccal attachment loss.
2. Grafting an RT3 recession can be expected to cover about 50 to 60% of the exposed root.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: in RT2 the interproximal loss is equal to or less than the buccal loss; more than the buccal is RT3. Statement 2 is false, not true: in RT3 a graft "would not end up achieving that root coverage at all"; the 50 to 60% figure he gave was for RT2.

Statement 1 is false: in RT2 the interproximal loss is equal to or less than the buccal loss; more than the buccal is RT3. Statement 2 is false: in RT3 a graft "would not end up achieving that root coverage at all"; the 50 to 60% figure he gave was for RT2.
Statement 1 is false, not true: in RT2 the interproximal loss is equal to or less than the buccal loss; more than the buccal is RT3.
Statement 2 is false, not true: in RT3 a graft "would not end up achieving that root coverage at all"; the 50 to 60% figure he gave was for RT2.

q9-S03.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. When plaque is under control and nothing traumatic is acting on the tissue, periodontal health does not depend on having a zone of attached gingiva.
2. When plaque control is suboptimal, a tooth needs 2 mm or more of keratinized gingiva to avoid losing attachment.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is true: it is the first half of the finding on the slide (Kennedy 1985; Scheyer 2015). Statement 2 is true: it is the second half: with suboptimal plaque control, at least 2 mm of KG is needed.

Statement 1 is true, not false: it is the first half of the finding on the slide (Kennedy 1985; Scheyer 2015). Statement 2 is true, not false: it is the second half: with suboptimal plaque control, at least 2 mm of KG is needed.
Statement 2 is true, not false: it is the second half of the slide's finding: with suboptimal plaque control, at least 2 mm of KG is needed.
Statement 1 is true, not false: it is the first half of the finding on the slide (Kennedy 1985; Scheyer 2015).

q9-T01.stem: True or false: If you can see the outline of the probe through the gingiva, the phenotype is thin (1 mm or less).
choices: True
False
why: True: that is the validated visibility test he described; seeing the probe means the tissue is 1 mm or less.
It is true: if the tissue hid the probe, that would mean a thick phenotype, over 1 mm.

q9-T02.stem: True or false: When the palatal vault is shallow, the CEJ-to-greater-palatine-bundle distance is roughly 17 mm.
choices: True
False
why: 17 mm belongs to a high palate; with a shallow palate the bundle is only about 7 mm from the CEJ.
It is false: a shallow palate puts the bundle about 7 mm away; 17 mm is the high palate's figure.

q9-T03.stem: True or false: Gingival recession that is not treated is likely to keep getting worse.
choices: True
False
why: True: the systematic review found that untreated recession progresses.
It is true: the review found progression, so simply watching it won't keep it where it is.

q9-T04.stem: True or false: The thin phenotype is the actual cause of recession, while inflammation only adds to the risk as a predisposing factor.
choices: True
False
why: The roles are reversed: inflammation is the cause of recession, and the thin phenotype is one of the factors that predispose to it.
It is false: "the key word here is inflammation," whether from brushing trauma or plaque; a thin phenotype only predisposes.

q9-T05.stem: True or false: Once a free gingival graft has been harvested, the wound on the palate heals by secondary intention.
choices: True
False
why: True: harvesting leaves the palate as an open wound that fills in by secondary intention.
It is true: the palatal wound isn't closed over, so it heals by secondary intention.

q9-T06.stem: True or false: For Type 2A altered passive eruption, the treatment is a gingivectomy by itself.
choices: True
False
why: A gingivectomy alone is reserved for Type 1A; Type 2A is treated with an apically positioned flap.
It is false: in Type 2A the band is just of normal width, so it is shifted with an apically positioned flap instead of trimmed.

q9-T07.stem: True or false: Of the forms of altered passive eruption, Types 1A and 1B are the ones seen most often.
choices: True
False
why: True: the slide names 1A and 1B, the forms with a wide band of gingiva, as the most frequently encountered.
It is true: 1A and 1B are the forms the slide names as most frequent.

q9-T08.stem: True or false: In a full smile, an upper lip with normal mobility moves up roughly 10-12 mm.
choices: True
False
why: 10-12 mm is hypermobile; a normal lip moves 6-8 mm.
It is false: normal mobility is 6-8 mm, and anything over 8 mm is a hypermobile lip.

q9-T09.stem: True or false: Normally, the gingival margin of a maxillary lateral incisor lies about 1 mm more apical than the margins of the central incisor and canine.
choices: True
False
why: The lateral's margin sits 1 mm coronal, toward the incisal edge, rather than apical.
It is false: the lateral sits 1 mm coronal to the line joining the central and canine margins.

q9-T10.stem: True or false: With a tunnel flap, the roots of several teeth can be reached while the papillae stay attached.
choices: True
False
why: True: leaving the papillae attached is what makes it a tunnel.
It is true: the papillae are not elevated; the sulci are joined beneath the tissue.

q9-N01.stem:
Dr. Abou-Arraj's slide lists predisposing factors for gingival recession. Which of these are on it?
1. Gingiva of the thin phenotype
2. Chewing or dipping smokeless tobacco
3. A broad zone of keratinized gingiva
4. A frenum or muscle that attaches high or aberrantly
choices: 1, 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
2 and 4 only
why: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are true. Statement 3 is false: a lack of keratinized gingiva is what predisposes; a broad zone resists recession.

It includes 3, which is false: a lack of keratinized gingiva is what predisposes; a broad zone resists recession. It leaves out 2, which is true: smokeless tobacco can produce severe localized recession.
It includes 3, which is false: a lack of keratinized gingiva is what predisposes; a broad zone resists recession. It leaves out 1, which is true: thin tissue is prone to recession.
It leaves out 1, which is true: thin tissue is prone to recession.

q9-N02.stem:
An acellular dermal matrix allograft is being considered. Which statements about it are true?
1. It is donated human dermis that has been processed so no cells remain
2. Living fibroblasts from the donor come with it and aid healing
3. The patient's own tissue gradually replaces it
4. The flap should cover it fully
choices: 1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
3 and 4 only
why: It includes 2, which is false: the matrix is acellular, "more or less a dead piece of skin" with nothing to contribute. It leaves out 4, which is true: without a blood supply it heals poorly, so it is covered completely.
Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 2 is false: the matrix is acellular, "more or less a dead piece of skin" with nothing to contribute.

It includes 2, which is false: the matrix is acellular, "more or less a dead piece of skin" with nothing to contribute. It leaves out 1, which is true: it is donated dermis with the epidermis and cells taken out.
It leaves out 1, which is true: it is donated dermis with the epidermis and cells taken out.

q9-N03.stem:
Consider altered passive eruption. Which statements are true?
1. Type 1 places the MGJ at the CEJ
2. Subcategory A has over 1 mm between the CEJ and the osseous crest
3. A gingivectomy by itself treats Type 1A
4. An apically positioned flap by itself treats Type 2B
choices: 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4
2 and 4 only
3 and 4 only
why: Statements 2 and 3 are true. Statement 1 is false: in Type 1 the MGJ is apical to the alveolar crest; an MGJ at the CEJ is Type 2. Statement 4 is false: in 2B the crest is close to the CEJ, so the flap needs osseous surgery too.
It includes 4, which is false: in 2B the crest is close to the CEJ, so the flap needs osseous surgery too.
It includes 4, which is false: in 2B the crest is close to the CEJ, so the flap needs osseous surgery too. It leaves out 3, which is true: Type 1A is the only one treated with a gingivectomy alone.
It includes 4, which is false: in 2B the crest is close to the CEJ, so the flap needs osseous surgery too. It leaves out 2, which is true: subcategory A has more than 1 mm from the CEJ to the crest.

q9-N04.stem:
A patient has a gummy smile. Which findings are matched with the right cause?
1. A lower facial third that is increased: vertical maxillary excess
2. An upper lip shorter than 20 mm: a short upper lip
3. The lip moving more than 8 mm: a hypermobile upper lip
4. Teeth of abnormal proportions with an asymmetric gingival line: vertical maxillary excess
choices: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3
1, 2 and 4
2, 3 and 4
why: It leaves out 3, which is true: more than 8 mm is the slide's sign of a hypermobile upper lip; 6-8 mm is normal.

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are true. Statement 4 is false: abnormal proportions with an asymmetric gingival line point to short clinical crowns, usually altered passive eruption; vertical maxillary excess shows as an increased lower facial third with normal teeth.

It includes 4, which is false: abnormal proportions with an asymmetric gingival line point to short clinical crowns, usually altered passive eruption; vertical maxillary excess shows as an increased lower facial third with normal teeth. It leaves out 3, which is true: more than 8 mm is the slide's sign of a hypermobile upper lip; 6-8 mm is normal.

It includes 4, which is false: abnormal proportions with an asymmetric gingival line point to short clinical crowns, usually altered passive eruption; vertical maxillary excess shows as an increased lower facial third with normal teeth. It leaves out 1, which is true: an increased lower facial third is the slide's sign of vertical maxillary excess.

q9-L37.stem: Three drug classes can enlarge the gingiva. In a typical general practice, which one are your patients most likely to be taking?
choices: Calcium channel blockers
Phenytoin and other anticonvulsants
Cyclosporine and other immunosuppressants
Bisphosphonates
why: These are common blood pressure drugs, so this is the class you'll see most, even though phenytoin is better documented.
Phenytoin is the best-documented cause, but far fewer patients take it than take blood pressure medicine.
Cyclosporine can cause it, but transplant patients are a small group.
Bisphosphonates belong to host modulation (and BRONJ); they are not a cause of gingival enlargement.

q9-L38.stem: A patient's drug-induced gingival enlargement persists even after good hygiene and scaling. What explains this?
choices: The enlarged tissue is fibrotic
The swelling is edema that resolves on its own
Plaque has no role in this condition
The overgrowth is located in the bone
why: The drug leads to extra collagen fibers being laid down, so the tissue has to be cut away with a gingivectomy.
Edematous tissue is the pseudopocket of gingivitis, which does respond to hygiene and scaling.
Plaque-induced gingivitis is always the primary factor; the drug only modifies it.
The overgrowth is gingival tissue, which is why a gingivectomy can remove it.

q9-L39.stem: Two patients both have altered passive eruption. Which finding would place one of them in subcategory B instead of A?
choices: Bone crest within 1 mm of the CEJ
A band of gingiva wider than normal
An MGJ level with the CEJ
Bone crest 1.5 to 2 mm from the CEJ
why: In B the crest is at the CEJ or within about 1 mm of it, leaving no room above it for the attachment.
The band's width sets the type (1 or 2), not the subcategory.
An MGJ at the CEJ is a sign of Type 2, the normal band.
1.5 to 2 mm is the normal distance, which is subcategory A.

q9-L40.stem: A patient with Type 1B altered passive eruption is treated with a gingivectomy and nothing else. Why won't the result last?
choices: The gingiva regrows over the crown
Too little gingiva is present to trim
Bone is lost after the gingivectomy
Every bit of keratinized gingiva is lost
why: The bone sits at or near the CEJ, leaving the supracrestal attachment no room, so the margin creeps back.
Type 1 has a wide band; it's Type 2 that can't spare any gingiva.
The bone stays where it is, at or near the CEJ, and that is the problem: the attachment has no room, so the tissue regrows.
Type 1's band is wider than normal, so trimming leaves enough; in 1B the issue is the bone.

q9-L41.stem: A patient has Type 2A altered passive eruption. What rules out a gingivectomy and calls for an apically positioned flap?
choices: Gingival band of only normal width
Bone sitting at the CEJ
A gingivectomy wound that will not heal
MGJ apical to the alveolar crest
why: Cutting it back would leave too little keratinized gingiva, so the flap shifts the whole band apically instead.
Bone at the CEJ describes a B subcategory, which needs osseous surgery as well.
A gingivectomy heals well; it is the band's width that rules it out in this case.
An MGJ apical to the crest is Type 1, the wide band, where a gingivectomy can work (in 1A).

q9-L42.stem: You are doing esthetic crown lengthening on a tooth whose crest sits at the CEJ, and you remove 2 mm of soft tissue. How much bone should you remove with it?
choices: 2 mm
None
1 mm
4 mm
why: Match the soft tissue, so the soft and hard tissue keep their relationship, just more apically.
With the crest at the CEJ, leaving the bone alone means the tissue grows back.
Removing only half leaves the attachment too little room, so the margin creeps back.
Taking twice what's needed removes supporting bone and attachment for no benefit.

q9-L43.stem: Esthetic crown lengthening is done. When can the final restorations be placed?
choices: At six months
At one week
At three weeks
At eighteen months
why: That gives the tissues time to settle, the attachment time to reach its final position and the bone time to remodel.
One week is suture removal.
Three weeks is the earliest point for provisionals, not the definitive restorations.
The 18-month photos show his patient's finals, but they were placed at six months.

q9-L44.stem: A patient with an ideal, medium smile line smiles fully. How much gingiva is visible?
choices: Up to 2 to 3 mm
No gingiva at all
Between 4 and 6 mm
6-8 mm, matching lip mobility
why: Showing up to 2-3 mm of gingiva is the medium smile line, the ideal.
Showing no gingiva in a full smile is a low smile line.
Showing more than 3 mm is a high smile line, a gummy smile.
6-8 mm is the upper lip's normal range of movement, not the gingiva on show.

q9-L45.stem: How wide should a maxillary central incisor be, as a share of its length?
choices: Roughly 75-80% of its length
Roughly half its length
Roughly 90-100% of its length
Roughly 62% of its length
why: A central 10 mm long should be no wider than about 8 mm; 70-75% is acceptable.
Half as wide as long is the shape of a mandibular incisor.
Almost as wide as long is a square tooth, which looks short.
0.618 is the golden proportion, which relates neighboring teeth seen from the front, not a single tooth's width and length.

q9-L46.stem: On a maxillary anterior tooth, where is the highest point of the gingival margin, the gingival zenith, located?
choices: A little distal to the tooth's midline
Right on the tooth's midline
A little mesial to the tooth's midline
On the mesial line angle
why: The height of contour sits just distal to the center, the canine included.
The canine's zenith can look centered from the front, but only because the canine sits at the corner of the arch.
The zenith sits distal to the midline, not mesial.
The zenith lies near the middle of the tooth, just distal to it, not at a line angle.

q9-L47.stem: A patient has a gray metal tattoo in the gingiva. What is its most common source?
choices: Amalgam from an apicoectomy
A calcium channel blocker
Long-standing gingivitis
Blood pigment after a graft
why: Apical surgery once retrofilled the canal with amalgam, which can leak into the tissue and stain it.
Calcium channel blockers cause gingival enlargement, not discoloration.
Inflammation makes the tissue red; it doesn't leave a gray stain.
A bruise after surgery fades; a tattoo is metal left behind in the tissue.

q9-L48.stem: In his amalgam tattoo case, what was the free gingival graft meant to do?
choices: Replace the stained tissue
Cover exposed root surfaces
Widen the keratinized gingiva
Make the vestibule deeper
why: The discolored tissue is removed and replaced with graft tissue that has no stain.
A bridge had replaced the teeth, so there were no roots to cover.
Widening the band is the usual reason for an FGG, but not in this case.
Deepening the vestibule was part of his lower incisor case, not this one.

q9-L49.stem: A tooth has receded farther than the teeth beside it. What is the most root coverage a graft can be expected to reach?
choices: Whichever neighbor's margin is more apical
Whichever neighbor's margin is more coronal
The CEJ, as long as a CTG is used
The tips of the two papillae
why: His ceiling: the adjacent teeth's gingival margin, "and likely the more apical one," whatever graft is used.
He put the ceiling at the more apical of the two neighbors' margins, not the more coronal.
Coverage to the CEJ needs intact interproximal support; the neighbors' margins set the ceiling whatever graft is chosen.
The graft lives on bone and attachment that sit well apical to the papilla tips, so coverage stops short of them.

q9-L50.stem: A tooth with 3 mm of recession and 2 mm of keratinized gingiva gets a CTG under a coronally advanced flap. Once healed, how much keratinized gingiva will it have?
choices: Roughly the same 2 mm
Roughly 5 mm
No keratinized gingiva
Roughly 4 mm, from graft epithelium
why: The graft lies under the flap and doesn't change the surface; the root is covered and the tissue is thicker.
The 3 mm of recession is covered, but by the advanced flap, not by new keratinized gingiva.
The flap keeps its own keratinized band, so nothing is lost.
A CTG has no epithelium; only an FGG left exposed creates new keratinized gingiva.

q9-L51.stem: You're planning esthetic crown lengthening and need to know how far the bone crest is from the CEJ. How do you find out?
choices: Anesthetize and sound to bone
Look at the probing depth
Do the rolling test at the MGJ
Take a CBCT of every case
why: Probing through the attachment down to bone locates the crest, which decides whether bone has to be removed.
The probe stops at the attachment when measuring probing depth; the bone lies beyond it.
The rolling test locates the MGJ and the band of gingiva (the type), not the bone.
A CBCT would show the bone, but it isn't routinely taken for this kind of crown lengthening.

q9-L52.stem: Lip repositioning surgery is offered for a hypermobile upper lip. What is its biggest weakness?
choices: Close to half of cases relapse
It must be redone about every six months
It leaves root surfaces exposed
It permanently shortens the lip
why: Results look great at first, but nearly 50% relapse; pairing it with Botox does better.
Repeating every six months is the drawback of Botox.
The surgery works on the lip, not the gingival margin.
It ties the lip down closer to the MGJ; relapse is the real problem.

q9-T11.stem: True or false: A gingivectomy without any other procedure gives lasting results in Type 1B altered passive eruption.
choices: True
False
why: The result isn't stable: with bone so close to the CEJ, the attachment has no room, and the tissue regrows.
It is false: in 1B the tissue grows back after a gingivectomy alone, so it needs a flap with osseous surgery.

q9-T12.stem: True or false: When Botox is used for a hypermobile upper lip, it needs to be given again roughly every six months.
choices: True
False
why: True: Botox wears off, so it is repeated about every six months.
It wears off, and the need to repeat it every six months is its drawback.

q9-T14.stem: True or false: His rule in crown lengthening is to always keep at least 2 mm, and ideally 3 mm, of keratinized gingiva.
choices: True
False
why: True: that minimum is the reason a band of normal width isn't trimmed.
It is his rule: not cutting a normal band below 2 mm is why Type 2 gets an apically positioned flap.

q9-S06.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Treating Type 1A altered passive eruption requires a flap along with osseous surgery.
2. Once esthetic crown lengthening is done, roughly six months should pass before the definitive restorations.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: in 1A the bone is at a normal distance, so a gingivectomy by itself works and leaves room for the supracrestal attachment.
Statement 2 is true, not false: the tissues, the attachment and the bone need about six months to settle; provisionals are possible from three weeks.

Statement 1 is false, not true: in 1A the bone is at a normal distance, so a gingivectomy by itself works and leaves room for the supracrestal attachment. Statement 2 is true, not false: the tissues, the attachment and the bone need about six months to settle; provisionals are possible from three weeks.

Statement 1 is false: in 1A the bone is at a normal distance, so a gingivectomy by itself works and leaves room for the supracrestal attachment. Statement 2 is true: the tissues, the attachment and the bone need about six months to settle; provisionals are possible from three weeks.

q9-S07.stem:
Read the two statements.
1. On a given tooth, a connective tissue graft under a coronally advanced flap covers more root than a free gingival graft would.
2. An FGG cannot cover any of an exposed root.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: an FGG can cover part of a root (his lower incisor case), only less than a CTG on the same tooth.
Statement 1 is true, not false: a CTG under a coronally advanced flap is the gold standard for root coverage.

Statement 1 is true: a CTG under a coronally advanced flap is the gold standard for root coverage. Statement 2 is false: an FGG can cover part of a root (his lower incisor case), only less than a CTG on the same tooth.

Statement 1 is true, not false: a CTG under a coronally advanced flap is the gold standard for root coverage. Statement 2 is false, not true: an FGG can cover part of a root (his lower incisor case), only less than a CTG on the same tooth.

q9-N05.stem:
A patient has gingival enlargement caused by a medication. Which statements are true?
1. Plaque-induced gingivitis is the primary factor in every case
2. Of the causative classes, calcium channel blockers are the one seen most in practice
3. Phenytoin, the best-documented cause, belongs to the immunosuppressants
4. Part of treatment may be asking the physician whether the drug can be changed
choices: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
why: It leaves out 4, which is true: even with everyone's best efforts, the drug may need to be switched.
Statements 1, 2 and 4 are true. Statement 3 is false: phenytoin is an anticonvulsant; the immunosuppressant is cyclosporine.
It includes 3, which is false: phenytoin is an anticonvulsant; the immunosuppressant is cyclosporine. It leaves out 2, which is true: they are common blood pressure drugs.
