It includes 3, which is false: phenytoin is an anticonvulsant; the immunosuppressant is cyclosporine. It leaves out 1, which is true: the drug modifies a gingival disease that plaque starts.

pc-a1.stem: Using the chart, work out how much attachment has been lost at #30 mesiofacial.
choices: 7 mm
6 mm
5 mm
1 mm
why: The pocket there is 6 mm and the margin sits 1 mm apical to the CEJ (1 mm of recession), so CAL is 6 + 1 = 7 mm.
That is only the probing depth, measured from the margin; attachment is measured from the CEJ, so the recession must be added.
This subtracts the recession (6 - 1); with the margin apical to the CEJ the recession is positive and gets added.
That is only the recession, CEJ to margin; the pocket below the margin still has to be counted.

pc-a2.stem: Putting together his chart, films and history, how should this man's periodontitis be stated?
choices: Localized Stage 3 Grade B periodontitis
Localized Stage 2 Grade B periodontitis
Generalized Stage 3 Grade B periodontitis
Localized Stage 3 Grade C periodontitis
why: His worst site (#30 mesial) has 7 mm of interdental CAL and bone loss into the middle third, Stage 3 by severity (the 6 mm pocket, a complexity factor, agrees); no tooth lost and no complex rehabilitation, so not Stage 4. 40% / 44 years is about 0.9, between 0.25 and 1.0, with no smoking or HbA1c to raise it: Grade B. Four of 28 teeth (14%): localized.
Stage 2 tops out at 3-4 mm of interdental CAL with coronal-third bone loss; #30 mesial has 7 mm of CAL and 40% bone loss, which is the middle third.
Generalized would need 30% or more of the teeth; only #30, #31, #3 and #14 are involved, 4 of 28.
Grade C would need a ratio over 1.0 or a modifier (10 or more cigarettes a day, HbA1c of 7% or more); his ratio is about 0.9 and he has neither.

pc-b1.stem: Based on her chart, films and history, which diagnosis fits this patient?
choices: Gingivitis on an intact periodontium
Generalized Stage 1 Grade A periodontitis
Generalized Stage 2 Grade B periodontitis
Clinical health on an intact periodontium
why: Her pockets reach 4-5 mm and 46% of sites bleed, but the CEJ is 3-5 mm under the margin, so CAL is 0 everywhere, and the crest sits where it should on the films. The depth is swollen gingiva (pseudopockets), not lost attachment.
Any stage requires attachment loss or bone loss; she has neither, so there is nothing to stage.

Stage 2 would need 3-4 mm of interdental CAL and coronal-third bone loss; this is Dr. Abou-Arraj's warning exactly: staging from a mouthful of 4s and 5s over-diagnoses a patient without periodontitis.
Health allows no bleeding and no depth beyond 3 mm; 46% of her sites bleed, far over the 10% threshold for gingivitis.

pc-b2.stem: Based on her findings, which procedure is appropriate?
choices: Scaling in the presence of gingival inflammation (D4346)
Scaling and root planing in each of the four quadrants
A routine adult prophylaxis, finished with polishing
Full-mouth debridement (D4355), with charting at a later visit
why: She has never had periodontitis and has no bone loss, but heavy, generalized inflammation from local factors: the code between a prophy and SRP, done with perio faculty and followed by a Phase I evaluation.
SRP is therapy for periodontitis, planing roots exposed by attachment loss. She has no attachment loss and no exposed roots.
A prophy is preventive care for health or gingivitis; for inflammation as heavy and widespread as hers, a simple prophy undersells the work.
Debridement is only for calculus so heavy the margin can't be found and nothing can be charted, and she has been charted.

q4-F01.stem: Subgingival calculus sits on the mesial root of #19 and you need to root plane it. Which instruments are made for this surface? Select all that apply.
choices: Gracey 11/12
Gracey 15/16
S204SD9 posterior sickle
H6/7 anterior sickle
why: Yes: the Gracey 11/12 is the area-specific curette for mesial surfaces of posterior teeth (and molar buccal/lingual surfaces).
Yes: the Gracey 15/16 is the alternative Gracey for mesial surfaces of posterior teeth.
No: the S204SD9 works on posterior interproximal surfaces, but above the gum; a sickle reaches only a short way below the margin (1-2 mm in the deck), and its use on exposed cementum is restricted.
No: the H6/7 sickle is for supragingival work on anterior teeth and molar buccal/lingual surfaces.

q4-F02.stem: While you scale the upper right molars, your ring finger rests on the lower right premolars. What type of finger rest are you using?
choices: Opposite-arch
Cross-arch
Conventional
Finger-on-finger
why: Correct: the rest is on the arch opposite the one you're working on, the mandible while you work on the maxilla.
A cross-arch rest would be on the other side of the same arch, here the maxillary left teeth.
A conventional rest would be on the teeth right next to the working area, the neighboring maxillary teeth.
A finger-on-finger rest is on the non-working hand's index finger or thumb, not on a tooth.

q4-F03.stem: Select every true statement about the Glickman furcation classes.
choices: Class II offers the best chance at regeneration
Class III is the toughest to treat because nothing is left to contain a graft
The patient can clean a Class IV with interdental aids or a water flosser
A Class I generally calls for regenerative surgery
Caries poses little risk to a Class IV's exposed root trunk
why: True: a Class II has depth and a bony wall on the other side (containability), making it the class most amenable to regeneration.
True: a Class III goes through-and-through; without containability it has lost its regenerative potential and is the hardest to treat.
True: with the soft tissue gone, the patient can clean the through-and-through furcation with interdental aids or a water flosser.
False: a Class I is only a catch and usually needs no treatment; it is easy to maintain if attachment loss and probing depth don't increase.
False: the exposed root trunk is at risk for sensitivity and root caries, and caries in the furcation makes the tooth hopeless.

q4-F04.stem: On a side with no molars, a mandibular first premolar probes 5 mm, has grade 2 mobility and is fremitus-positive; the patient also clenches at night. If you do SRP and nothing else, what outcome should you expect?
choices: The pocket may improve, but mobility persists until the occlusion is dealt with
Both will resolve, since the mobility is caused by the inflammation in the pocket
Neither will get better, since SRP can't be performed on a tooth with grade 2 mobility
The tooth needs extraction first, since grade 2 mobility means it is depressible
why: SRP treats the pocket, but mobility from occlusal trauma on a reduced periodontium (no posterior support, clenching) remains until the occlusion is addressed.
Here the mobility comes from occlusal load, not just the pocket, so treating a 5 mm pocket won't resolve grade 2 mobility by itself.
Mobility doesn't keep SRP from working on the pocket; it's the mobility that won't respond without fixing the occlusion.
A depressible tooth is Miller Class 3 and ready for extraction; grade 2 is more than 1 mm but under 2 mm, with no vertical displacement.

q4-F05.stem: How should the clinic's piezoelectric ultrasonic fit into your SRP sequence?
choices: Ultrasonic for gross deposits, hand instruments to plane, ultrasonic to lavage
Ultrasonic only, since it both removes subgingival deposits and leaves a planed root
Hand instruments only, since piezo tips aren't meant to go below the gingival margin
Hand instruments for the gross deposits, then the ultrasonic to give a planed root
why: The ultrasonic takes off gross deposits, hand instruments do the root planing it can't do, and a final ultrasonic pass flushes the pocket with its irrigation.
The piezo works subgingivally but can't root plane, so used alone it won't leave a smooth root.
Piezoelectric tips can be used subgingivally; leaving them out loses both the gross removal and the final lavage.
Root planing is the one thing the ultrasonic can't do, so it can't be the planing step.

q4-F06.stem: During perio instrumentation, which jobs does the mouth mirror do? Select all that apply.
choices: Lets you see surfaces indirectly
Lights up the working area
Holds back the cheek, lips or tongue
Measures the probing depth
Detects root roughness
why: Yes: the mirror provides indirect vision of surfaces you can't view directly.
Yes: the mirror reflects light onto the working area (illumination).
Yes: the mirror retracts the cheek, lips or tongue to open up the working area.
No: probing depth is read with the periodontal probe (the UNC-15), not the mirror.
No: root roughness is felt with an explorer such as the ODU 11/12, not seen in a mirror.

pc-c1.stem: Using the chart for #24, which recession type should be recorded?
choices: RT2
RT1
RT3
None until a radiograph is read
why: #24 has lost attachment interproximally (2 mm of CAL mesial and distal: 2 mm pockets with the margin at the CEJ), but less than on the buccal, where CAL is 6 mm (2 mm pocket plus 4 mm of recession). Interproximal loss that doesn't exceed buccal loss is RT2.
RT1 means no interproximal attachment loss; #24 shows 2 mm of CAL at both its mesial and distal. #25 and #26 are the RT1 teeth.
RT3 means more interproximal loss than buccal loss; at #24 the interproximal CAL (2 mm) is far below the buccal (6 mm). #23 is the RT3 tooth.
Recession type is read from the chart, interproximal CAL against buccal CAL; the radiograph confirms it but isn't needed.

pc-c2.stem: If root coverage surgery were done, which of these teeth could be expected to end up fully covered?
choices: None of them, given the thin tissue
why: #25 has 3 mm of facial recession with no interproximal attachment loss (mesial and distal CAL 0): RT1, so full coverage is predictable.
#24 is RT2: its 2 mm of interproximal attachment loss limits how far the tissue can come back, so only partial coverage is expected.
#23 is RT3: 5 mm of interproximal loss against 3 mm facially. Coverage isn't attempted because it won't succeed.
In this lecture it is the recession type, not tissue thickness, that predicts coverage, and an RT1 site predicts full coverage.

pc-d1.stem: Based on the Nabers probe findings, how would you classify #19's buccal furcation in Glickman's system?
choices: Class II
Class I
Class III
Class IV
why: The probe goes about 4 mm into the furcation but meets bone and never reaches the lingual: horizontal loss with a bony wall left, Class II.
Class I is incipient: the probe only catches the entrance and the interradicular bone is intact. Here it goes 4 mm in.
Class III would let the probe pass between the roots to the other side, but from the lingual it doesn't even enter.
Class IV is through-and-through and visible because of recession, and she has neither.

pc-d2.stem: From her chart, Nabers probe findings, films and history, what is the correct periodontal diagnosis?
choices: Localized Stage 3 Grade C periodontitis
Localized Stage 2 Grade B periodontitis
Localized Stage 2 Grade C periodontitis
Localized Stage 3 Grade B periodontitis
why: Severity alone (worst interdental CAL 4 mm, 30% bone loss) would be Stage 2, but a Class II furcation is one of the three findings that send a case straight to Stage 3 or 4; with no tooth lost and no complex rehabilitation, it is Stage 3. The ratio (30 / 50 = 0.6) says B, but 15 cigarettes a day raises it to C. Five of 28 teeth: localized.
Her CAL and bone loss match Stage 2, but the Class II furcation forces Stage 3, and smoking 15 a day forces Grade C.
The grade is correct (smoking), but a Class II or III furcation forces Stage 3 or 4 no matter what the CAL is.
The stage is correct, but grading doesn't end at the ratio: 10 or more cigarettes a day moves it to C regardless.

pc-d3.stem: The Class II furcation options are furcation plasty, regeneration, root resection and extraction. For this patient, which one fits worst?
choices: Regenerating it under a membrane
Reshaping it with furcation plasty
Resecting or hemisecting a root
Extracting, then an implant later
why: The site is ideal (a mandibular buccal Class II), but she smokes, and smokers are not candidates for regeneration, any more than uncontrolled diabetics, the immunocompromised or patients with poor compliance or hygiene.
Making the entrance shallower and cleanable is a Class II option, and smoking doesn't remove it from the list.
Resective options are listed for Class II and III; they commit the tooth to endodontics and a restoration, but smoking doesn't rule them out.
Extraction is the choice when too much is against the tooth; it isn't the worst fit, though her smoking would count against an implant too.

q5-F01.stem: In a stable mouth that probes 2-3 mm everywhere, #19, a crowned molar with a root canal, has a single 7 mm site. Which of these could account for it? Select all that apply.
choices: Crown cement left behind
A root fractured vertically
A crown margin that overhangs
Diabetes that isn't controlled
A pack-a-day smoking habit
why: Fits: cement left under the gingiva is a plaque trap on that one tooth, one of the local causes he named.
Fits: a vertical fracture on a root-canal-treated molar gives one deep site, and it means the tooth comes out.
Fits: an overhang holds plaque and drives inflammation, bone loss and attachment loss on that tooth.
Doesn't fit: diabetes is systemic and would show at many sites, not one.
Doesn't fit: smoking acts on the whole mouth; a single deep site points to something on that tooth.

q5-F02.stem: Whether he was talking about Phase I or surgery, Dr. Litz kept coming back to the same therapeutic goal for nearly every patient. Which goal was it?
choices: A mouth the patient is able to keep clean daily
Positive bony architecture at every site
Growing back all the lost bone and attachment
Clearing every bacterium from the pockets
why: His repeated point: we clean their teeth two to four times a year and they clean them 700 to 800 times, so the goal is a mouth they can keep clean.
Positive architecture is what osseous surgery aims for, and he accepts flat when getting there would cost too much bone.
Regeneration suits selected defects and patients; most therapy aims for sites the patient can clean, not regrowth of everything.
No therapy removes every bacterium for good; surgery cures nothing alone, it only makes the sites cleanable.

q5-F03.stem: #19 and #20 in the same patient have each lost 5 mm of buccal attachment. On #19, a molar, the loss has reached the furcation (Glickman Grade II); #20 is a single-rooted premolar. How do their prognoses compare?
choices: #19 is worse, since its furcation can't be cleaned well
They are equal, since the attachment loss is equal
#20 is worse, since one root has less support than two
#19 is better, since two roots share what support is left
why: Loss into a furcation dramatically lowers the prognosis: most entrances are narrower than a curette, and the concave furcal surfaces hide calculus the patient can't reach.
The same millimeters don't give the same prognosis; once the loss reaches a furcation, the tooth does worse.
A single-rooted tooth with the same loss and no furcation is easier to clean, so it usually fares better.
Extra roots don't help once the furcation is open; the space between them is what can't be cleaned.

q5-F04.stem: At the mid-buccal of a mandibular first molar you record a 5 mm probing depth. What should that tell you, as taught?
choices: Its buccal furcation may be open; check with a Nabers probe
Its furcation is safe, since the entrance is about 8 mm down
Its furcation is safe until an arrow appears on a radiograph
A 5 mm depth only reaches the furcation of a maxillary molar
why: Its buccal entrance is about 2.4 mm from the CEJ, so a 5 mm depth may already reach it; the Nabers probe will tell you.
About 8 mm is the maxillary premolar's mean entrance depth; this molar's buccal entrance is about 2.4 mm from the CEJ.
Only about 30-55% of involved furcations show an arrow; the clinical exam comes first, and no arrow rules nothing out.
The mandibular entrances are the shallowest (about 2.4-2.5 mm), so they are reached first; the maxillary ones lie at 3.6-4.8 mm.

pc-e1.stem: Looking at the chart and the radiograph at this re-evaluation, how much can you tell about the wall count of the defect on the mesial of #19?
choices: Nothing definite yet: walls are confirmed at surgery
It has three walls, since the radiolucency is narrow
It has one wall, since the crest by the root is lost
It has two walls, since it's a crater with #20
why: The walls are confirmed at surgery, after the flap is raised and the defect debrided. A radiograph is a flat picture of a 3-D defect, and the deck's dry-skull films show how hard walls are to tell apart on one.
A narrow, deep radiolucency is a good sign for regeneration, but it doesn't count walls: a 2-D film can't show which buccal and lingual walls remain.
The film shows the bone beside the mesial root sitting below the crest at #20: that is the defect's depth, not its number of walls.
A crater is bone lost from both neighboring proximal surfaces, leaving only buccal and lingual walls; here the crest at #20 is intact, and craters aren't read from a film anyway.

pc-e3.stem: At today's re-evaluation, what is the right next step for the #19 mesial site?
choices: Regenerative surgery, followed by maintenance
Resective osseous surgery to level the defect
Another round of SRP, re-checked in 6 weeks
Extraction of #19 and an implant plan
why: Phase I is complete, and re-evaluation leaves one 8 mm pocket at #19 mesial over a 5 mm vertical defect, in a nonsmoker with a 12% plaque score who keeps every visit: a Phase II site, and this kind of vertical defect is what regenerative surgery (graft, membrane or both) rebuilds.
Resective surgery reshapes bone into a cleansable form by removing bone; it fits horizontal loss and craters, not a deep vertical defect that can be regrown.
Re-evaluation is where the surgical decision is made; a residual 8 mm pocket over a 5 mm intrabony defect is more than another round of instrumentation can clean.
Extraction is for a tooth with too much against it; this is a single residual defect in a compliant nonsmoker, a good candidate for rebuilding.

q1-F01.stem: What can be concluded from the Becker et al. tooth-loss figures discussed in lecture? Select all that apply.
choices: Without treatment, patients lose about three times as many teeth as treated ones
After treatment, skipping maintenance roughly doubles the rate of tooth loss
Once therapy has reduced the pockets, skipping maintenance costs no more teeth
After treatment, skipping maintenance means losing teeth as fast as if never treated
why: Belongs: patients who refused treatment lost about three times as many teeth as treated patients.
Belongs: treated patients who skipped maintenance lost teeth about twice as fast as those who kept their recalls.
Doesn't belong: the doubled tooth loss in treated patients who skipped maintenance is exactly the price of stopping after active therapy.
Doesn't belong: skipping maintenance about doubles tooth loss, but untreated patients still lost the most, around three times as many as treated ones.

q1-F02.stem: Which of these go into a patient's stage, as opposed to the grade? Select all that apply.
choices: The interdental CAL at the worst site
The radiographic bone loss at the worst site
How many teeth were lost to periodontitis
The percent bone loss divided by the age
A glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) of 7% or more
why: Belongs: interdental CAL is the staging gold standard, taken from the single worst site.
Belongs: radiographic bone loss is the second-choice staging measure after interdental CAL.
Belongs: tooth loss from periodontitis is a staging finding; losing any tooth to it means Stage 3 or 4, and losing 5 or more points to Stage 4.
Doesn't belong: bone loss divided by age is the ratio that estimates the grade, the speed of the disease.
Doesn't belong: an HbA1c of 7% or more is a grade modifier that pushes the case to Grade C; it never changes the stage.

pc-f1.stem: Setting today's findings beside the baseline, how should #30 be diagnosed?
choices: Peri-implantitis at #30
Mucositis at #30
A healthy implant
Expected crestal remodeling
why: It bleeds and suppurates on probing, probes 5-7 mm where it read 3 mm at the baseline, and the bone, at the first thread (1.5 mm below the platform) at the baseline, is now 4-5 mm below it: 2.5-3.5 mm lost since the crown, more than the ~2 mm of remodeling, and still going 2.5 years later.
Mucositis has the inflammation (bleeding, suppuration, deeper probing from swelling) but no bone loss past the initial remodeling; this implant has lost 2.5-3.5 mm of bone since the baseline.
Health means no bleeding or suppuration on gentle probing and no deeper probing than at earlier exams; he has all three.
Remodeling is about 2 mm, happens in the first year and then levels off; this loss goes past that, 2.5 years after the crown, and comes with bleeding and pus.

pc-f2.stem: Which of Meffert's categories fits this #30 implant?
choices: A failing implant
An ailing implant
A failed implant
Surviving, and therefore successful
why: Bone loss that is still progressing, with inflammation and no mobility, makes a failing implant: handled case by case, or kept in function.
An ailing implant has static bone loss with no inflammation and no mobility; this loss is new since the baseline, and the site bleeds and suppurates.
A failed implant has progressive bone loss plus clinical mobility and loss of function; this crown is firm, and the mobility would have to be of the implant body, not the crown or abutment.

Survival only means it is still in the mouth and loaded; success (Albrektsson) needs no radiolucency and no infection, with 1.5 mm or less of bone loss in the first year and no more than 0.2 mm a year after. "Be cautious of the terms used, success versus survival."

pc-g1.stem: How would you diagnose the tissues around #19 at today's visit?
choices: Peri-implant health
Mucositis around the implant
Peri-implantitis
Meffert's ailing implant
why: Nothing bleeds or suppurates on gentle probing, probing is the same as at the baseline (4-5 mm), and the bone is only 1 mm lower than at the crown seating, inside the ~2 mm of first-year remodeling.
Mucositis needs inflammation: profuse bleeding and/or suppuration and deeper probing than at the baseline. Her 4-5 mm sites read what they did at the crown seating, and none bleed.
Peri-implantitis needs inflammation plus bone loss past the initial remodeling. Her 1 mm drop in the first year of function is that remodeling, and nothing bleeds.
An ailing implant has pathologic bone loss that has stopped and is monitored. A 1 mm drop in the first year after loading is physiologic remodeling, not disease.

pc-g2.stem: The mesial and distal of #19 read 5 mm today. How should you interpret that number?
choices: On its own, nothing: it equals her baseline
Those 5 mm pockets need scaling
She has lost bone since the crown was seated
It is a failing implant that needs a closer look
why: There is no 3 mm cutoff at implants. Depth depends on how deep the implant sits, the abutment height and the tissue, so each implant is judged against its own baseline, and hers was 4-5 mm.
A 5 mm reading at an implant isn't disease in itself; with no bleeding and no change from the baseline, there is nothing to treat.
Bone loss can deepen a probing reading, but hers hasn't deepened at all: it matches the crown seating.
A failing implant (Meffert) has progressive bone loss with inflammation, and she has neither.

pc-g3.stem: Compared with the film at the crown seating, today's film puts the bone 1 mm lower. What does that change represent?
choices: Normal, physiologic remodeling at the crest
Early peri-implantitis with pathologic loss
Retrograde peri-implantitis
Failure of an Albrektsson success criterion
why: Once an implant is in function, about 2 mm of crestal remodeling is expected, leveling off within about the first year; a 1 mm drop in her first year falls inside it.
Only bone loss past the initial remodeling is pathologic, and peri-implantitis also needs inflammation; she has neither.
Retrograde peri-implantitis is a radiolucency at the apical third of an implant; her change is at the crest.
Albrektsson allows up to 1.5 mm of vertical bone loss at 1 year in function, and 1 mm is within that.

pc-g4.stem: After today's film, when should #19 get its next routine radiograph?
choices: A year from now, then yearly
Six months from now, and every 6 months for life
Only once clinical signs show up
At each maintenance visit
why: Films are every 6 months for the first year after the baseline (the final restoration), then yearly; today's is her 12-month film.
The 6-month films are for the first year only; after that they are yearly.
Clinical signs (deeper probing, bleeding, suppuration) call for an extra film, but the routine yearly film still happens.
Implant films are confirmatory, not exploratory, so they aren't taken at every visit.

pc-h1.stem: Given today's findings, which diagnosis fits the implant at #5?
choices: Mucositis around the implant
Peri-implantitis
A healthy implant
Soft and hard tissue deficiency
why: The mucosa is red and swollen, it bleeds profusely on gentle probing and probes 1-2 mm deeper than at the baseline, yet the bone is where it was at the crown seating: inflammation without bone loss past remodeling.
Peri-implantitis also needs bone loss past the initial remodeling; today's film puts the bone 1.5 mm below the platform, just as at the baseline.
A healthy implant doesn't bleed on gentle probing or probe deeper than at earlier exams; his does both.
A deficiency is mucosa lost together with the bone beneath it; his mucosa is swollen, not lost, and his bone hasn't changed.

pc-h2.stem: What explains why his implant now reads about 2 mm deeper than at the baseline?
choices: Inflamed, swollen mucosa adds tissue volume
Bone has been lost since the crown was seated
The crestal bone is still remodeling
The baseline measurement was wrong
why: Inflammation bulks up the tissue, so the probe goes deeper without any bone lost; his film shows the bone unchanged.
Real bone loss is one of the three reasons a reading deepens, but his film shows the bone right where it was.
Remodeling (about 2 mm) levels off within about the first year in function, and his crown went on 4 years ago.
A measuring error is one of the three reasons, but his tissue is red, swollen and bleeding: the inflammation accounts for the change.

choices: Debride now and coach his home care
Record it and recheck at the annual visit
Raise a flap, decontaminate and graft
Remove the implant and graft the site
why: Mucositis reverses like gingivitis, so treat it now: remove the plaque with implant instruments and work on his hygiene and his smoking before it turns into peri-implantitis.
Dr. Kaur said mucositis isn't put on watch: it can be reversed now and can progress to peri-implantitis.
Opening, cleaning and grafting is for peri-implantitis with bone loss, and he has no bone loss to rebuild.
Only a mobile implant (lost osseointegration) has to be removed; his is firm and has lost no bone.

pc-h5.stem: Today's film came 6 months before his annual one was due. Was it justified?
choices: Yes: his signs called for a confirming film
No: films should follow the annual schedule
Yes: a film is taken at every maintenance visit
No: films can't show peri-implant disease
why: An extra film is taken at a maintenance visit when clinical signs point to disease (deeper probing, bleeding, suppuration); it confirms what probing found.
The schedule is the minimum; clinical signs of disease are the reason for an extra film.
Implant films aren't taken at every visit: radiographs confirm, they don't explore.
The film is how bone loss past remodeling is confirmed, which is what separates mucositis from peri-implantitis.

pc-i1.stem: Which of her findings is the one that puts #14 in peri-implantitis instead of mucositis?
choices: Bone far below where it sat at baseline
Pus at the mesial
Pockets of 6-8 mm
Profuse bleeding, in a line, on gentle probing
why: At the baseline the bone was 1 mm below the platform; now it is 5-5.5 mm below, well past the ~2 mm of first-year remodeling. Mucositis never has that.
Pus means active disease, but mucositis can suppurate too: bleeding and/or suppuration is in both definitions.
Both diagnoses probe deeper than at the baseline, and swelling alone can add millimeters.
Profuse bleeding is part of the mucositis definition too; it shows inflammation, not bone loss.

pc-i2.stem: Of her findings, which appear on the slide's list of peri-implantitis risk factors? Select all that apply.
choices: Her diabetes is poorly controlled
She is a former smoker who quit 2 years ago
Her teeth were lost to periodontitis
Her soft tissue phenotype is thin
She is 63 years old
why: Belongs: uncontrolled diabetes is on the peri-implantitis list.
Belongs: the list counts smoking whether current or former.
Belongs: a history of periodontitis is on both lists.
Doesn't belong: a thin phenotype is on the mucositis list, not the peri-implantitis one.
Doesn't belong: age is on neither list.

pc-i3.stem: Pus is coming from the mesial of #14. What should happen at this visit?
choices: Debride it, possibly adding a local antibiotic
Note it and reprobe in 3 months
Take the implant out, since pus means it has failed
Rely on a systemic antibiotic alone
why: Suppuration is active disease: whatever the long-term plan, respond today with local debridement, and at a deep site possibly a local antibiotic.
"Whenever you see suppuration, you have to do something." It is never put on watch.
A failed implant has a mobile body, and hers is firm. Pus means active disease, not lost osseointegration.
An antibiotic alone can't remove a biofilm; only mechanical debridement does (Session 8).

pc-i4.stem: What started her peri-implantitis in the first place?
choices: Plaque biofilm, meaning bacteria
Her diabetes, which is poorly controlled
Her three decades of heavy smoking
An IL-1 gene variant that overreacts
why: "If somebody has to ask you" how the disease starts: bacteria, the plaque biofilm. Her other findings raise the risk; plaque starts it.
It is a risk factor on the list, not the cause: it raises her risk once plaque is present.
Smoking, current or former, is a risk factor: it favors the pathogens but doesn't start the disease.
Genes play a part in a multifactorial disease, but the primary cause is plaque.

pc-i5.stem: How does the fact that she lost teeth to periodontitis bear on this implant?
choices: It marks her as a susceptible host
It no longer matters once the teeth are gone
Treated periodontitis contraindicates implants
The implant should have been placed at extraction
why: Someone who lost teeth to periodontitis is a susceptible host; periodontitis and peri-implantitis share bacteria, and putative pathogens can linger a year after the teeth come out.
Pathogens can linger even a year after extraction, and the susceptibility remains: it raises peri-implant risk even in an edentulous mouth.
Only untreated periodontitis is a contraindication; a treated, arrested, compliant patient can have implants.
No immediate implants during disease control: extract, heal, re-evaluate, do any Phase II surgery, then plan implants.

q7-F02.stem: Three and a half years ago this implant's crown was seated; at that visit it probed 4 mm without bleeding, and the film put the bone 1 mm below the platform. The annual film 6 months ago looked the same. Today the mucosa is red and swollen, gentle probing reads 6 mm with bleeding and pus, and the crown is firm. Today's film still shows the bone 1 mm below the platform. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The diagnosis is peri-implant mucositis
It should be debrided locally today
The clinical signs justified today's film
The pus means this is peri-implantitis
It can be left alone until the next annual visit
why: Belongs: it is inflamed, bleeds and suppurates, and probes 2 mm deeper than at the baseline, but the bone sits exactly where the baseline film showed it: no bone loss past the initial remodeling.
Belongs: suppuration signals active disease and always needs a response now, whatever the long-term plan: local debridement, and at a deep site sometimes a local antibiotic.
Belongs: deeper probing, bleeding and suppuration are the signs that call for an extra film; radiographs confirm rather than explore, and this one is what rules out peri-implantitis.
Doesn't belong: bleeding and/or suppuration is part of the mucositis definition too; only bone loss past the initial remodeling makes it peri-implantitis.
Doesn't belong: suppuration is never put on watch, and mucositis is reversible, so it is treated now, before it progresses.

q9-P01.stem: For #24, what should treatment set out to achieve, and with which procedure?
choices: Gain KG: an exposed FGG with an apically positioned flap
Cover the root fully: a CTG under a coronally advanced flap
Cover several roots: an ADM under a tunnel flap
Trim excess gingiva: a gingivectomy
why: There is no keratinized gingiva on #24 and plaque collects there; an FGG left exposed carries its own keratinization, as in Dr. Abou-Arraj's case.
#24 is RT2, so full coverage isn't possible, and a CTG covered by mucosa adds no keratinized gingiva.
Only #24 needs treating, and an ADM, covered by mucosa, carries no keratinization of its own.
No excess gingiva is present; a gingivectomy would take away tissue the tooth already lacks.

q9-P02.stem: Using the chart, classify #24's recession by Cairo type and say how much root a graft can cover.
choices: RT2: coverage will be partial
RT2: coverage will be complete
RT1: coverage will be complete
RT3: no coverage is expected
why: The 3 mm interproximal CAL is less than the 4 mm buccal CAL, which is RT2: coverage up to about the interproximal attachment level.
RT2 has interproximal attachment loss, which limits coverage; complete coverage belongs to RT1.
RT1 has no interproximal attachment loss, but #24's mesial and distal sites show 3 mm of CAL.
RT3 requires interproximal loss greater than the buccal; here 3 mm is less than 4 mm.

choices: A CTG covered by a coronally advanced flap
An exposed FGG with an apically positioned flap
An ADM left uncovered over both roots
Watch it, as painless recession stays stable
why: The aim is root coverage, so the graft is buried: connective tissue only, with the flap advanced over it without tension.
An exposed FGG is for creating keratinized gingiva; he still has KG, and his concern is the exposed roots.
An acellular dermal matrix has no cells or blood supply of its own, so it must be fully covered.
Recession left untreated tends to progress (Chambrone and Tatakis), and he has both sensitivity and an esthetic concern.

q9-P04.stem: Based on the chart, what share of #11's exposed root should a graft be able to cover?
choices: Close to 100%
Roughly 50 to 60%
None, given 3 mm of recession
About 25%, given his hard brushing
why: The mesial and distal CAL are 0, so there is no interproximal attachment loss: RT1, where full coverage can be reached.
50 to 60% is what to expect in RT2; #11 has no interproximal attachment loss.
How much the tooth has receded doesn't decide coverage; the interproximal attachment does.
His hard brushing is something to correct, not what predicts coverage.

q9-F02.stem: The goal for a sensitive, hard-to-clean lower incisor is to gain a band of keratinized gingiva. Its RT2 recession leaves the margin in alveolar mucosa, with no KG at all. What should the plan include? Select all that apply.
choices: A palatal free gingival graft
Leaving the graft uncovered to heal
An apically positioned flap
A coronally advanced flap covering the graft
A gingivectomy at the gingival margin
why: Belongs: an FGG keeps its epithelium and palatal connective tissue, which carry their own determination to keratinize.
Belongs: an uncovered FGG heals into a band of keratinized gingiva; covering it "would deny it the ability" to become keratinized tissue.
Belongs: a trapezoidal flap positioned apically prepares the bed for the FGG, as in his case.
Doesn't belong: the only tissue to cover it with is alveolar mucosa, which gains no keratinized gingiva; a coronally advanced flap goes with a CTG for root coverage.
Doesn't belong: a gingivectomy takes gingiva away, and this tooth has none to spare; it is used for gingival excess.

q9-F03.stem: A patient's #9 looks shorter than #8 because its gingival margin is about 1.5 mm more coronal. Both teeth probe 2 mm with no bleeding, no roots are exposed, and the lip and facial thirds are normal. How should this mismatch of the gingival margins be treated?
choices: Gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap
Better oral hygiene and scaling
Botox or surgery to reposition the lip
A CTG under a coronally advanced flap
why: A gingival line discrepancy between contralateral teeth, an inconsistent margin, is treated with a gingivectomy or an apically positioned full-thickness flap.
Hygiene and scaling resolve a pseudopocket, the swollen, bleeding gingivitis tissue that probes 4-5 mm; these margins are healthy and won't move with hygiene.
Botox or lip repositioning treats a hypermobile upper lip that moves more than 8 mm; here the lip is normal and the problem is one tooth's margin.
A CTG under a coronally advanced flap covers recession; no root is exposed here, and #9 has extra tissue, not too little.

q9-F04.stem: A trap door is one way to harvest a connective tissue graft from the palate. What is the other way?
choices: Harvest an FGG and de-epithelialize it
Harvest just the submucosal fat layer
Order processed dermis from a tissue bank
Elevate palatal mucosa with the periosteum
why: The whole rectangle is taken with its epithelium, like an FGG, and the epithelium is removed afterwards: harvested as an FGG, delivered as a CTG.
The submucosa's fat and glands are trimmed off a graft so they don't slow healing; a CTG is the lamina propria.
Processed donor dermis is an acellular dermal matrix, an allograft; a CTG is the patient's own palatal connective tissue.
A CTG is the lamina propria without epithelium; the periosteum stays on the bone and isn't part of the graft.
